In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Ta, Sin, Mim.﴾ ﴿These are the verses of the clear Book.﴾ ﴿We recite to you from the news of Moses and Pharaoh in truth, for a people who believe.﴾ ﴿Indeed, Pharaoh exalted himself in the land and made its people into factions, oppressing a group among them: he slaughters their sons and spares their women. Indeed, he was among the corrupters.﴾ ﴿And We wished to bestow favour upon those who were oppressed in the land, to make them leaders and to make them the inheritors.﴾ ﴿And to establish them in the land, and to show Pharaoh and Haman and their hosts from them that which they feared.﴾

Know that His words, exalted is He, ﴿Ta, Sin, Mim﴾, are like the other opening letters, and the discussion of them has already preceded. ﴿Those﴾ is a pointer to the verses of the surah, and ﴿the clear Book﴾ is either the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawḥ) or the Book which God promised to send down upon Muhammad (ﷺ). So He clarified that the verses of this surah are the verses of that Book, and described it as "clear" (mubīn) because it makes clear the lawful and the unlawful in it; or because by its eloquence it makes clear that it is the speech of God and not the speech of creatures; or because it makes clear the truthfulness of the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ); or because it makes clear the news of the former and the latter peoples; or because it makes clear the way of being freed from the doubts of the people of misguidance.

As for His words ﴿We recite to you﴾, that is, through the tongue of Gabriel, peace be upon him, because he used to recite to Muhammad until he memorised it. And His words ﴿from the news of Moses and Pharaoh﴾ are the object of ﴿We recite to you﴾, meaning: We recite to you some of the report of the two of them, in truth, being truthful, like His words ﴿grows with oil﴾ (al-Mu'minūn: 20). And His words ﴿for a people who believe﴾ have two aspects:

The first: He, exalted is He, indeed intended by this also those who do not believe, but He singled out the believers for mention because they accepted and benefited, so it is like His words ﴿a guidance for the God-fearing﴾ (al-Baqarah: 2).

The second: It is possible that He, exalted is He, knew that the goodness in its recitation is their belief, and that His intention for those who do not believe is secondary.

His words, exalted is He, ﴿Indeed, Pharaoh exalted himself in the land﴾: It was read as "Fur'awn" with a ḍamma on the fā' and with a kasra, and the kasra is better, and it is like al-qusṭās and al-qisṭās. ﴿ʿAlā﴾ means he became arrogant, tyrannical, magnified himself and transgressed. What is meant by it is the strength of rule and exaltation in the land, that is, the land of his kingdom. Then God, exalted is He, explained some of that by His words ﴿and made its people into shiyaʿan﴾, that is, factions who follow him in what he wills and obey him, none of them being able to oppose him; or some of them support others in serving him; or categories in serving him; or diverse factions among whom he had incited enmity so that they would be more obedient to him. Or what is meant is what He explained with His words ﴿oppressing a group among them﴾, that is, he makes them serve him, and ﴿he slaughters their sons and spares their women﴾; this is what is meant by the shiyaʿ.

His words ﴿oppressing a group among them﴾: That group were the Children of Israel. And regarding the cause of the slaughter of the sons there are several aspects:

The first: that a soothsayer said to him: "A child will be born among the Children of Israel on such-and-such night, and your kingdom will be lost at his hand." So twelve boys were born on that night, and he killed them. According to most exegetes, this punishment remained upon the Children of Israel for many years. Wahb said: The Copts killed ninety thousand of the Children of Israel in search of Moses, peace be upon him. Some of them said: In this there is evidence of the foolishness of Pharaoh, for if he believed the soothsayer, the killing did not prevent what was to occur, and if he was lying, what was the purpose of the killing? This question may be raised in refuting the knowledge of judgments from the science of the stars. Its parallel is what those who deny moral obligation (takālīf) say: If Zayd is among the fortunate in the knowledge and decree of God, there is no need for obedience, and if he is among the wretched, there is no benefit in obedience. Also, this question, if it were sound, would nullify the science of interpreting dreams and its benefit. Also, the astrologer's answer is that the stars indicated that a child would be born who, if he were not killed, would become such-and-such; and on this assumption, the effort to kill him is not vain.

Know that this aspect is weak, because attributing such a report to the soothsayer is an acknowledgement that he may inform of the unseen in detail, and if we permitted this, the proof of the reports of the unseen for the truthfulness of the messengers would be nullified, and that is false by the consensus (ijmāʿ) of the Muslims.

The second: and this is the saying of al-Suddī, that Pharaoh saw in his dream that a fire came from Jerusalem and enveloped Egypt, burning the Copts but not the Children of Israel. So he asked about his vision, and they said: "A man will come out of this land from which the Children of Israel came, and at his hand will be the ruin of Egypt." So he ordered the killing of the males.

The third: The prophets who were before Moses, peace be upon him, gave good news of his coming, and Pharaoh had heard of that. For this reason he used to slaughter the sons of the Children of Israel. And this aspect is the most worthy of acceptance.

The author of al-Kashshāf (al-Kashshāf, the Qur'anic commentary of al-Zamakhsharī) said: "yastaḍʿifu" is a ḥāl (circumstantial clause) from the pronoun in ﴿wa-jaʿala﴾, or a ṣifah (qualifier) of "shiyaʿan", or a new independent clause; or "yudhabbiḥu" is a badal (substitute) for "yastaḍʿifu". And His words ﴿Indeed, he was among the corrupters﴾ indicate that this slaughter produced nothing from him except corruption, and that it has no effect in repelling the decree of God, exalted is He.

As for His words ﴿And We wished to bestow favour﴾, it is a clause conjoined (maʿṭūfah) to His words ﴿Indeed, Pharaoh exalted himself in the land﴾, because it is similar to that in its occurrence as an explanation of the news of Moses, peace be upon him, and Pharaoh, and as a narration of it. The wording in His words ﴿We wish﴾ is for the future, but what is intended by it is the narration of a past state. It is also permissible that it be a ḥāl from ﴿yastaḍʿifu﴾, meaning: Pharaoh oppresses them, while We wish to bestow favour upon them. If it is said: How can their oppression coexist with God's intention to bestow favour upon them, and when God wills something it occurs and is not delayed until another time? We say: Since God's favour upon them by delivering them from Pharaoh was near in occurrence, the intention of its occurrence was made as if it were concurrent with their oppression.

[Page 194]

As for His words ﴿and make them leaders﴾, that is, foremost in this world and in religion. From Mujāhid: "callers to good." From Qatādah: "rulers", like His words ﴿and made you kings﴾ (al-Mā'idah: 20). ﴿And make them the inheritors﴾, meaning: to the kingdom of Pharaoh, his land and what was in his hands.

As for His words ﴿and to establish them in the land﴾: know that it is said "mukkina lahu" when a place is made for him to sit or lie down, so he is given a settled place and it is prepared for him; its parallel is "arraḍa lahu". The meaning of establishing them in the land, which is the land of Egypt and the Levant, is that their command is executed and their hands are set free. And His words ﴿and to show Pharaoh and Haman and their hosts from them that which they feared﴾: it was read "wa-yaraā Fir'awnu wa-Hāmānu wa-junūduhumā" (and that Pharaoh and Haman and their hosts may see), meaning: they see from them what they were afraid of, namely the loss of their kingdom and their destruction at the hand of a boy of the Children of Israel.

﴿Ta, Sin, Mim.﴾ ﴿These are the verses of the clear Book.﴾ ﴿We recite to you from the news of Moses and Pharaoh in truth, for a people who believe.﴾ ﴿Indeed, Pharaoh exalted himself in the land and made its people into factions, oppressing a group among them: he slaughters their sons and spares their women. Know that His words, exalted is He, ﴿Ta, Sin, Mim﴾, are like the other opening letters, and the discussion of them has already preceded. ﴿Those﴾ is a pointer to the verses of the surah, and ﴿the clear Book﴾ is either the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawḥ) or the Book which God promised to send down upon Muhammad (ﷺ). So He clarified that the verses of this surah are the verses of that Book, and described it as "clear" (mubīn) because it makes clear the lawful and the unlawful in it; or because by its eloquence it makes clear that it is the speech of God and not the speech of creatures; or because it makes clear the truthfulness of the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ); or because it makes clear the news of the former and the latter peoples; or because it makes clear the way of being freed from the doubts of the people of misguidance.

As for His words ﴿We recite to you﴾, that is, through the tongue of Gabriel, peace be upon him, because he used to recite to Muhammad until he memorised it. And His words ﴿from the news of Moses and Pharaoh﴾ are the object of ﴿We recite to you﴾, meaning: We recite to you some of the report of the two of them, in truth, being truthful, like His words ﴿grows with oil﴾ (al-Mu'minūn: 20). And His words ﴿for a people who believe﴾ have two aspects:

The first: He, exalted is He, indeed intended by this also those who do not believe, but He singled out the believers for mention because they accepted and benefited, so it is like His words ﴿a guidance for the God-fearing﴾ (al-Baqarah: 2).

The second: It is possible that He, exalted is He, knew that the goodness in its recitation is their belief, and that His intention for those who do not believe is secondary.

His words, exalted is He, ﴿Indeed, Pharaoh exalted himself in the land﴾: It was read as "Fur'awn" with a ḍamma on the fā' and with a kasra, and the kasra is better, and it is like al-qusṭās and al-qisṭās. ﴿ʿAlā﴾ means he became arrogant, tyrannical, magnified himself and transgressed. What is meant by it is the strength of rule and exaltation in the land, that is, the land of his kingdom. Then God, exalted is He, explained some of that by His words ﴿and made its people into shiyaʿan﴾, that is, factions who follow him in what he wills and obey him, none of them being able to oppose him; or some of them support others in serving him; or categories in serving him; or diverse factions among whom he had incited enmity so that they would be more obedient to him. Or what is meant is what He explained with His words ﴿oppressing a group among them﴾, that is, he makes them serve him, and ﴿he slaughters their sons and spares their women﴾; this is what is meant by the shiyaʿ.

His words ﴿oppressing a group among them﴾: That group were the Children of Israel. And regarding the cause of the slaughter of the sons there are several aspects:

The first: that a soothsayer said to him: "A child will be born among the Children of Israel on such-and-such night, and your kingdom will be lost at his hand." So twelve boys were born on that night, and he killed them. According to most exegetes, this punishment remained upon the Children of Israel for many years. Wahb said: The Copts killed ninety thousand of the Children of Israel in search of Moses, peace be upon him. Some of them said: In this there is evidence of the foolishness of Pharaoh, for if he believed the soothsayer, the killing did not prevent what was to occur, and if he was lying, what was the purpose of the killing? This question may be raised in refuting the knowledge of judgments from the science of the stars. Its parallel is what those who deny moral obligation (takālīf) say: If Zayd is among the fortunate in the knowledge and decree of God, there is no need for obedience, and if he is among the wretched, there is no benefit in obedience. Also, this question, if it were sound, would nullify the science of interpreting dreams and its benefit. Also, the astrologer's answer is that the stars indicated that a child would be born who, if he were not killed, would become such-and-such; and on this assumption, the effort to kill him is not vain.

Know that this aspect is weak, because attributing such a report to the soothsayer is an acknowledgement that he may inform of the unseen in detail, and if we permitted this, the proof of the reports of the unseen for the truthfulness of the messengers would be nullified, and that is false by the consensus (ijmāʿ) of the Muslims.

The second: and this is the saying of al-Suddī, that Pharaoh saw in his dream that a fire came from Jerusalem and enveloped Egypt, burning the Copts but not the Children of Israel. So he asked about his vision, and they said: "A man will come out of this land from which the Children of Israel came, and at his hand will be the ruin of Egypt." So he ordered the killing of the males.

The third: The prophets who were before Moses, peace be upon him, gave good news of his coming, and Pharaoh had heard of that. For this reason he used to slaughter the sons of the Children of Israel. And this aspect is the most worthy of acceptance.

The author of al-Kashshāf (al-Kashshāf, the Qur'anic commentary of al-Zamakhsharī) said: "yastaḍʿifu" is a ḥāl (circumstantial clause) from the pronoun in ﴿wa-jaʿala﴾, or a ṣifah (qualifier) of "shiyaʿan", or a new independent clause; or "yudhabbiḥu" is a badal (substitute) for "yastaḍʿifu". And His words ﴿Indeed, he was among the corrupters﴾ indicate that this slaughter produced nothing from him except corruption, and that it has no effect in repelling the decree of God, exalted is He.

As for His words ﴿And We wished to bestow favour﴾, it is a clause conjoined (maʿṭūfah) to His words ﴿Indeed, Pharaoh exalted himself in the land﴾, because it is similar to that in its occurrence as an explanation of the news of Moses, peace be upon him, and Pharaoh, and as a narration of it. The wording in His words ﴿We wish﴾ is for the future, but what is intended by it is the narration of a past state. It is also permissible that it be a ḥāl from ﴿yastaḍʿifu﴾, meaning: Pharaoh oppresses them, while We wish to bestow favour upon them. If it is said: How can their oppression coexist with God's intention to bestow favour upon them, and when God wills something it occurs and is not delayed until another time? We say: Since God's favour upon them by delivering them from Pharaoh was near in occurrence, the intention of its occurrence was made as if it were concurrent with their oppression.

[Page 194]

As for His words ﴿and make them leaders﴾, that is, foremost in this world and in religion. From Mujāhid: "callers to good." From Qatādah: "rulers", like His words ﴿and made you kings﴾ (al-Mā'idah: 20). ﴿And make them the inheritors﴾, meaning: to the kingdom of Pharaoh, his land and what was in his hands.

As for His words ﴿and to establish them in the land﴾: know that it is said "mukkina lahu" when a place is made for him to sit or lie down, so he is given a settled place and it is prepared for him; its parallel is "arraḍa lahu". The meaning of establishing them in the land, which is the land of Egypt and the Levant, is that their command is executed and their hands are set free. And His words ﴿and to show Pharaoh and Haman and their hosts from them that which they feared﴾: it was read "wa-yaraā Fir'awnu wa-Hāmānu wa-junūduhumā" (and that Pharaoh and Haman and their hosts may see), meaning: they see from them what they were afraid of, namely the loss of their kingdom and their destruction at the hand of a boy of the Children of Israel.

It is also said that the exception is one verse, which is ﴿Indeed, He who has imposed the Qur'an upon you﴾, the verse. The surah has seven or eighty-eight verses.

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

When she felt the labour pains, she sent for her and said to her, "What has befallen me has befallen me, and let your love for me benefit me today." So the midwife sat with her. When Moses (peace be upon him) fell to the ground, a light between his eyes overwhelmed her, every joint of her body trembled, and love for Moses (peace be upon him) entered her heart. She said, "O woman, I did not come to you except to kill your newborn. But I have found for this son of yours a great love, so keep your son hidden, for I see him as our enemy." When the midwife left her, one of the spies saw her and came to the door to enter upon the mother of Moses. Moses' sister said, "O mother, this is the guard!" So she wrapped him and placed him in a heated oven (tannur), and her mind was confused, so she did not know what she was doing. They entered and found the oven heated, and they saw that the mother of Moses' colour had not changed, nor had milk appeared for her. They said, "Why did the midwife enter upon you?" She said, "She is a beloved friend of mine; she came to visit." So they left her, and her mind returned to her. She said to Moses' sister, "Where is the boy?" She said, "I do not know." Then she heard crying from the oven, so she went to it, and Allah had made the fire cool and safe for him, so she took him. Then, when the mother of Moses (peace be upon him) saw that Pharaoh was earnestly pursuing the male infants, she feared for her son. So Allah cast into her heart that she should make for him a chest (tabut), and then cast the chest into the Nile. She went to a carpenter from the people of Egypt and bought a chest from him. He said to her, "What will you do with it?" She said, "A son of mine, whom I fear the plot of Pharaoh against, I will hide him." She did not realise that he would spread that news. When she departed, the carpenter went to inform the slaughterers (the executioners). When he came to them, Allah held his tongue, and he began to gesture with his hand. They beat him and drove him away. When he returned to his place, Allah restored his speech to him, and he went again to inform them, but they beat him and drove him away. When he returned to his place, Allah restored his speech. He went a third time to inform them, and they beat him and drove him away, so Allah took away his sight and his tongue. He then made a pledge to Allah that if He restored his sight and his tongue, he would not point them (the boy) out to them. Allah knew his sincerity, so He restored his sight and his tongue. Each day she had three needs that she would raise to her father, and she had a severe leprosy. Pharaoh had consulted the physicians and the magicians about her condition. They said, "O king, she will not be cured except through the sea: a creature resembling a human is found in it. Its saliva is taken and smeared upon her leprosy, and she will be healed of it. That will be on such-and-such a day, in such-and-such a month, when the sun rises." When that day came, Pharaoh went out in the morning to a gathering place he had on the edge of the Nile, with Asiya the daughter of Muzahim with him. The daughter of Pharaoh came with her maids and sat on the shore. Then the Nile brought a chest, tossed about by the waves, and it became caught on a tree. Pharaoh said, "Bring it to me!" So they hurried to it with boats from every side until they placed it before him. They tried to open the lid but could not, and they tried to break it but could not. Asiya looked and saw a light inside the chest that no one but she saw. She treated it and opened it, and there was a small child in the cradle, and a light between his eyes. Allah cast His love into the hearts of the people. The daughter of Pharaoh went to his saliva and smeared her leprosy with it, and she was healed. She embraced him to her chest. The deluded ones among the people of Pharaoh said, "We think this is the one we fear, who was cast into the sea out of fear of you." Pharaoh was about to kill him, but the wife of Pharaoh pleaded with him to spare him, and she adopted him, so he abandoned killing him.

* * *

As for His words, ﴿Then the family of Pharaoh picked him up﴾: al-iltiqat (picking up) is coming upon a thing without seeking it. The "family of Pharaoh" here means his maidservants.

As for His words, ﴿so that he would become for them an enemy and a source of grief﴾: it is well known that this lam (the lam) is intended to express the outcome (al-'aqiba). They said: otherwise it would contradict His words, ﴿And the wife of Pharaoh said, "A comfort of the eye for me and for you"﴾, and His words, ﴿And I cast upon you love from Me﴾ (Ta-Ha: 39). A parallel to this lam is His words, ﴿And We have certainly created for Hell﴾ (al-A'raf: 179), and the saying of the poet:

Give birth for death, and build for ruin.

Know that the correct position is what the author of "al-Kashshaf" mentioned, namely that this lam is the lam of causation (lam al-ta'lil) used figuratively. This is because the purpose and aim of a thing is the outcome to which its matter ends, so they used this lam for what a thing ends up in, by way of comparison, just as the word "lion" is applied to a brave man and "donkey" to a dullard. Hamza and al-Kisa'i read (huznan) with a dammah on the ha' and sukun on the za', while the rest read it with a fatha. Both are dialectal forms, like al-suqm and al-saqam.

As for His words, "they were sinners" (kanu khati'in), there are two interpretations:

The first: al-Hasan said: the meaning of ﴿they were sinners﴾ is not from sin (al-khati'a), but rather the meaning is: "while they did not perceive that it was he who would take away their kingdom."

The majority of the exegetes said: its meaning is that they were sinners in what they were upon of disbelief and wrongdoing, so Allah punished them by raising up as their enemy the very one who would be the cause of their destruction at their hands. It is also read (khati'in) as a lightened form of khati'in, meaning those who turn the right into the wrong. Allah the Exalted has made clear that she picked him up so that he would be a comfort of the eye for her and for him, all together. Ibn Ishaq said: Allah the Exalted cast His love into her heart, because he had a beauty in his face, so whoever saw him loved him. Also, when she opened the chest she saw the light, and when she opened the chest she saw him sucking his finger. Also, when the daughter of Pharaoh smeared her leprosy with his saliva, it went away. It is also said that she had no child and so she loved him. Ibn 'Abbas said: When she (the wife of Pharaoh) said, ﴿A comfort of the eye for me and for you﴾, Pharaoh said, "Let it be for you; as for me, I have no need of him." The reading of Ibn Mas'ud is evidence that it is a predicate: he read, "Do not kill him, a comfort of the eye for me and for you," placing "do not kill him" first. Then the woman said, ﴿Perhaps he will benefit us﴾, so that we may gain some good from him, ﴿or we may adopt him as a son﴾ because he is fit for adoption (tabanni).

As for His words, ﴿while they did not perceive﴾: most exegetes hold that it is a new statement from Allah the Exalted, meaning that they did not perceive that their destruction would be through him and at his hand. This is the view of Mujahid, Qatada, al-Dahhak and Muqatil. Ibn 'Abbas said: he means they did not perceive where the affair of Moses (peace be upon him) would end. Others said: this is part of the woman's own speech, meaning that the Children of Israel and the people of Egypt did not perceive that we had picked him up. This is the view of al-Kalbi.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 28, verses 10–11:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And the heart of Moses' mother became void; she was about to disclose him, had We not fortified her heart so that she might be among the believers.﴾ ﴿And she said to his sister, "Follow him," so she watched him from afar, while they did not perceive.﴾

They have mentioned several interpretations of His saying: ﴿the heart of Moses' mother became void﴾.

The first: al-Hasan said, "void of every concern except concern for Moses, peace be upon him."

The second: Abu Muslim said, "The void of the heart is fear and anxiety, as in His saying: ﴿and their hearts are air﴾ (Ibrahim: 43)."

The third: the author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) said, "void (safiran) of intellect. The meaning is that when she heard that he had fallen into the hand of Pharaoh, her reason flew away from excess of distress and fear."

The fourth: al-Hasan and Muhammad ibn Ishaq said, "void of the revelation that We had revealed to her: that you should cast him into the river, and do not fear and do not grieve; indeed We will return him to you. Then Satan came to her and said: 'You disliked that Pharaoh should kill your son, so that you would have a reward; you undertook to destroy him.' And when the news reached her that Moses, peace be upon him, had fallen into Pharaoh's hand, the magnitude of the trial made her forget what had been the covenant of God with her."

The fifth: Abu 'Ubayda said, "void of grief, because she knew that he would not be killed, relying on God's guarantee of his welfare." Ibn Qutaybah said, "This is among the wonders: how could her heart be void of grief when God, Exalted is He, says: ﴿had We not fortified her heart﴾? Is a heart fortified except one that is distressed and grieving?" It may be answered that there is no impossibility in this: that, owing to the intensity of her trust in God's promise, she was not afraid when his name was disclosed, and she was certain that, even if she disclosed it, he would be safe by virtue of that promise; but it was known that disclosure would harm, so God fortified her heart. And His saying: ﴿she was about to disclose him, had We not fortified her heart﴾ may be taken to mean with the revelation, so that she felt secure and grief departed from her heart; according to this interpretation, it is valid to understand that her heart was entirely free of grief over Moses.

There is a third aspect: that she heard that Pharaoh's wife had shown affection for him and adopted him, so she was about to disclose that he was her son, because she could not control herself out of joy at what she had heard, had it not been that the intensity of her joy and elation was calmed ﴿so that she might be among the believers﴾, those who are certain of God's promise, not those who rely on the adoption of Pharaoh's accursed wife and her affection.

It has been read as (fariqan), meaning empty, from their saying: "I seek refuge in God from the emptiness of the vessel and the emptiness of the courtyard," and (faraghan) from their saying:

"Their blood among them is faragh,"

meaning wasted, void of recompense; that is: her heart was rendered null from the intensity of what came upon her.

As for His saying: ﴿she was about to disclose him﴾, know that according to those who interpret the void as freedom from grief, we have already mentioned the explanation of His saying: ﴿she was about to disclose﴾. As for those who interpret the void as the occurrence of fear, they have mentioned several aspects:

The first: Ibn 'Abbas said, "She was about to inform them that the one you found is my son." In a narration from 'Ikrimah he said, "She was about to say: 'Woe, my son!' from the intensity of her yearning for him, when she saw the waves rising and falling." Al-Kalbi said, "That was when she heard the people saying: 'He is the son of Pharaoh.'" Al-Suddi said, "When her son was taken, she was about to say: 'He is my son,' so God, Exalted is He, preserved her."

Then He said: ﴿had We not fortified her heart﴾ with the inspiration of patience, as one ties down a thing that is slipping away so that it may settle and be at rest, ﴿so that she might be among the believers﴾, among those who affirm God's promise, which is His saying: ﴿We will return him to you﴾.

As for His saying: ﴿And she said to his sister, "Follow him"﴾, meaning: follow his trace, and look to where he has landed and to whom he has come. His sister was from both his father and mother, and her name was Maryam. ﴿So she watched him﴾: Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with him, said, "She saw him." Al-Mubarrad said, "abṣarathu and baṣurat bihi have the same meaning." His saying: ﴿from afar (‘an junub)﴾ means from a distance; it has been read as ‘an jani b and ‘an janb. The janb is the side; that is, she looked a sidelong, furtive glance. ﴿while they did not perceive﴾ her condition and her purpose.

﴿And We had forbidden wet-nurses to him from before, so she said, "Shall I direct you to a household that will take care of him for you, and they will be sincere toward him?"﴾ ﴿So We returned him to his mother, that her eye might be comforted and she would not grieve, and that she would know that the promise of Allah is true; but most of them do not know.﴾

Know that His saying, ﴿And We had forbidden wet-nurses to him from before﴾, requires that they were forbidden to him from before. If that was not achieved through worship and prohibition, then the distinction would be impossible, so there must be another act. That act may be that Allah, Exalted, although he needed milk, caused in him an aversion to the milk of other women, so he would not suckle from them; or He caused in their milk a taste that his nature rejected; or He placed in his mother's milk a pleasure, so that once he became accustomed to it, he naturally disliked the milk of others.

It is reported from al-Dahhak that his mother had nursed him for three months until he recognized her scent. The word al-marāḍi‘ (المراضع) is the plural of murḍi‘ (مُرْضِع), meaning a woman who nurses, or the plural of mar­ḍa‘ (مَرْضَع), meaning the place of nursing, that is, the breast, or the act of nursing. His saying, ﴿from before﴾, means: from before We returned him to his mother, and from before the coming of the sister of Musa, peace be upon him, and from before his birth in Our judgment and decree. At that point his sister said, ﴿Shall I direct you to a household that will take care of him for you﴾, meaning, they will guarantee his nursing and the attending to his welfare, ﴿and they will be sincere toward him﴾, not withholding from him what benefits him in his upbringing and nourishment, and not betraying you concerning him. Al-nuṣḥ (النُّصْح) is the sincere performance of an act free from any admixture of corruption.

Al-Suddi said: When she said, ﴿and they will be sincere toward him﴾, the apparent meaning indicated that the household knew him. So Haman said to her, "You have recognized this boy, so direct us to his family." She said, "I do not know him, but I only said, 'They are sincere to the king,' so that the anxiety of his heart would be removed."

Everything that has been related on this subject indicates that Pharaoh was in the same position as Asiya in his intense love for Musa, peace be upon him, not as one who claimed that she was singled out for this alone.

Then Allah, Exalted, said, ﴿So We returned him to his mother﴾ with this kind of gentleness, ﴿that her eye might be comforted and she would not grieve, and that she would know that the promise of Allah is true﴾, meaning, in what He had promised her, that He would return him to her. She had indeed known this, but the report is not like seeing with one's own eyes, so she was assured by the existence of what had been promised.

﴿But most of them do not know﴾. Concerning this there are four aspects:

First: most people in that era and afterward do not know, because of their turning away from reflecting on the signs of Allah.

Second: al-Dahhak and Muqatil said: it refers to the people of Egypt, who did not know that Allah had promised her his return to her.

Third: this is like an allusion to what had escaped from her when she heard the news of Musa, peace be upon him, and she grieved and her heart became empty.

Fourth: the meaning may be: We only returned him to her ﴿and that she would know that the promise of Allah is true﴾, and the primary purpose of that return is this religious aim, but most do not know that this is the primary aim, and that what is other than it, such as the comforting of the eye and the removal of grief, is a consequence. Al-Dahhak said: When he accepted her breast, Haman said, "You are surely his mother." She said, "No." He said, "Then why did he accept your breast from among all the women?" She said, "O king, I am a woman of pleasant scent and sweet milk; no infant smells my scent except that he turns to my breast." They said, "You have spoken the truth." So none of the family of Pharaoh remained except that he sent her gifts and honored her with gold and jewels.

The commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 28, verse 14:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And when he reached his full strength and became mature, We gave him judgement and knowledge. Thus do We reward the good-doers﴾ ﴿And he entered the city at a time of heedlessness among its people, and he found in it two men fighting, one of his own party (shi'ah) and the other of his enemy. The one from his party sought his help against the one from his enemy, so Moses struck him and killed him. He said: "This is from the work of Satan. Indeed, he is a misleading, manifest enemy."﴾ ﴿He said: "My Lord, I have wronged myself, so forgive me." So He forgave him. Indeed, He is the Forgiving, the Merciful.﴾ ﴿He said: "My Lord, by what You have bestowed upon me, I will never be a supporter of the criminals."﴾

Know that in His saying ﴿reached his full strength (ashudd) and became mature﴾ there are two views:

The first: that both phrases have one meaning, namely the completion of strength and the balance of temperament and physique.

The second, which is the more correct: that they are two different meanings. Then they differed in several ways:

The first, which is the closest: that ashudd (full strength) is an expression for the completion of physical, bodily strength, and istiwa' (maturity) is an expression for the completion of intellectual strength.

The second: ashudd is an expression for the completion of strength, and istiwa' is an expression for the completion of build and natural constitution.

The third: ashudd is an expression for puberty (bulugh), and istiwa' is an expression for the completion of natural constitution.

The fourth: Ibn 'Abbas said: ashudd is the period from eighteen years to thirty, then from thirty to forty he remains level, without increase or decrease, and from forty he begins to decline. What Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him) said is true, because a person at the beginning of life is in growth and increase, then he remains without increase or decrease, then he begins to decline. The end of the period of increase is from the beginning of life to twenty; from twenty to thirty the increase is small and the strength is very strong; then from thirty to forty he stops, neither increasing nor decreasing; from forty to sixty he begins a hidden decline; and from sixty to the end of life he begins a clear, evident decline.

It is related that no prophet was sent except at the age of forty. The wisdom in this is evident, because a person until the age of forty has his bodily powers of appetite, anger and sense strong and complete, so the person is drawn toward them. When he reaches forty, the bodily powers begin to decline while the intellectual power continues to increase, and there the man is at his most complete. For this reason Allah, may He be exalted, chose this age for revelation.

Second issue: They differed about the singular of ashudd. Al-Farra' said: the singular of ashudd is shadd by analogy, though it has not been heard with this singular. Abu al-Haytham said: the singular of ashudd is shiddah, just as the singular of al-an'um is ni'mah, and shiddah means strength and vigour.

As for His saying ﴿We gave him judgement and knowledge﴾, there are two views:

The first: that they refer to prophethood and what accompanies it of knowledge and good character. On this interpretation, the verse provides no proof as to whether this prophethood was before or after the killing of the Egyptian (al-Qibti), because the particle "wa" (and) in His saying ﴿and he entered the city﴾ does not indicate sequence.

The second: We gave him wisdom and knowledge. He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿And remember what is recited in your houses of the verses of Allah and the wisdom﴾ (al-Ahzab: 34). This view is preferable for several reasons:

The first: prophethood is the highest of human ranks, so it must be preceded by completeness in knowledge and in a pleasing conduct, which are the characters of the noble and the wise.

The second: His saying ﴿Thus do We reward the good-doers﴾ indicates that He gave him judgement and knowledge only as a reward for his good-doing, and prophethood is not a reward for deeds.

The third: if judgement and knowledge meant prophethood, then prophethood would have to be granted to everyone who was among the good-doers, based on His saying ﴿Thus do We reward the good-doers﴾, because His saying ﴿thus﴾ refers to what was mentioned before, namely judgement and knowledge, and then He explained His favour upon him before the killing of the Egyptian. There are issues in this:

First issue: They differed about al-Madinah (the city). The majority hold that it is the city in which Pharaoh used to live, a village two farsakhs from Egypt. al-Dahhak said: it is 'Ayn Shams.

Second issue: They differed about the meaning of His saying ﴿at a time of heedlessness among its people﴾, and there are several views:

The first view: when Moses, peace be upon him, reached his full strength and became mature, and Allah gave him judgement and knowledge in his religion and the religion of his forefathers, he knew that Pharaoh and his people were upon falsehood. So he spoke the truth and found fault with their religion, and this became well known from him, until the matter reached the point where they feared him and he feared them. He had among the Children of Israel a party who followed him and listened to him. He reached such a level of fear that he would not enter Pharaoh's city except in fear. So he entered it one day at a time of heedlessness among its people. The majority hold that he, peace be upon him, entered it at midday, when they were taking their afternoon rest. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas that he meant between maghrib and 'isha'. The first is preferable, because Allah attributed the heedlessness to its people, and when a man enters hidden out of fear, the heedlessness is not attributed to the people.

The second view: al-Suddi said: when Moses, peace be upon him, grew up, he used to ride the mounts of Pharaoh, wear the same clothes as him, and be called "Moses, son of Pharaoh." One day he rode after him and was overtaken by the midday rest in a place, so he entered it at midday, when the streets were empty. This is His saying ﴿at a time of heedlessness﴾.

The third view: Ibn Zayd said: what is meant by His saying ﴿at a time of heedlessness among its people﴾ is not the occurrence of heedlessness at that hour, but rather heedlessness from the mention of Moses and his affair. When Moses was young, he struck the head of Pharaoh with a staff and plucked his beard, so Pharaoh wanted to kill him. A burning coal was brought, and he took it and put it in his mouth, and from this came the impediment in his tongue. Pharaoh said: "I will not kill him, but expel him from the house and the land." So he was expelled, and he did not enter upon them until he grew up, while the people had forgotten his mention. This is His saying ﴿at a time of heedlessness﴾. There is no way to prefer some of these reports over others, because nothing in the Qur'an indicates any of them.

Fourth issue: "He found in it two men fighting, one from his own party and the other from his enemy" (28:15). Al-Zajjaj said: "He said 'this one' and 'this one', while they were absent, in the manner of narration (hikayah), meaning: he found in it two men fighting; when the observer looks at them, he says, 'this one is from his party, and this one is from his enemy.'" Then the scholars differed. Muqatil said: the two men were both disbelievers, except that one of them was from the Children of Israel and the other from the Copts. He argued for this by the fact that Musa, peace be upon him, said to him on the second day, "Indeed, you are clearly a deviator" (28:18). The well-known view, however, is that the one from his party was a Muslim, because one does not say of someone who opposes a man in his religion and way that he is "from his party." It was also said that the Copt who was subjugating the Israelite was the cook of Pharaoh, who had conscripted him to carry firewood to his kitchen. It was also said: the two men fighting were, one of them the Samiri, who was from his party, and the other the cook of Pharaoh; but God knows best the exact state of affairs. So the one from his party called on him for help against the one from his enemy, that is, he asked him to rescue him from him and sought his support against him. Then Musa, peace be upon him, struck him (fa-wakazahu). The wakz is pushing with the tips of the fingers, and it was said it is pushing with the palm gathered together. Ibn Mas'ud recited: "fa-lakazahu Musa" (then Musa punched him). Some said: the wakz is to the chest and the lakz is to the back. He, peace be upon him, was extremely forceful in his grip. Some exegetes said: "he struck him with his staff." Al-Mufaddal said: this is an error, because one does not say "he struck him with a staff" (wakazahu bi-l-'asa). "So he dispatched him" (faqada 'alayhi), that is, he caused him to die and killed him.

* * *

Fifth issue: Those who challenge the infallibility of the prophets, peace be upon them, have argued from this verse in several respects:

First: As for that Copt, it is either said that he deserved to be killed or not. If the first, then why did he say, "This is from the work of Satan" (28:15), and why did he say, "My Lord, I have wronged myself, so forgive me. And He forgave him" (28:16), and why did he say in another surah, "I did it then while I was of those astray" (26:20)? And if the second, namely that this Copt did not deserve to be killed, then his killing was a disobedience and a sin.

Second: His saying, "and this one is from his enemy" (28:15), indicates that he was a disbelieving combatant (harbi), so his blood was permissible. Why then did he seek forgiveness for it? Seeking forgiveness for a permissible act is not allowed, because it suggests that the permissible is forbidden.

Third: Striking does not ordinarily aim at killing, so that killing was an accidental killing (qatl khata'). Why then did he seek forgiveness for it?

The answer to the first: Why is it not permissible to say that he was, because of his disbelief, one whose blood is permissible?

As for his saying, "This is from the work of Satan," there are several views:

One: Perhaps God, although He permitted the killing of the disbeliever, preferred that their killing be delayed to another time. When he killed, he abandoned that recommended act (mandub). So his saying, "This is from the work of Satan," means: my undertaking to abandon the recommended act is from the work of Satan.

Two: His saying "this" (hadha) refers to the deed of the one killed, not to his own deed. So "This is from the work of Satan" means: the deed of this one killed is from the work of Satan. The purpose of this is to show that he opposed God Most High and deserved to be killed.

Three: His saying "this" refers to the one killed, meaning that he is from the troops and party of Satan. It is said, "So-and-so is from the work of Satan," meaning from his partisans.

As for his saying, "My Lord, I have wronged myself, so forgive me," it follows the manner of Adam's saying, peace be upon him, "Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves" (7:23). The commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 28, verses 18–21:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So he woke up in the city, fearful and watchful, when behold, the one who had sought his help the day before was crying out to him for help. Musa said to him, "Indeed, you are clearly a misguided man."﴾ ﴿Then when he wanted to seize the one who was an enemy to both of them, he said, "O Musa, do you intend to kill me as you killed a man yesterday? You only want to be a tyrant in the land, and you do not want to be among the reformers."﴾ ﴿And a man came running from the farthest part of the city and said, "O Musa, the chiefs are conspiring against you to kill you, so leave. Indeed, I am one of your sincere advisors."﴾ ﴿So he left it, fearful and watchful, and said, "My Lord, deliver me from the wrongdoing people."﴾

Know that after the death of that man from the blow, Musa (peace be upon him) woke up the next day in fear that it might become known that he was the killer, and he would then be pursued for it. He went out while concealing himself. ﴿When behold, the one who had sought his help﴾, who was an Israelite, ﴿the day before was crying out to him﴾, seeking his help with shouting and crying out. Musa said to him: ﴿Indeed, you are clearly a misguided man.﴾

The lexicographers said: "Al-ghawiyy" may be an adjective of the pattern fa'il in the sense of mufil (causing error), meaning: indeed you are a cause of misguidance for my people, for I fell into what I fell into yesterday because of you. It may also mean "al-ghawi" (one who is misguided). Those who criticised the infallibility (ʿisma) of the prophets (peace be upon them) used this verse as evidence, saying: How is it permissible for Musa (peace be upon him) to say to a man from his own group who was calling for his help, ﴿Indeed, you are clearly a misguided man﴾? The answer is in two respects.

The first: The people of Musa (peace be upon him) were coarse and rough. Do you not see their saying after witnessing the signs: ﴿Make for us a god just as they have gods﴾ (Al-A'raf 7:138)? So the intended meaning of "clearly misguided" is this.

The second: He (peace be upon him) only called him "misguided" because the one who engages in excessive quarrelling, in a manner that makes it impossible for him to repel his opponent from the harm he intends, is acting contrary to the way of right guidance.

They differed concerning His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿He said, "O Musa, do you intend to kill me as you killed..."﴾ Is it from the words of the Israelite or of the Qibti (Egyptian)? Some said: When Musa addressed the Israelite as "misguided" and saw him in anger, he thought, when he (the Israelite) moved to strike, that he (the Israelite) wanted to strike him, so he said this statement. They claimed that he (the Israelite) did not know that Musa was the one who had killed the man the day before, and that this became a cause for the killing to become known and for fear to increase. Others said: Rather, it is the saying of the Qibti, who had learned the story from the Israelite. The apparent view is this one, because He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿Then when he wanted to seize the one who was an enemy to both of them, he said, "O Musa"﴾.

So this statement is therefore from him and not from anyone else. Also, His saying ﴿You only want to be a tyrant in the land﴾ is fitting only if it is the saying of the disbeliever.

Know that the tyrant (jabbar) is one who does what he wills of striking and killing through injustice, does not consider the consequences, and does not repel evil with what is better. It was also said: he is the one who considers himself great and does not humble himself before anyone's command. When this incident occurred, the news spread in the city and reached Pharaoh, and they resolved to kill him.

As for His saying: ﴿And a man came running from the farthest part of the city﴾, the author of "al-Kashshaf" said: "Yas'a" (running) may be in the nominative as an adjective of "rajul" (a man), and in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl) of it, because it has been specified by His saying ﴿from the farthest part of the city﴾. "Al-i'timar" means consultation. It is said: "The two men ta'tamirani," because each of them commands his companion with something or advises him concerning a matter. The meaning is: they are consulting one another because of you. Most of the exegetes hold that this man was a believer from the family of Pharaoh, and he hurried to him out of compassion, to frighten him that the chiefs were conspiring against him to kill him.

As for His saying: ﴿So he left it, fearful and watchful﴾, meaning: fearful for his own self from the family of Pharaoh, awaiting whether a pursuit would overtake him and he would be seized. Then he turned to Allah, may He be exalted, knowing that there is no refuge other than Him, and said: ﴿My Lord, deliver me from the wrongdoing people.﴾ This indicates that his killing of that Qibti was not a sin, for otherwise he would have been the wrongdoer towards them, and they would not have been wrongdoers towards him by seeking him in order to kill him as retaliation (qisas).

**Al-Razi's commentary (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 28, verses 22–24**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And when he turned toward Madyan, he said, "Perhaps my Lord will guide me to the sound way."﴾ ﴿And when he arrived at the water of Madyan, he found upon it a community of people watering [their flocks], and he found besides them two women keeping back [their sheep]. He said, "What is your circumstance?" They said, "We cannot water until the shepherds have finished sending [their flocks away], and our father is an old man."﴾ ﴿So he watered [the flocks] for them; then he turned back to the shade and said, "My Lord, indeed I am, for whatever good You would send down to me, in need."﴾ ﴿Then came to him one of the two women, walking shyly. She said, "Indeed, my father invites you that he may give you the reward for what you watered for us." And when he came to him and related to him the story, he said, "Fear not. You have escaped from the wrongdoing people."﴾ ﴿One of them said, "O my father, hire him; indeed, the best one you could hire is the strong, the trustworthy."﴾ ﴿He said, "Indeed, I intend to marry you to one of these two daughters of mine on [the condition] that you serve me eight years; but if you complete ten, it will be [a favor] from you. And I do not intend to make it difficult for you. You will find me, if Allah wills, of the righteous."﴾ ﴿He said, "That is [settled] between me and you. Whichever of the two terms I fulfill, there shall be no injustice against me. And Allah is Witness over what we say."﴾

People have differed regarding His saying: ﴿And when he turned toward Madyan﴾. Some said: He set out without intending Madyan, but he committed himself to Allah, may He be exalted, and began walking without knowing [the way], so Allah, may He be exalted, brought him to Madyan. This is the view of Ibn Abbas. Others said: When he set out, he intended Madyan, because it occurred to him that there was kinship between them and him, since they were descendants of Madyan ibn Ibrahim, peace be upon him, and he was from the Children of Israel. But he had no knowledge of the route; rather, he relied upon the grace of Allah, may He be exalted. Among the people there are those who said: Rather, Jibril, peace be upon him, came to him and taught him the way. Ibn Jarir reported from al-Suddi that when Musa, peace be upon him, began his journey, an angel came to him on a horse, and Musa prostrated to him out of joy, so he said: "Do not do that, but follow me." So he followed him toward Madyan.

Those who held that he set out without intending Madyan argued with two points:

The first: His saying, ﴿he turned toward Madyan﴾. Had he been intending to go to Madyan, He would have said, "When he turned toward Madyan." Since He did not say that, but said, ﴿turned toward Madyan﴾, we know that he only turned toward that direction without knowing where that direction would end.

The second: His saying, ﴿Perhaps my Lord will guide me to the sound way.﴾ This is the speech of one who is doubtful, not of one who knows. The closer view is that it should be said: he intended to go to Madyan, but he was not knowledgeable of the route. Then he would ask people about the manner of the route, because it is unlikely, given Musa's intellect and intelligence, that he would not ask. Then Ibn Ishaq said: He went out from Egypt to Madyan without provisions or a mount, and between them was a distance of eight days, and he had no food except the leaves of trees.

As for His saying, ﴿Perhaps my Lord will guide me to the sound way﴾, it is similar to the saying of his forefather Ibrahim, peace be upon him: ﴿Indeed, I am going to my Lord; He will guide me﴾ (al-Saffat: 99). Musa, peace be upon him, rarely speaks words in argument, answer, supplication, and humble entreaty except what Ibrahim, peace be upon him, had mentioned. Likewise is the righteous successor to the righteous predecessor, may the blessings of Allah be upon them and upon all the pure and purified.

﴿And when he arrived at the water of Madyan﴾, and it is the water from which they watered, and it was a well according to what has been narrated. His arrival means his coming and reaching it. ﴿He found upon it﴾, that is, above its edge and its watering place, ﴿a community﴾, a large group in number, ﴿of people﴾, of various people. ﴿And he found besides them﴾, in a place lower than their place, ﴿two women keeping back﴾. Al-dhawd means pushing away and driving off, so His saying "keeping back" means holding back. Then there are several opinions about it:

The first: They were holding back their sheep. People differed about the cause of that holding back in several ways:

One: Al-Zajjaj said: Because those on the water were stronger than they were, so they could not manage to water.

Second: They disliked crowding at the water.

Third: So that their sheep would not mix with their sheep.

Fourth: So that they would not mix with men.

The second opinion: They were keeping back [people] from their faces, [so that] the gaze of the one looking would not see them.

The third opinion: They were keeping people back from their sheep.

The fourth opinion: Al-Farra' said: They were holding them back so that they would not scatter and disperse.

﴿He said, "What is your circumstance?"﴾, that is, what is your matter? Its literal sense is: what is your subject of asking, that is, what you seek in driving off, so the thing sought is called a khatb (affair), just as the thing that is in question is called sha'n (matter), as in your saying: "What is your matter?" ﴿They said, "We cannot water until the shepherds have finished sending [their flocks away], and our father is an old man."﴾ That indicates their weakness in watering in several ways:

One: The custom of watering is for men, and women are weak in that.

Second: The manifest fact of their driving the livestock in a manner of delay.

Third: Their saying: "until the shepherds have finished sending [their flocks away]."

Fourth: Their waiting for what remains of the people from the water.

Fifth: Their saying: ﴿and our father is an old man﴾, and the indication of this is that had he been strong, he would have come, and had he come, the watering would not have been delayed. At that point, he watered for them before the shepherds finished sending [their flocks away], and they returned to their father before the customary time.

Abu Amr, Ibn Amir, and Asim read [yusdira] with an open ya' and a damma on the dal, while the rest read with a damma on the ya' and a kasra on the dal. The meaning in the first recitation is: until they turn away from the water and return from their watering; and sadara is the opposite of warada. As for the one who read with a damma on the ya', the meaning in the recitation is: until the people send their livestock away.

As for His saying, ﴿So he watered [the flocks] for them﴾, that is, he watered their flocks on their behalf. Regarding the manner of the watering, there are several opinions:

One: He, peace be upon him, asked the people to permit him, and they permitted him.

Second: Some people said: He went to a well over whose mouth was a stone that only ten could lift, and it was said forty, and it was said a hundred. He moved it himself and drew water from that well.

Third: When the people crowded Musa, peace be upon him, they deliberately threw that stone over the mouth of the well. So he, peace be upon him, threw that stone and watered for them. The explanation of this is not in the Qur'an, and Allah knows best its correctness.

However, the woman described Musa, peace be upon him, with strength, which indicates that she had witnessed from him something that showed the excellence of his strength. And He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿Then he turned back to the shade﴾, and in it is an indication that he watered for them in sunshine and heat, and in it is also an indication of the perfection of Musa's strength, peace be upon him. Al-Kalbi said: Musa came to the people of the water and asked them for a bucket of water. They said to him: If you wish, go to the bucket and draw for them. He said: Yes. Forty men would gather at the bucket until they brought it out of the well. So Musa, peace be upon him, took the bucket, drew with it alone, poured it into the trough, and invoked blessing. Then he brought their flock near, and they drank until they were satisfied, then he sent them back with their flock.

If it is said: How was it proper for the Prophet of Allah, who was Shu'ayb, to consent that his two daughters should water livestock? We say: There is nothing in the Qur'an that indicates that their father was Shu'ayb, and people differ about it. Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: Their father was Bayrun, the nephew of Shu'ayb, and Shu'ayb died after he had become blind. This is the view chosen by Abu Ubayd. Al-Hasan said: He was a Muslim man who accepted the religion from Shu'ayb. Furthermore, even if we concede that he was Shu'ayb, peace be upon him, there is no corruption in it, because religion does not forbid it. As for propriety (muruwwah), people differ regarding it, and the conditions of the people of the desert are not the conditions of the people of the settled towns, especially when the situation is one of necessity.

* * *

As for His saying, ﴿So he said, "My Lord, indeed I am, for whatever good You would send down to me, in need."﴾ the meaning is: Indeed, for whatever good You have sent down to me, whether little or much, meager or plentiful, I am in need. He used the preposition lam with faqir (in need) because it was implicitly given the meaning of "seeking" and "requesting."

Know that this statement indicates need, whether for food or for something else, except that the exegetes understood it as referring to food. Ibn Abbas said: He means food that he would eat. Al-Dahhak said: He remained seven days, tasting no food during them except the herbs of the earth. It is narrated that when Musa, peace be upon him, said that, he raised his voice so that the two women would hear it. If it is said: When there remained with him enough strength by which he could lift that great bucket, how is it fitting for his lofty aspiration to ask for food? Did he not, peace be upon him, say: "Charity is not lawful for a rich person or for one who has sound strength"? We say: As for raising the voice with that in order to make the two women hear and asking for food, that is absolutely not fitting for Musa, peace be upon him, so that narration is not accepted. Rather, perhaps he, peace be upon him, said that within himself to his Lord, may He be exalted. There is another aspect in the verse: as if he said, "My Lord, indeed, because of what You have sent down to me of the good of religion, I have become poor

in the world, since he had been with Pharaoh in dominion and wealth. So he said this in contentment with this exchange, joy in it, and gratitude to Him. And this interpretation is more fitting to the state of Musa, peace be upon him."

Its literal sense is: what is your subject of asking, that is, what you seek in driving off, so the thing sought is called a khatb (affair), just as the thing that is in question is called sha'n (matter), as in your saying: "What is your matter?" ﴿They said, "We cannot water until the shepherds have finished sending [their flocks away], and our father is an old man."﴾ That indicates their weakness in watering in several ways:

One: The custom of watering is for men, and women are weak in that.

Second: The manifest fact of their driving the livestock in a manner of delay.

Third: Their saying: "until the shepherds have finished sending [their flocks away]."

Fourth: Their waiting for what remains of the people from the water.

Fifth: Their saying: ﴿and our father is an old man﴾, and the indication of this is that had he been strong, he would have come, and had he come, the watering would not have been delayed. At that point, he watered for them before the shepherds finished sending [their flocks away], and they returned to their father before the customary time.

Abu Amr, Ibn Amir, and Asim read [yusdira] with an open ya' and a damma on the dal, while the rest read with a damma on the ya' and a kasra on the dal. The meaning in the first recitation is: until they turn away from the water and return from their watering; and sadara is the opposite of warada. As for the one who read with a damma on the ya', the meaning in the recitation is: until the people send their livestock away.

As for His saying, ﴿So he watered [the flocks] for them﴾, that is, he watered their flocks on their behalf. Regarding the manner of the watering, there are several opinions:

One: He, peace be upon him, asked the people to permit him, and they permitted him.

Second: Some people said: He went to a well over whose mouth was a stone that only ten could lift, and it was said forty, and it was said a hundred. He moved it himself and drew water from that well.

Third: When the people crowded Musa, peace be upon him, they deliberately threw that stone over the mouth of the well. So he, peace be upon him, threw that stone and watered for them. The explanation of this is not in the Qur'an, and Allah knows best its correctness.

However, the woman described Musa, peace be upon him, with strength, which indicates that she had witnessed from him something that showed the excellence of his strength. And He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿Then he turned back to the shade﴾, and in it is an indication that he watered for them in sunshine and heat, and in it is also an indication of the perfection of Musa's strength, peace be upon him. Al-Kalbi said: Musa came to the people of the water and asked them for a bucket of water. They said to him: If you wish, go to the bucket and draw for them. He said: Yes. Forty men would gather at the bucket until they brought it out of the well. So Musa, peace be upon him, took the bucket, drew with it alone, poured it into the trough, and invoked blessing. Then he brought their flock near, and they drank until they were satisfied, then he sent them back with their flock.

If it is said: How was it proper for the Prophet of Allah, who was Shu'ayb, to consent that his two daughters should water livestock? We say: There is nothing in the Qur'an that indicates that their father was Shu'ayb, and people differ about it. Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: Their father was Bayrun, the nephew of Shu'ayb, and Shu'ayb died after he had become blind. This is the view chosen by Abu Ubayd. Al-Hasan said: He was a Muslim man who accepted the religion from Shu'ayb. Furthermore, even if we concede that he was Shu'ayb, peace be upon him, there is no corruption in it, because religion does not forbid it. As for propriety (muruwwah), people differ regarding it, and the conditions of the people of the desert are not the conditions of the people of the settled towns, especially when the situation is one of necessity.

* * *

As for His saying, ﴿So he said, "My Lord, indeed I am, for whatever good You would send down to me, in need."﴾ the meaning is: Indeed, for whatever good You have sent down to me, whether little or much, meager or plentiful, I am in need. He used the preposition lam with faqir (in need) because it was implicitly given the meaning of "seeking" and "requesting."

Know that this statement indicates need, whether for food or for something else, except that the exegetes understood it as referring to food. Ibn Abbas said: He means food that he would eat. Al-Dahhak said: He remained seven days, tasting no food during them except the herbs of the earth. It is narrated that when Musa, peace be upon him, said that, he raised his voice so that the two women would hear it. If it is said: When there remained with him enough strength by which he could lift that great bucket, how is it fitting for his lofty aspiration to ask for food? Did he not, peace be upon him, say: "Charity is not lawful for a rich person or for one who has sound strength"? We say: As for raising the voice with that in order to make the two women hear and asking for food, that is absolutely not fitting for Musa, peace be upon him, so that narration is not accepted. Rather, perhaps he, peace be upon him, said that within himself to his Lord, may He be exalted. There is another aspect in the verse: as if he said, "My Lord, indeed, because of what You have sent down to me of the good of religion, I have become poor

[Page 206]

in the world, since he had been with Pharaoh in dominion and wealth. So he said this in contentment with this exchange, joy in it, and gratitude to Him. And this interpretation is more fitting to the state of Musa, peace be upon him."

**Al-Razi's commentary (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 28, verses 22–24**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And when he turned toward Madyan, he said, "Perhaps my Lord will guide me to the sound way."﴾ ﴿And when he arrived at the water of Madyan, he found upon it a community of people watering [their flocks], and he found besides them two women keeping back [their sheep]. He said, "What is your circumstance?" They said, "We cannot water until the shepherds have finished sending [their flocks away], and our father is an old man."﴾ ﴿So he watered [the flocks] for them; then he turned back to the shade and said, "My Lord, indeed I am, for whatever good You would send down to me, in need."﴾ ﴿Then came to him one of the two women, walking shyly. She said, "Indeed, my father invites you that he may give you the reward for what you watered for us." And when he came to him and related to him the story, he said, "Fear not. You have escaped from the wrongdoing people."﴾ ﴿One of them said, "O my father, hire him; indeed, the best one you could hire is the strong, the trustworthy."﴾ ﴿He said, "Indeed, I intend to marry you to one of these two daughters of mine on [the condition] that you serve me eight years; but if you complete ten, it will be [a favor] from you. And I do not intend to make it difficult for you. You will find me, if Allah wills, of the righteous."﴾ ﴿He said, "That is [settled] between me and you. Whichever of the two terms I fulfill, there shall be no injustice against me. And Allah is Witness over what we say."﴾

People have differed regarding His saying: ﴿And when he turned toward Madyan﴾. Some said: He set out without intending Madyan, but he committed himself to Allah, may He be exalted, and began walking without knowing [the way], so Allah, may He be exalted, brought him to Madyan. This is the view of Ibn Abbas. Others said: When he set out, he intended Madyan, because it occurred to him that there was kinship between them and him, since they were descendants of Madyan ibn Ibrahim, peace be upon him, and he was from the Children of Israel. But he had no knowledge of the route; rather, he relied upon the grace of Allah, may He be exalted. Among the people there are those who said: Rather, Jibril, peace be upon him, came to him and taught him the way. Ibn Jarir reported from al-Suddi that when Musa, peace be upon him, began his journey, an angel came to him on a horse, and Musa prostrated to him out of joy, so he said: "Do not do that, but follow me." So he followed him toward Madyan.

Those who held that he set out without intending Madyan argued with two points:

The first: His saying, ﴿he turned toward Madyan﴾. Had he been intending to go to Madyan, He would have said, "When he turned toward Madyan." Since He did not say that, but said, ﴿turned toward Madyan﴾, we know that he only turned toward that direction without knowing where that direction would end.

The second: His saying, ﴿Perhaps my Lord will guide me to the sound way.﴾ This is the speech of one who is doubtful, not of one who knows. The closer view is that it should be said: he intended to go to Madyan, but he was not knowledgeable of the route. Then he would ask people about the manner of the route, because it is unlikely, given Musa's intellect and intelligence, that he would not ask. Then Ibn Ishaq said: He went out from Egypt to Madyan without provisions or a mount, and between them was a distance of eight days, and he had no food except the leaves of trees.

As for His saying, ﴿Perhaps my Lord will guide me to the sound way﴾, it is similar to the saying of his forefather Ibrahim, peace be upon him: ﴿Indeed, I am going to my Lord; He will guide me﴾ (al-Saffat: 99). Musa, peace be upon him, rarely speaks words in argument, answer, supplication, and humble entreaty except what Ibrahim, peace be upon him, had mentioned. Likewise is the righteous successor to the righteous predecessor, may the blessings of Allah be upon them and upon all the pure and purified.

﴿And when he arrived at the water of Madyan﴾, and it is the water from which they watered, and it was a well according to what has been narrated. His arrival means his coming and reaching it. ﴿He found upon it﴾, that is, above its edge and its watering place, ﴿a community﴾, a large group in number, ﴿of people﴾, of various people. ﴿And he found besides them﴾, in a place lower than their place, ﴿two women keeping back﴾. One: Al-Zajjaj said: Because those on the water were stronger than they were, so they could not manage to water.

Third: So that their sheep would not mix with their sheep.

Fourth: So that they would not mix with men.
