in the world, since he had been with Pharaoh in dominion and wealth. So he said this in contentment with this exchange, joy in it, and gratitude to Him. And this interpretation is more fitting to the state of Musa, peace be upon him."

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 28, verse 25–28:

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then there came to him one of the two women, walking shyly﴾, His saying ﴿shyly﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial phrase (hal), meaning bashfully. ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab said: She had covered herself with the sleeve of her shirt. It was also said: she was walking at a distance, keeping away from the men. ʿAbd al-ʿAziz ibn Abi Hazim said: "out of reverence for him." Some readers pause at His saying ﴿walking﴾ and then begin, saying ﴿shyly﴾. She said: ﴿Indeed my father invites you﴾, meaning that she was speaking this word in a state of shyness, because a noble person who invites another to hospitality feels shy, especially a woman. This indicates that Shuʿayb had no helper other than the two of them. It is related that when they returned to their father earlier than the people, he said to them: "What has made you hasten?" They said: "We found a righteous man who had mercy on us and watered for us." So he said to one of them: "Go and call him to me."

As for the disagreement over whether that elderly man was Shuʿayb, peace be upon him, or someone else, it has already been discussed, and most scholars hold that he was Shuʿayb. Muhammad ibn Ishaq said regarding the two daughters: the name of the elder is Safura, and the younger is Liya. Others said: Safra and Safira. al-Dahhak said: Safura. And the one who came to Musa, peace be upon him, was the elder according to the majority. al-Kalbi said: it was the younger. There is no indication in the Qur'an of any of these details.

As for His saying: ﴿She said: Indeed my father invites you that he may reward you with the wage for what you watered for us﴾, there are several difficulties in it:

The first: How was it permissible for Musa, peace be upon him, to act upon the word of a woman, and to walk with her while she was a non-mahram? For that leads to a great suspicion, and he, peace be upon him, said: "Avoid the places of suspicion"?

The second: He watered their flocks seeking nearness to God, so how is it fitting for him to take a wage for it? For that is not permissible in terms of manliness (muruwwa) nor in the Shariʿa?

The third: He knew their poverty, their father's poverty and his incapacity, and that he, peace be upon him, was at the height of strength, such that he could earn much with little effort. So how is it fitting for the manliness of someone like him to seek a wage for that amount of watering from an elderly poor man and a poor woman?

The fourth: How is it fitting for Shuʿayb, the Prophet, peace be upon him, to send his young daughter to a young man before knowing whether that man was chaste or dissolute?

As for the answer to the first: we say that acting upon the word of a woman is like acting upon the word of one person, whether free or slave, male or female, in reports; and she was only reporting on behalf of her father. As for walking with a woman, there is no harm in it together with caution and abstention.

As for the answer to the second: even though the woman said that, perhaps Musa, peace be upon him, did not go to them seeking a wage, but rather seeking blessing through seeing that elderly man. It is related that when she said "that he may reward you," he disliked that, and when the food was presented to him he refused, and said: "We are a household that does not sell our religion for our worldly life, nor take a price for kindness," until Shuʿayb, peace be upon him, said: "This is our custom with everyone who comes to us." Furthermore, it is not unlikely that hunger had reached a point he could not bear, so he accepted it out of necessity. This is the answer to the third, for necessities make forbidden things permissible.

As for the answer to the fourth: perhaps he, peace be upon him, had known by revelation her purity and innocence, so he relied upon her.

As for His saying: ﴿So when he came to him﴾, ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, said: He got up walking while the girl was in front of him, then the wind blew and uncovered her. Musa, peace be upon him, said: "I am from the lineage of Ibrahim, peace be upon him, so walk behind me, so that the wind does not lift your clothes, and I see what is not lawful for me." When he entered upon Shuʿayb, the food was laid out, and Shuʿayb said: "Partake, young man." Musa, peace be upon him, said: "I seek refuge in Allah." Shuʿayb said: "Why?" He said: "Because we are from a household that does not sell its religion for a fill of the earth in gold." Shuʿayb said: "But my custom and the custom of my forefathers is to feed the guest." So Musa, peace be upon him, sat down and ate. He only disliked eating the food out of fear that it would be a wage for him for his work. He did not dislike that with al-Khidr when he said: ﴿Had you wished, you could have taken a wage for it﴾. The difference is that taking a wage for charity is not permissible, but hiring from the outset is not disliked.

As for His saying: ﴿And he related to him the narratives﴾, al-qasas is a verbal noun like al-ʿalal, and the thing related is called by it. al-Dahhak said: When he entered upon him, he said to him: "Who are you, servant of Allah?" He said: "I am Musa son of ʿImran son of Yasahar son of Qahath son of Lawi son of Yaʿqub," and he mentioned to him his whole matter from his birth onwards, and the matter of the midwives, the wet-nurses, the casting into the river, the killing of the Copt, and that they were seeking him to kill him. Then Shuʿayb said: ﴿Do not fear; you have escaped from the wrongdoing people﴾, meaning he has no authority in our land, for we are not in his kingdom. There is no indication in the verse that he said this by revelation or in accordance with what custom would require. If it is said: the exegetes said that when Pharaoh rode after Musa, peace be upon him, he rode with a thousand thousand and six hundred thousand men; so how is it conceivable that a king of such standing should have no village in his realm at a distance of eight days from the seat of his kingdom? We say: although this is rare, it is not impossible.

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿One of them said: O father, hire him; indeed the best one you could hire is the strong, the trustworthy﴾, there are several issues:

First issue: She described him as strong because of what she witnessed of the manner of the watering, and as trustworthy because of what we have related of his lowering his gaze when they drove the flock away, when he watered for them, and when he walked before them toward their father.

Second issue: Why did He make ﴿the best one you hire﴾ the subject and ﴿the strong, the trustworthy﴾ the predicate, although the reverse would be more appropriate? Because concern is the cause of priority.

Third issue: Strength and trustworthiness do not suffice to achieve the aim unless shrewdness and astuteness are joined to them, so why was the matter of astuteness omitted? It may be said that it is included within trustworthiness. It is related from Ibn Masʿud, may Allah be pleased with him: "The most perceptive of people are three: the daughter of Shuʿayb, the companion of Yusuf, and Abu Bakr concerning ʿUmar."

As for His saying: ﴿He said: Indeed I wish to marry you to one of these two daughters of mine﴾, there is no doubt that this expression, although it is in an indefinite form, was specified at the time of the marriage. And there is no doubt that the contract was concluded on the lesser of the two terms, so the extra was like a voluntary gift. Jurists have sometimes used this as evidence that work may serve as a dowry like property, and that adding an extra to the price and the priced good is permissible. But it is the law of those before us, so it does not bind us. It indicates that in that law it was permissible to stipulate a benefit for the guardian, and that it was permissible in that law for a woman to be married without a due that the woman is entitled to, and that the marriage contract is not invalidated by conditions that the contract does not necessitate. Then he said: ﴿On condition that you serve me for eight years﴾. "Serve me" (ta'jurani) is from ajartuhu when you made him a hired worker for you; "eight years" is its time frame. Or it is from ajartuhu kadhā when you granted him that, and from it: "May Allah reward you (ajarakum) and have mercy on you." And "eight years" is the object, and its meaning is "as a shepherd for eight years." Then he said: ﴿And I do not wish to make it hard for you﴾, and in it there are two views:

The first: I do not wish to burden you by imposing the sin of the two men. If it is said: what is the reality of their saying "I made it hard for him" and "the matter was hard upon him"? We say: its reality is that when a matter overwhelms you, it is as if your assumption of two things made it hard for you; you say at one time "I can bear it" and at another "I cannot bear it."

The second: I do not wish to make it hard for you in the herding, but I will be lenient with you in it and accommodate you as far as possible, and I will not burden you with extreme caution in the manner of herding. Thus were the prophets, peace be upon them, taking the easiest course in their dealings with people, and from it is the hadith: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ was my partner, and he was the best partner: he would not be contentious, nor would he dispute, nor would he argue." Then he said: ﴿You will find me, if Allah wills, among the righteous﴾, and in it there are two views:

The first: by righteousness he means good dealing and gentleness of manner.

The second: he means righteousness in general, which includes good dealing; and he said "if Allah wills" out of reliance upon His success and help.

If it is said: how does the contract come into being with this condition? For if you said "my wife is divorced if Allah wills," she would not be divorced? We say: this is among the matters that differ according to the laws.

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿He said: That is between me and you﴾, know that "that" (dhalika) is the subject, and "between me and you" is its predicate, and it is a reference to what Shuʿayb had covenanted with him. He means: that which you have said and which you have pledged to me stands between us both; neither of us departs from it, neither I from what I stipulated for myself, nor you from what you stipulated upon yourself. Then he said: ﴿Whichever of the two terms I fulfill﴾: of the two terms, the longer one, which is ten years, or the shorter one, which is eight years. ﴿Then there shall be no transgression against me﴾, meaning no one shall transgress against me by seeking an increase; he intended by this to establish the matter of choice, meaning: if I wish this, and if I wish that, and the choice of the longer term is left to his opinion without anyone having compulsion over him. Then he said: ﴿And Allah is Witness over what we say﴾. The wakil is the one to whom the matter is entrusted, and when "wakil" was used in the sense of "witness," it was made to govern "ʿala" for this reason.

The third: He knew their poverty, their father's poverty and his incapacity, and that he, peace be upon him, was at the height of strength, such that he could earn much with little effort. So how is it fitting for the manliness of someone like him to seek a wage for that amount of watering from an elderly poor man and a poor woman?

The fourth: How is it fitting for Shuʿayb, the Prophet, peace be upon him, to send his young daughter to a young man before knowing whether that man was chaste or dissolute?

As for the answer to the first: we say that acting upon the word of a woman is like acting upon the word of one person, whether free or slave, male or female, in reports; and she was only reporting on behalf of her father. As for walking with a woman, there is no harm in it together with caution and abstention.

As for the answer to the second: even though the woman said that, perhaps Musa, peace be upon him, did not go to them seeking a wage, but rather seeking blessing through seeing that elderly man. It is related that when she said "that he may reward you," he disliked that, and when the food was presented to him he refused, and said: "We are a household that does not sell our religion for our worldly life, nor take a price for kindness," until Shuʿayb, peace be upon him, said: "This is our custom with everyone who comes to us." Furthermore, it is not unlikely that hunger had reached a point he could not bear, so he accepted it out of necessity. This is the answer to the third, for necessities make forbidden things permissible.

As for the answer to the fourth: perhaps he, peace be upon him, had known by revelation her purity and innocence, so he relied upon her.

Musa, peace be upon him, said: "I am from the lineage of Ibrahim, peace be upon him, so walk behind me, so that the wind does not lift your clothes, and I see what is not lawful for me." When he entered upon Shuʿayb, the food was laid out, and Shuʿayb said: "Partake, young man." Musa, peace be upon him, said: "I seek refuge in Allah." Shuʿayb said: "Why?" He said: "Because we are from a household that does not sell its religion for a fill of the earth in gold." Shuʿayb said: "But my custom and the custom of my forefathers is to feed the guest." We say: although this is rare, it is not impossible.

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿One of them said: O father, hire him; indeed the best one you could hire is the strong, the trustworthy﴾, there are several issues:

First issue: She described him as strong because of what she witnessed of the manner of the watering, and as trustworthy because of what we have related of his lowering his gaze when they drove the flock away, when he watered for them, and when he walked before them toward their father.

Second issue: Why did He make ﴿the best one you hire﴾ the subject and ﴿the strong, the trustworthy﴾ the predicate, although the reverse would be more appropriate? Because concern is the cause of priority.

Third issue: Strength and trustworthiness do not suffice to achieve the aim unless shrewdness and astuteness are joined to them, so why was the matter of astuteness omitted? It may be said that it is included within trustworthiness. It is related from Ibn Masʿud, may Allah be pleased with him: "The most perceptive of people are three: the daughter of Shuʿayb, the companion of Yusuf, and Abu Bakr concerning ʿUmar."

As for His saying: ﴿He said: Indeed I wish to marry you to one of these two daughters of mine﴾, there is no doubt that this expression, although it is in an indefinite form, was specified at the time of the marriage. And there is no doubt that the contract was concluded on the lesser of the two terms, so the extra was like a voluntary gift. Jurists have sometimes used this as evidence that work may serve as a dowry like property, and that adding an extra to the price and the priced good is permissible. But it is the law of those before us, so it does not bind us. It indicates that in that law it was permissible to stipulate a benefit for the guardian, and that it was permissible in that law for a woman to be married without a due that the woman is entitled to, and that the marriage contract is not invalidated by conditions that the contract does not necessitate. Then he said: ﴿On condition that you serve me for eight years﴾. "Serve me" (ta'jurani) is from ajartuhu when you made him a hired worker for you; "eight years" is its time frame. Or it is from ajartuhu kadhā when you granted him that, and from it: "May Allah reward you (ajarakum) and have mercy on you." And "eight years" is the object, and its meaning is "as a shepherd for eight years." Then he said: ﴿And I do not wish to make it hard for you﴾, and in it there are two views:

The first: I do not wish to burden you by imposing the sin of the two men. If it is said: what is the reality of their saying "I made it hard for him" and "the matter was hard upon him"? We say: its reality is that when a matter overwhelms you, it is as if your assumption of two things made it hard for you; you say at one time "I can bear it" and at another "I cannot bear it."

The second: I do not wish to make it hard for you in the herding, but I will be lenient with you in it and accommodate you as far as possible, and I will not burden you with extreme caution in the manner of herding. Thus were the prophets, peace be upon them, taking the easiest course in their dealings with people, and from it is the hadith: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ was my partner, and he was the best partner: he would not be contentious, nor would he dispute, nor would he argue." The first: by righteousness he means good dealing and gentleness of manner.

The second: he means righteousness in general, which includes good dealing; and he said "if Allah wills" out of reliance upon His success and help.

If it is said: how does the contract come into being with this condition? For if you said "my wife is divorced if Allah wills," she would not be divorced? We say: this is among the matters that differ according to the laws.

Then he said: ﴿And Allah is Witness over what we say﴾. The wakil is the one to whom the matter is entrusted, and when "wakil" was used in the sense of "witness," it was made to govern "ʿala" for this reason.

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿He said: That is between me and you﴾, know that "that" (dhalika) is the subject, and "between me and you" is its predicate, and it is a reference to what Shuʿayb had covenanted with him. He means: that which you have said and which you have pledged to me stands between us both; neither of us departs from it, neither I from what I stipulated for myself, nor you from what you stipulated upon yourself. Then he said: ﴿Whichever of the two terms I fulfill﴾: of the two terms, the longer one, which is ten years, or the shorter one, which is eight years. ﴿Then there shall be no transgression against me﴾, meaning no one shall transgress against me by seeking an increase; he intended by this to establish the matter of choice, meaning: if I wish this, and if I wish that, and the choice of the longer term is left to his opinion without anyone having compulsion over him. Then he said: ﴿And Allah is Witness over what we say﴾. The wakil is the one to whom the matter is entrusted, and when "wakil" was used in the sense of "witness," it was made to govern "ʿala" for this reason.

[Page 209]

The Almighty's words: ﴿So when Moses had fulfilled the term and set out with his family, he perceived a fire from the side of the mount. He said to his family, "Wait, I have perceived a fire. Perhaps I will bring you news from it, or a burning brand from the fire, so that you may warm yourselves."﴾ ﴿And when he came to it, he was called from the right side of the valley, in the blessed spot, out of the tree: "O Moses, indeed I am Allah, the Lord of the worlds."﴾ ﴿And throw down your staff." But when he saw it moving as if it were a snake, he turned back in flight and did not return. "O Moses, come forward and do not fear. Indeed, you are among the secure."﴾ ﴿Insert your hand into your pocket; it will come out white without harm. And draw your arm to your side against fear. These are two proofs from your Lord to Pharaoh and his chiefs. Indeed, they have been a defiant people.﴾

Know that it has been narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "He married the younger of the two daughters, and fulfilled the more complete of the two terms." That is, he fulfilled the fuller of the two terms. Mujahid said: "He fulfilled the term of ten years, and then remained with him for ten more years." And His words: ﴿So when Moses had fulfilled the term and set out with his family﴾

[Page 209]

﴿Perceived﴾ indicates that this perceiving took place after the combination of the two matters, and does not indicate that it took place after only one of them, namely the fulfilling of the term. Thus what the al-Qadi said is refuted, namely that this indicates he did not add anything beyond it. His words ﴿and set out with his family﴾ do not indicate that he went out alone with her. His words ﴿Wait﴾ indicate plurality.

As for His words ﴿Indeed, I have perceived a fire﴾, its explanation has already passed in Surah Ta-Ha and Surah al-Naml.

As for His words ﴿Perhaps I will bring you news from it, or a burning brand from the fire, so that you may warm yourselves﴾, there are several discussions concerning it:

The first: The author of al-Kashshaf said: "The jadhwa (burning brand) is pronounced in the three dialects, and it has been read in all three. It is a thick stick, whether or not it has fire at its end." Al-Zajjaj said: "The jadhwa is a thick piece of firewood."

The second: We have related in Surah Ta-Ha that the night fell upon him in the desert, a strong wind blew which scattered his livestock, he lost his way, and rain fell upon them, so they found intense cold. At that point he saw a distant fire, so he set out toward it seeking someone who would guide him to the road. This is His words ﴿I will bring you news from it﴾, or "I will bring you from this fire a burning brand of firewood, so that you may warm yourselves." His words ﴿Perhaps I will bring you news from it﴾ indicate that he had lost his way, and His words ﴿so that you may warm yourselves﴾ indicate the cold.

As for His words ﴿And when he came to it, he was called from the right side of the valley, in the blessed spot, out of the tree: "O Moses, indeed I am Allah, the Lord of the worlds."﴾ Know that the shore of the valley is its side. The call came from Moses' right, from the side of the valley, from the direction of the tree. His words ﴿out of the tree﴾ are a substitute for His words ﴿from the side of the valley﴾, a substitution of inclusion (badal al-ishtimal), because the tree was growing on the shore, as in His words: ﴿Had We not made for those who disbelieve in the Most Merciful silver roofs for their houses﴾ (al-Zukhruf: 33). He described the spot as blessed only because the beginning of prophethood and Allah's speaking to him took place there.

* * *

Here are some issues:

The first issue: The Mu'tazilah argued for their doctrine that Allah the Exalted speaks by a speech which He creates in a body, using His words ﴿out of the tree﴾. For this is explicit that Moses, peace be upon him, heard the call from the tree, and the one speaking that call is Allah, glorified is He, and He, the Exalted, is far above being in a body. Thus it is established that He, the Exalted, speaks only by creating speech in a body. Those who hold the eternity of speech responded and said: We have two positions:

The first: the statement of Abu Mansur al-Maturidi and the imams of Transoxiana, which is that the eternal speech subsisting in the essence of Allah the Exalted is not heard; what is heard is only the sound and the letter. That was created in the tree and heard from it. On this assumption the question disappears.

The second: the statement of Abu al-Hasan al-Ash'ari, which is that speech which is neither a letter nor a sound can be heard, just as the essence, which is neither a body nor an accident, can be seen. According to this position, it is not improbable that he heard the letter and the sound from the tree, and heard the eternal speech from Allah the Exalted and not from the tree. So there is no contradiction between the two matters. The People of the Sunnah argued: if the locus of His words ﴿Indeed, I am Allah, the Lord of the worlds﴾ were the tree, then the tree would have said: "Indeed, I am Allah." The Mu'tazilah replied that this follows only if the one speaking the speech were the locus of the speech and not its agent, and this is the core of the issue. The People of the Sunnah replied: the poisoned foreleg said: "Do not eat from me, for I am poisoned." The agent of that speech is Allah the Exalted. If the speaker of the speech were the agent of that speech, it would follow that Allah had said: "Do not eat from me, for I am poisoned," and this is false. And if the speaker were the locus of the speech, it would follow that the tree had said: "Indeed, I am Allah," and all of this is false.

* * *

The second issue: It may be said that He, the Exalted, created in him a necessary knowledge that this speech is the speech of Allah. The Mu'tazilah do not accept this. They said: if he knew by necessity that this speech was the speech of Allah, it would be necessary for him to know by necessity the existence of Allah the Exalted, because it is impossible for an attribute to be known by necessity while the essence is known only by reasoning. And if Moses knew by necessity that it was Allah the Exalted, the obligation (taklif) would be removed.

It may be said that when He, the Exalted, made him hear the speech which is neither a letter nor a sound, he knew that such speech could not be the speech of created beings.

It may be said that the manifestation of speech from the tree is like the manifestation of glorification from pebbles, in that he would know that such a thing cannot occur except from Allah the Exalted.

It may be that the miracle was that he saw the fire in the green tree, and so he knew that no one can combine fire and the greenness of a tree except Allah the Exalted.

It may be that what is related is sound: that when Iblis said to him, "How did you know that it was the call of Allah the Exalted?" he said, "Because I heard it with all my parts." When he found the sensation of hearing from all the parts, he knew that this is something no one can do except Allah the Exalted. This holds only according to our position, where we say that a proof (bayyinah) is not a condition.

* * *

The third issue: In Surah al-Naml He said: ﴿Blessed is whoever is in the fire and whoever is around it﴾ (al-Naml: 8). Here He said: ﴿Indeed, I am Allah, the Lord of the worlds﴾, and in Ta-Ha He said: ﴿O Moses﴾ ﴿Indeed, I am your Lord﴾ (Ta-Ha: 11–12). There is no contradiction among these matters. He, the Exalted, mentioned all of it, but in each surah He related some of what that call contained.

The fourth issue: al-Hasan said that Moses, peace be upon him, was called with the call of revelation, not the call of speech. The evidence for this is His words: ﴿So listen to what is revealed﴾ (Ta-Ha: 13). The majority said: Allah the Exalted spoke to him without an intermediary. The evidence for this is His words: ﴿And Allah spoke to Moses directly﴾ (al-Nisa': 164), and the rest of the verses. As for what al-Hasan relied upon, it is weak, because His words ﴿So listen to what is revealed﴾ were not by revelation. For if that too were by revelation, the matter would end at a speech which the one under obligation hears not by revelation; otherwise an infinite regress would follow. Rather, what is meant by His words ﴿So listen to what is revealed﴾ is His charge that he should be steadfast in matters that will reach him in the future by revelation.

Regarding His statement: ﴿And throw down your staff. But when he saw it moving as if it were a snake, he turned back fleeing and did not return. "O Musa, come forward and do not fear. Indeed, you are among the secure."﴾ The interpretation of all of this has already been given. His statement ﴿as if it were a snake﴾ clearly indicates that He likened it to a snake; it does not say that it was in itself a snake. Therefore this does not contradict its being a serpent (thu'ban). Rather, He likened it to a snake in terms of its quivering and movement, not in terms of its size. The discussion of his fear has already been covered. The meaning of ﴿did not return﴾ is that he did not come back. It is said: "'aqqaba al-muqatil" when a fighter charges again after fleeing. Wahb said: "It left no tree or rock without swallowing it, until Musa, peace be upon him, heard the grinding of its teeth and heard the crunching of rocks in its belly. At that point he turned and fled."

The scholars differed concerning the staff in several respects:

First: They said that Shu'ayb had the staves of the prophets, peace be upon them. He told Musa at night: "When you enter that room, take one staff from those staves." So he took a staff that Adam, peace be upon him, had descended with from Paradise, and the prophets had continued to inherit it until it came to Shu'ayb, peace be upon him. Shu'ayb said: "Show me the staff," and he touched it. Shu'ayb was blind, so he was reluctant to give it up and said: "Take another instead." But nothing came into his hand except that one, seven times. So he knew that it had a special status with him. It is also narrated that Shu'ayb, peace be upon him, instructed his daughter to bring a staff for Musa, peace be upon him. She entered the room, took the staff and brought it to him. When the old man saw it he said: "Bring him another." She threw it down and tried to take another, but no other came into her hand. When the old man saw this he was content with it, but afterward he regretted it and went out seeking Musa, peace be upon him. When he met him he said: "Give me the staff." Musa said: "It is my staff," and he refused to give it to him, so they disputed. Then they agreed to make the first man who met them the judge between them. An angel came walking, and he judged between them, saying: "Put it on the ground. Whoever lifts it, it is his." The old man tried to lift it but could not, while Musa, peace be upon him, lifted it easily. So the old man left it to him and tended sheep for him for ten years.

Second: Ibn Salih narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: In the house of Bayrun, the son of Shu'ayb's brother, there was a room that no one entered except Bayrun and his daughter whom he married to Musa, peace be upon him. She used to sweep it and clean it. In that room there were thirteen staves, and Bayrun had eleven sons. Whenever one of them reached maturity, he would order him to enter the room and bring out one of those staves. One day Musa returned to his home and did not find his family, and he needed a staff for herding, so he entered that room, took a staff from those staves and went out with it. When the woman learned of this, she went to her father and informed him. Bayrun was pleased and said to her: "Indeed, this husband of yours is a prophet, and he has a special status with this staff."

Third: Some reports state that when Musa, peace be upon him, concluded the contract with Shu'ayb, and it was morning, and he wished to herd, Shu'ayb, peace be upon him, said to him: "Go with these sheep. When you reach the fork in the road, take the left and do not take the right, even if the pasture is richer that way, for there is a great dragon (tinnin) there, and I fear for you and the sheep from it." Musa went with the sheep, and when he reached the fork in the road, the sheep turned to the right. Musa strove to turn them back but could not, so he followed their trail and found abundant grass. Then Musa, peace be upon him, slept while the sheep were grazing, and suddenly the dragon came. Musa's staff rose up and fought it until it killed it, and then returned to Musa's side, bloodied. When Musa, peace be upon him, awoke, he saw the staff bloodied and the dragon slain, and he was relieved by that, and he knew that God, exalted is He, had power and a sign in that staff. He returned to Shu'ayb, peace be upon him, who was blind, and he touched the sheep, and they were in better condition than before. He asked him about this, and Musa, peace be upon him, told him the story. Shu'ayb rejoiced at this and knew that Musa, peace be upon him, and his staff had a special status. He wished to reward Musa, peace be upon him, for his good herding, out of honor and as a gift to his daughter, so he said: "I have granted you from the young that my sheep bear this year every spotted and white-spotted one." God, exalted is He, then revealed to Musa, peace be upon him, that he should strike the water from which the sheep drink with his staff. He did so and then gave the sheep to drink from it, and not one of them failed to give birth to its young, all of them being spotted and white-spotted. Shu'ayb then knew that this was a provision that God, exalted is He, had sent to Musa, peace be upon him, and his wife, so he fulfilled his condition for him.

Fourth: Some said: That staff was the staff of Adam, peace be upon him, and Jibril, peace be upon him, took that staff after Adam's death, and it remained with him until Musa, peace be upon him, met his Lord with it at night.

Fifth: Al-Hasan said: It was only a staff of wood that he picked up haphazardly (i'tirādan), meaning he took it from among the random wood. It is said: "i'taraḍa" when one does not choose carefully. And from al-Kalbi: The tree from which he was called was the tree of al-'awsaj (a thorny shrub), and his staff was from it.

There is no certainty in preferring one of these opinions over another, because nothing in the Qur'an indicates any of them, and the reports conflict. God knows best about them.

[Page 211]

Regarding His words, may He be exalted: ﴿Insert your hand into your bosom; it will come out white, without harm﴾, know that Allah, exalted is He, has expressed this meaning in three expressions.

The first of them is this one.

The second is His words in Ta-Ha: ﴿And draw your hand to your side; it will come out white﴾ [Ta-Ha: 22].

The third is His words in an-Naml: ﴿And insert your hand into your bosom﴾ [an-Naml: 12]. Al-Azizi said in Gharib al-Qur'an: ﴿Usluk yadaka fi jaybika﴾ means insert it into it (the bosom).

As for His words: ﴿And draw your wing to you against fear﴾, the best of people in speaking about it is the author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari), who said: it has two meanings.

The first: when Allah turned the staff into a serpent for him, Musa, peace be upon him, was frightened and agitated, and he shielded himself with his hand as a frightened person does from something. It was said to him: shielding yourself with your hand carries a disgrace before the enemies; so when you cast it down and it turns into a serpent, insert your hand under your armpit in place of shielding yourself with it, then bring it out white, so that two things are achieved: avoiding what is a disgrace to you, and displaying another miracle. The "wing" here means the hand, because a person's hands are like the two wings of a bird; and when he inserts his right hand under his left armpit, he has drawn his wing to himself.

The second: that by drawing his wing to himself is meant his steadfastness, his self-restraint and his firmness when the staff turns into a serpent, so that he does not become agitated and does not dread. It is a metaphor borrowed from the action of a bird, for when it fears it spreads its wings and loosens them; otherwise its wings are folded to it and held close. The meaning of His words ﴿from the fear﴾ is: if dread befalls you at the sight of the serpent, then draw your wing to you. His words ﴿Insert your hand into your bosom﴾ are, according to one of the two interpretations, one and the same; but the two expressions are varied because the purposes differ, for the purpose of one is the hand coming out white, and the purpose of the second is the removal of fear. If it is said: the wing, which is the hand, has been described in one place as "folded" and in another as "drawn to" (something), namely His words ﴿And draw your wing to you﴾ and His words ﴿And draw your hand to your wing﴾, then how is the harmony between them? We say: by the folded wing is meant the right hand, and by that to which it is drawn is the left hand; each of the two hands' right and left is a wing. This is all the words of the author of al-Kashshaf, and it is of the utmost excellence.

As for His words, exalted is He: ﴿So these two﴾, it has been read with light and with heavy emphasis. The light reading is the dual of (dha), and the heavy reading is the dual of (dhanin). His words ﴿are two proofs from your Lord﴾: two clear arguments for his truthfulness in prophethood and for the soundness of what he called them to of monotheism. The apparent sense of the speech requires that Allah commanded him with this before meeting Pharaoh, so that he knew what miracles he would display before him, because Allah, exalted is He, afterwards related of Musa, peace be upon him, that he said: ﴿I killed a soul from among them, so I fear that they will kill me﴾. The judge (al-Qadi) said: if that is so, then at the time of the manifestation of the two proofs there must have been someone there from his family or others who invited him to his mission, since miracles only appear upon messengers at the time of sending, not before it, and they appear so that others may be guided by them to the message. This is weak; for it has been established that there must be wisdom in the manifestation of a miracle, and there is no greater wisdom than that others be guided by it to the truthfulness of the claimant. As for the claim that there is no wisdom here, we do not concede it; there may be other kinds of wisdoms and purposes besides that, especially since these verses agree that there was no one with Musa, peace be upon him, at that time.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 28, verses 33–37:**

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿He said, "My Lord, I killed a soul from them, so I fear that they will kill me. And my brother Harun, he is more eloquent in tongue than me, so send him with me as a supporter, to confirm me. Indeed, I fear that they will deny me."﴾ ﴿He said, "We will strengthen your arm through your brother, and We will grant you both authority, so they will not reach you. By Our signs, you and whoever follows you will be the victorious."﴾ ﴿So when Musa came to them with Our clear signs, they said, "This is nothing but fabricated magic, and we have not heard of this among our first forefathers."﴾ ﴿And Musa said, "My Lord knows best who has come with guidance from Him and whose will be the good outcome of the abode. Indeed, the wrongdoers will not succeed."﴾

[p. 213]

Know that when Allah the Exalted said, ﴿So these two are proofs from your Lord to Pharaoh and his chiefs﴾, this implied that Musa should go to Pharaoh and his people with these two proofs. At that point, he asked Allah the Exalted for what would strengthen his heart and remove his fear. So he said, ﴿My Lord, I killed a soul from them, so I fear that they will kill me.﴾ ﴿And my brother Harun, he is more eloquent in tongue than me.﴾ This is because there was a speech impediment (ḥubsah) in his tongue, either from his natural creation or because he placed a burning coal in his mouth when he plucked Pharaoh's beard.

The evidence for this is His saying, the Exalted: (﴿For them is the good outcome of the abode﴾ ﴿Gardens of Eden﴾ [al-Ra'd: 22–23]) and His saying: ﴿And the disbelievers will know to whom belongs the good outcome of the abode﴾ [al-Ra'd: 42]. The "abode" here means the worldly life, and its outcome and final end is that the servant be sealed with mercy, good pleasure, and the angels receiving him with glad tidings at death. Whoever acts in it contrary to what Allah set it for has distorted it. Thus its original outcome is the outcome of good, and as for the outcome of evil, it is not counted, because it is a result of the distortion of the wicked. Then he, peace be upon him, emphasized this by his saying: ﴿Indeed, the wrongdoers will not succeed﴾. The meaning is that they will not attain success, salvation, and benefits, but will obtain the opposite of that. This is the utmost in warning them against the obstinacy that has appeared from them.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 28, verses 33–37:**

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿He said, "My Lord, I killed a soul from them, so I fear that they will kill me. And my brother Harun, he is more eloquent in tongue than me, so send him with me as a supporter, to confirm me. Indeed, I fear that they will deny me."﴾ ﴿He said, "We will strengthen your arm through your brother, and We will grant you both authority, so they will not reach you. By Our signs, you and whoever follows you will be the victorious."﴾ ﴿So when Musa came to them with Our clear signs, they said, "This is nothing but fabricated magic, and we have not heard of this among our first forefathers."﴾ ﴿And Musa said, "My Lord knows best who has come with guidance from Him and whose will be the good outcome of the abode. Indeed, the wrongdoers will not succeed."﴾

[p. 213]

Know that when Allah the Exalted said, ﴿So these two are proofs from your Lord to Pharaoh and his chiefs﴾, this implied that Musa should go to Pharaoh and his people with these two proofs. At that point, he asked Allah the Exalted for what would strengthen his heart and remove his fear. The first discussion: *ridʾ* (رِدْء) is a name for that by which one is helped. It is a noun in the sense of a passive object, just as *difʾ* (دِفْء) is a name for that by which one is warmed. It is said: *radaʾtu al-ḥāʾiṭa arduʾuhu* (رَدَأْتُ الحائِطَ أرْدَؤُهُ) when you prop up a wall with wood or other material so that it does not fall.

The second discussion: Nafi' read *ridʾan* without a hamza, while the others read it with a hamza. ʿĀṣim and Ḥamzah read *yuṣaddiqunī* (يُصَدِّقُنِي) with a raised *qāf* (i.e., indicative, *rafʿ*), and this is also related from Abu ʿAmr, while the rest read it with a jussive *qāf* (*jazm*), which is the well-known reading from Abu ʿAmr. Whoever reads it with *rafʿ*, the implied meaning is: "a supporter who confirms me." Whoever reads it with *jazm* understands it in the sense of a conditional: "if you send him, he will confirm me." A parallel to this is His saying, ﴿So grant me from Yourself an heir﴾ ﴿who will inherit me﴾ (Maryam: 5–6), with the *thāʾ* of *yarithunī* jussive. The third discussion: The majority hold that the confirmation is for Harun. Muqatil said: the meaning is "so that Pharaoh may believe me," and the meaning is: send my brother with me so that he may support me in manifesting the argument and clarity; when the two proofs are combined, the intended result, that Pharaoh confirms him, may perhaps be achieved.

The fourth discussion: The purpose of Harun's confirmation is not that he would say to him, "You are right," or that he would say to the people, "Musa speaks the truth." Rather, it is that he would, with his eloquent tongue, summarize the aspects of the proofs, answer doubts, and argue with the disbelievers with it. This is the beneficial confirmation. قَوْلُهُ تَعالى: ﴿وقالَ فِرْعَوْنُ يا أيُّهَا المَلَأُ ما عَلِمْتُ لَكُمْ مِن إلَهٍ غَيْرِي فَأوْقِدْ لِي يا هامانُ عَلى الطِّينِ فاجْعَلْ لِي صَرْحًا لَعَلِّي أطَّلِعُ إلى إلَهِ مُوسى وإنِّي لَأظُنُّهُ مِنَ الكاذِبِينَ﴾ ﴿واسْتَكْبَرَ هو وجُنُودُهُ في الأرْضِ بِغَيْرِ الحَقِّ وظَنُّوا أنَّهم إلَيْنا لا يُرْجَعُونَ﴾ ﴿فَأخَذْناهُ وجُنُودَهُ فَنَبَذْناهُمْ في اليَمِّ فانْظُرْ كَيْفَ كانَ عاقِبَةُ الظّالِمِينَ﴾ ﴿وجَعَلْناهُمْ أئِمَّةً يَدْعُونَ إلى النّارِ ويَوْمَ القِيامَةِ لا يُنْصَرُونَ﴾ ﴿وأتْبَعْناهُمْ في هَذِهِ الدُّنْيا لَعْنَةً ويَوْمَ القِيامَةِ هم مِنَ المَقْبُوحِينَ﴾ ﴿ولَقَدْ آتَيْنا مُوسى الكِتابَ مِن بَعْدِ ما أهْلَكْنا القُرُونَ الأُولى بَصائِرَ لِلنّاسِ وهُدًى ورَحْمَةً لَعَلَّهُمْ يَتَذَكَّرُونَ﴾

Let me know that Pharaoh's habit, whenever the proof of Musa appeared, was to resort, in repelling that proof, to a dubious argument (shubhah) that he would circulate among his foolish people. Here he mentions two such doubts.

The first: his saying ﴿ما عَلِمْتُ لَكُمْ مِن إلَهٍ غَيْرِي﴾ ("I know of no god for you other than me"). In reality this comprises two statements:

First, the denial of any god other than himself.

Second, the affirmation of his own divinity.

As for the first, his reliance was on the principle that what has no proof cannot be affirmed. That there is no proof for it is because these stars and spheres suffice for the variation of the conditions of this lower world, so there is no need to affirm a Creator. As for the principle that what has no proof cannot be affirmed, the matter in it is clear.

But know that the first premise is false. We do not accept that there is no proof for the existence of the Creator. For when we know by proof that bodies are originated (ḥudūth), we know the origination of the spheres and stars, and we know by necessity that what is originated must have an originator. Then, at that point,

[Page 216]

we know by proof that this world has a Creator. What is strange is that a group relied, in denying many things, on saying: "There is no proof for it, so its denial is obligatory." They said: "We only said there is no proof because we searched and examined and found no proof for it." The upshot of their statement, after verification, comes to this: every thing for which no proof is known must be denied. Pharaoh, however, did not assert the denial with certainty; rather he said: "There is no proof for it, so I do not affirm it, but I think he is lying in his claim." Thus Pharaoh, at the height of his ignorance, is in a better state than this inferring person.

As for the second, namely his affirmation of his own divinity, know that what is meant by it is not that he claimed to be the creator of the heavens, the earth, the seas, the mountains, and the essences and attributes of people. For knowledge of the impossibility of that is among the first intellects, so doubt about it would imply the loss of reason. Rather, "god" (ilāh) means the one worshipped. So the man was denying the Creator and saying: "There is no obligation upon people except that they obey their king and submit to his command." This is what is meant by his claim to divinity, not what the masses supposed, namely that he claimed to be the creator of the sky and earth. Especially since we have demonstrated, in Surah Ṭāhā, in the commentary on his saying ﴿فَمَن رَبُّكُما يا مُوسى﴾ ("Who then is your Lord, O Musa?") [Ṭā Hā 20:49], that he was knowing of God, Exalted, and that he was saying that to deceive the foolish among the people.

The second doubt: his saying ﴿فَأوْقِدْ لِي يا هامانُ عَلى الطِّينِ فاجْعَلْ لِي صَرْحًا لَعَلِّي أطَّلِعُ إلى إلَهِ مُوسى وإنِّي لَأظُنُّهُ مِنَ الكاذِبِينَ﴾. Here there are several discussions.

The first: the anthropomorphists (al-Mushabbihah, those who liken God to creatures) cling to this verse to claim that God is in the sky. They said: "Had Musa, peace be upon him, not called to that, Pharaoh would not have said this statement." The reply: Musa, peace be upon him, indicated to Pharaoh by his saying ﴿رَبُّ السَّماواتِ والأرْضِ﴾ ("Lord of the heavens and the earth") and did not say: "He is the one who is in the sky rather than the earth." So Pharaoh gave the impression that he was saying his god is in the sky. This too is from the cunning, deceit and craftiness of Pharaoh.

The second: they differed as to whether Pharaoh actually built this tower (ṣarḥ). Some said he built it. They said: when he ordered the building of the tower, Hāmān gathered the workers until fifty thousand builders were assembled, besides the followers and hired laborers. He ordered the baking of bricks, the plastering with gypsum, the carving of wood, and the driving of nails. They raised it until it reached a height no structure of any creature had reached. Then God, Exalted, sent Gabriel, peace be upon him, at sunset; he struck it with his wing and cut it into three pieces. One piece fell upon Pharaoh's army and killed a million men; one piece fell into the sea; and one piece fell into the west. None of his workers remained but that he perished. It is also narrated in this story that Pharaoh ascended to its top and shot an arrow toward the sky. God wanted to test them, so it was returned to them smeared with blood. He said: "I have killed the god of Musa." At that, God, Exalted, sent Gabriel, peace be upon him, to demolish it.

Some people said: he did not build that tower, because it is far-fetched for intelligent people to think that by ascending the tower they would come near the sky, while knowing that whoever is on the top of high mountains sees the sky just as he saw it when he was on the ground. Whoever doubts this has left the bounds of reason. The same applies to what is said about the shooting of an arrow toward the sky and its return smeared with blood, for every person of sound mind knows that it is impossible to make an arrow reach the sky, and that whoever attempts this is a madman. It is not fitting for reason and religion to take the story that God related in the Qur'an as meaning something whose falsehood is known by necessity of reason, for that would become a strong avenue for those who wish to attack the Qur'an. Rather, the closer view is that he only pretended to build and did not build, or that this was part of his saying ﴿ما عَلِمْتُ لَكُمْ مِن إلَهٍ غَيْرِي﴾, meaning: there is no way to affirm Him by proof, since the movements of the stars suffice for the change of this world, and there is no way to affirm Him by the senses, since sensing Him is impossible except after ascending to the sky, and that is not something attainable. Then he said at that point to Hāmān: ﴿ابْنِ لِي صَرْحًا لَعَلِّي أبْلُغُ الأسْبابَ * أسْبابَ السَّماواتِ﴾ ("Build for me a tower that I may reach the ways, the ways of the heavens") [Ghāfir 40:36-37]. He said that only by way of mockery. By the sum of these matters, he established that there is no proof for the Creator. Then he arranged the conclusion upon it, saying:

[Page 217]

﴿وإنِّي لَأظُنُّهُ مِنَ الكاذِبِينَ﴾ ("And indeed I think him to be among the liars"). This interpretation is preferable to what is other than it.

The third: he said ﴿فَأوْقِدْ لِي يا هامانُ عَلى الطِّينِ﴾ ("Kindle for me, O Hāmān, a fire upon the clay") and did not say: "Bake the bricks for me and make them." This is because he was the first to make bricks, so he was teaching him the craft. Also, this expression is more fitting to the eloquence of the Qur'an and more similar to the speech of tyrants. He commanded Hāmān, his vizier, to kindle the fire upon the clay. Calling his name with "yā" (O) in the middle of the speech is a sign of exaltation and arrogance. The verbs ṭalaʿa (to ascend) and iṭṭalaʿa (to look upon/mount) mean ascending; one says "ṭalaʿa al-jabal" and "iṭṭalaʿa" with one meaning.

As for his saying ﴿واسْتَكْبَرَ هو وجُنُودُهُ في الأرْضِ بِغَيْرِ الحَقِّ﴾ ("He and his soldiers acted arrogantly in the land without right"), know that arrogance (kibriyāʾ) in truth belongs only to God, Exalted, and He is the Mutakabbir in the true sense, that is, the one who is extreme in the greatness of His standing. He, peace be upon him, said, relating what he related from his Lord: "Greatness is My cloak and majesty is My garment; whoever contends with Me over either of them, I will cast into the Fire." Every other arrogant person's arrogance is without right.

* * *

Second issue: al-Jubbāʾī (Abū ʿAlī al-Jubbāʾī, the Muʿtazilī theologian) said: the verse indicates that God did not give him the kingdom, for otherwise that would be by right, and likewise every usurper. This is unlike what the kings of the Banu Umayyah claimed when they gained dominance, that their kingdom was from God, Exalted. For God, Exalted, has made clear regarding every usurper of God's judgment that he took that without right. Know that this is weak, because the arrival of that kingdom to him either came from himself, or from God, Exalted, or from neither himself nor God, Exalted. If it came from himself, then why was no one else able to attain it? Often the weaker person is much stronger and wiser than the one who holds the affair. If it came from God, Exalted, then the point is established. If it came from the rest of the people, then why did the people's motives converge upon supporting one of them and abandoning the other? Know that this is clearer than that a person of sound mind could doubt it.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 28, verses 39–43:**

As for His saying, ﴿And they thought that they would not be returned to Us﴾, this indicates that they knew God, exalted is He, but they denied the Resurrection, and for this reason they rebelled and transgressed.

As for His saying, ﴿So We seized him and his hosts, and cast them into the sea﴾, this is from the awe-inspiring kind of speech by which He shows the greatness of His affair and the majesty of His dominion. He likened them, belittling them and making their number seem insignificant, though they were the great, the numerous, and the vast multitude, to pebbles that someone takes in his palm and throws into the sea, and the like. His saying, ﴿And We placed in it firm, towering mountains﴾, ﴿and the earth and the mountains are lifted and crushed with one blow﴾, ﴿They did not measure God with His true measure, while the whole earth will be His handful on the Day of Resurrection, and the heavens will be folded up in His right hand﴾, exalted is He, has no purpose except to depict that everything within capability, however great, is insignificant in comparison with His power.

As for His saying, ﴿And We made them leaders calling to the Fire﴾, the Companions (i.e. the Mu'tazila) have relied on it to argue that He, exalted is He, is the creator of good and evil. Al-Jubba'i said: the meaning of His saying ﴿And We made them﴾ is that We made clear this about their condition and named them by it. Among its parallels is His saying, ﴿And they made the angels, who are servants of the Most Merciful, females﴾ (al-Zukhruf 43:19). The people of language, in explaining "fasaqahu" and "bakhkhalahu," say: "he made him a wrongdoer (fasiq) and a miser (bakhil)," not that He created them as leaders, because at the time of their creation they were children. Al-Ka'bi said: He only said ﴿And We made them leaders﴾ because He allowed them to be free to do what they did and did not hasten punishment against them, and because they disbelieved and He did not prevent them by compulsion. This is like His saying, ﴿So it increased them in uncleanness﴾ (al-Tawba 9:125), since they increased in it at that time. A parallel to this is that a man is asked for something that is burdensome to him, and though he is able to give it, he withholds it; then it is said to the one asking: "You made so-and-so a miser," meaning: "I made him stingy." Abu Muslim said: the meaning of leadership (imama) is precedence. When God hastened the punishment for them, they became precursors for those among the disbelievers who came after them.

Know that the discussion of this has already preceded in surah Maryam, in His saying, ﴿We sent the devils upon the disbelievers﴾ (Maryam 19:83). The meaning of calling them to the Fire is calling them to what necessitates it of disbelief and sins, for no one at all calls to the Fire. God made them leaders in this domain because they reached the utmost extremes in it, and whoever is like that deserves to be a leader who is followed in that domain. Then God made clear that this punishment will befall them in a manner from which escape is impossible, and this is the meaning of His saying, ﴿and on the Day of Resurrection they will not be helped﴾. Or its meaning may be: ﴿and on the Day of Resurrection they will not be helped﴾, as He helps the leaders who call to Paradise.
* * *
As for His saying, ﴿And they were followed in this world by a curse﴾, its meaning is the curse of God and of the angels upon them, and His command to the believers to curse them in this world. He made clear that on the Day of Resurrection they will be among the reviled (al-maqbuhin), that is, the banished and cursed. Qubh (reviling) is distancing. Al-Layth said: it is said, "qabbahahu Allah," meaning He removed him from every good. Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with him and his father, said: they will be among those marked by blackened faces and blue eyes. In sum, the first group understood qubh as spiritual qubh, which is expulsion and distancing from the mercy of God, exalted is He, while the rest understood it as ugliness in appearance.

It has also been said: God makes their forms ugly and makes their deeds ugly upon them, and He combines the two disgraces.

Then God, exalted is He, made clear that what must be held fast to is what Moses, peace be upon him, brought. He said: ﴿And We gave Moses the Book after We had destroyed the earlier generations﴾. The Book is the Torah. God described it as ﴿insights for mankind﴾, in that by it one gains insight in matters of religion; and as ﴿guidance﴾, in that one is guided by it; and in that whoever holds fast to it attains his goal of reward. He described it as ﴿mercy﴾, because it is one of the blessings of God upon whoever worships by it. Abu Sa'id al-Khudri narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "God, exalted is He, has not destroyed any generation of generations with a punishment from the heavens or from the earth since He sent down the Torah, except the people of the town whom He transformed into apes."

As for His saying, ﴿So that they may remember﴾, the meaning is: in order that they may remember. The Qadi said: this indicates the will of remembrance from every accountable person, whether he chooses it or does not choose it. Therefore it refutes the doctrine of the Mujbira (those who hold that man is compelled), who say: "He did not will remembrance except from one who remembers; as for one who does not remember, He has disliked that from him." But the text of the Qur'an refutes this view. We say: Did you not interpret His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And We have created many of the jinn and humans for Hell﴾ (al-A'raf 7:179), as referring to the outcome? Then why not interpret it here as referring to the outcome? For the outcome for all is the attainment of this remembrance, and that is in the Hereafter.

Abu Sa'id al-Khudri narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "God, exalted is He, has not destroyed any generation of generations with a punishment from the heavens or from the earth since He sent down the Torah, except the people of the town whom He transformed into apes."

As for His saying, ﴿So that they may remember﴾, the meaning is: in order that they may remember. The Qadi said: this indicates the will of remembrance from every accountable person, whether he chooses it or does not choose it. Therefore it refutes the doctrine of the Mujbira (those who hold that man is compelled), who say: "He did not will remembrance except from one who remembers; as for one who does not remember, He has disliked that from him." But the text of the Qur'an refutes this view. We say: Did you not interpret His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And We have created many of the jinn and humans for Hell﴾ (al-A'raf 7:179), as referring to the outcome? Then why not interpret it here as referring to the outcome? For the outcome for all is the attainment of this remembrance, and that is in the Hereafter.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 28, verses 39–43:**

As for His saying, ﴿And they thought that they would not be returned to Us﴾, this indicates that they knew God, exalted is He, but they denied the Resurrection, and for this reason they rebelled and transgressed.

As for His saying, ﴿So We seized him and his hosts, and cast them into the sea﴾, this is from the awe-inspiring kind of speech by which He shows the greatness of His affair and the majesty of His dominion. He likened them, belittling them and making their number seem insignificant, though they were the great, the numerous, and the vast multitude, to pebbles that someone takes in his palm and throws into the sea, and the like. His saying, ﴿And We placed in it firm, towering mountains﴾, ﴿and the earth and the mountains are lifted and crushed with one blow﴾, ﴿They did not measure God with His true measure, while the whole earth will be His handful on the Day of Resurrection, and the heavens will be folded up in His right hand﴾, exalted is He, has no purpose except to depict that everything within capability, however great, is insignificant in comparison with His power.

As for His saying, ﴿And We made them leaders calling to the Fire﴾, the Companions (i.e. the Mu'tazila) have relied on it to argue that He, exalted is He, is the creator of good and evil. Al-Jubba'i said: the meaning of His saying ﴿And We made them﴾ is that We made clear this about their condition and named them by it. Among its parallels is His saying, ﴿And they made the angels, who are servants of the Most Merciful, females﴾ (al-Zukhruf 43:19). The people of language, in explaining "fasaqahu" and "bakhkhalahu," say: "he made him a wrongdoer (fasiq) and a miser (bakhil)," not that He created them as leaders, because at the time of their creation they were children. Al-Ka'bi said: He only said ﴿And We made them leaders﴾ because He allowed them to be free to do what they did and did not hasten punishment against them, and because they disbelieved and He did not prevent them by compulsion. This is like His saying, ﴿So it increased them in uncleanness﴾ (al-Tawba 9:125), since they increased in it at that time. A parallel to this is that a man is asked for something that is burdensome to him, and though he is able to give it, he withholds it; then it is said to the one asking: "You made so-and-so a miser," meaning: "I made him stingy." Abu Muslim said: the meaning of leadership (imama) is precedence. When God hastened the punishment for them, they became precursors for those among the disbelievers who came after them.

Know that the discussion of this has already preceded in surah Maryam, in His saying, ﴿We sent the devils upon the disbelievers﴾ (Maryam 19:83). The meaning of calling them to the Fire is calling them to what necessitates it of disbelief and sins, for no one at all calls to the Fire. God made them leaders in this domain because they reached the utmost extremes in it, and whoever is like that deserves to be a leader who is followed in that domain. Then God made clear that this punishment will befall them in a manner from which escape is impossible, and this is the meaning of His saying, ﴿and on the Day of Resurrection they will not be helped﴾. Or its meaning may be: ﴿and on the Day of Resurrection they will not be helped﴾, as He helps the leaders who call to Paradise.
* * *
As for His saying, ﴿And they were followed in this world by a curse﴾, its meaning is the curse of God and of the angels upon them, and His command to the believers to curse them in this world. He made clear that on the Day of Resurrection they will be among the reviled (al-maqbuhin), that is, the banished and cursed. Qubh (reviling) is distancing. Al-Layth said: it is said, "qabbahahu Allah," meaning He removed him from every good. Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with him and his father, said: they will be among those marked by blackened faces and blue eyes. In sum, the first group understood qubh as spiritual qubh, which is expulsion and distancing from the mercy of God, exalted is He, while the rest understood it as ugliness in appearance.

It has also been said: God makes their forms ugly and makes their deeds ugly upon them, and He combines the two disgraces.

[Page 219]

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿You were not on the western side when We decreed the command to Moses, nor were you among the witnesses﴾ ﴿But We produced generations, and the lifetime grew long for them. And you were not dwelling among the people of Madyan, reciting Our verses to them; but We were the ones who sent [messengers]﴾ ﴿And you were not on the side of the Mount when We called [to Moses]; but it is a mercy from your Lord, that you may warn a people to whom no warner had come before you, that they may remember﴾ ﴿And had it not been that a calamity might befall them for what their hands have sent forth, and they should say, "Our Lord, why did You not send to us a messenger so that we might follow Your verses and be among the believers?"﴾

Know that in this verse there are questions:

The first question: The "side" (al-jānib) is a qualified noun (mawṣūf), and "western" (al-gharbī) is a qualifier (ṣifah). How then is the qualified noun annexed to its qualifier?

The answer: This is a point of disagreement among the grammarians. According to the Basrans, it is not permissible to annex a qualified noun to its qualifier except under a specific condition that we shall mention. According to the Kufans, it is permissible in all cases. The argument of the Basrans is that annexing a qualified noun to its qualifier entails annexing a thing to itself, and this is impermissible, so that too is impermissible. The proof of the implication is that when you say, "Zayd the witty came to me," the word "witty" indicates a thing that is specific in itself, unknown from this word alone, to which wittiness has occurred. When you specify Zayd, we know that the thing to which wittiness has occurred is Zayd. If this is established, then if you annexed Zayd to "the witty," you would have annexed Zayd to Zayd, and annexing a thing to itself is impermissible. Therefore annexing a qualified noun to its attribute must also be impermissible. However, some expressions have come contrary to this rule, namely His saying in this verse, ﴿You were not on the western side﴾, and His saying: ﴿And that is the upright religion﴾ [al-Bayyinah: 5], and His saying: ﴿Indeed, this is the certain truth﴾ [al-Ḥāqqah: 51], ﴿And the home of the Hereafter﴾ [Yūsuf: 109]. It is also said: "the prayer of the first [time]," "the mosque of the congregation," and "the herb of the foolish [one]." They said the interpretation of these is: the side of the western place, the religion of the upright creed, the truth of the certain thing, the home of the final hour, the prayer of the first hour, the mosque of the congregational place, and the herb of the foolish seed. Then they said, in these instances, the annexed noun is not the qualifier but the qualified noun, except that the qualified noun has been omitted and the qualifier has been placed in its position. Here one looks: if that qualifier is as if specific to that qualified noun, it is acceptable; otherwise it is not. Do you not see that you may not say, "Indi jayyid" (I have something good) meaning "Indi dirham jayyid" (I have a good dirham)? But it is permissible to say, "Marartu bil-faqīh" (I passed by the jurist), meaning "Marartu bil-rajul al-faqīh" (I passed by the jurist man), because the jurist is known to be only among people, whereas "good" may be a dirham or other than a dirham. Since that is so, the phrase "the side of the western [place]" is acceptable, because the thing described as western to which the side is annexed can only be a place or something resembling it. Therefore this annexation is indeed acceptable, and the same applies to the rest. And Allah knows best.

The second question: What is the meaning of His saying: ﴿when We decreed the command to Moses﴾?

The answer: The western side is the place lying on the western side, and it is the place where Moses' appointed time at the Mount took place, and where Allah wrote [the commandments] on the tablets. The command decreed to Moses, peace be upon him, is the revelation that was revealed to him. The address is to the Messenger ﷺ. The meaning is: You were not present at the place where We revealed to Moses, peace be upon him, nor were you among those who witnessed the revelation to him, or witnessed the one to whom it was revealed. This is because a witness must necessarily be present, and they were his chosen men whom he selected for the appointed time.

The third question: Since He said, ﴿You were not on the western side﴾, it is established that he was not a witness, because a witness must be present. So what is the benefit of repeating His saying: ﴿nor were you among the witnesses﴾?

The answer: Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: The meaning is: you were not present at that place. Even had you been present, you would not have witnessed those events, for it is possible for one to be there and yet not witness and not see.

[Page 220]

The fourth question: How does His saying ﴿But We produced generations﴾ connect with this statement, and in what way is it an exception (istidrāk) to it?

The answer: The meaning of the verse is: But We produced, after the time of Moses, peace be upon him, until your time, many generations, and the lifetime grew long for them. This is the generation in which you are. The knowledge was effaced, so it became necessary to send you to them. So We sent you and informed you of the states of the prophets and the states of Moses. The summary is as if He said: You were not a witness to Moses and what happened to him, but We revealed it to you. He mentioned the cause of revelation, which is the lengthening of the interval (between prophets), and by it indicated the effect. Thus this exception is similar to the two exceptions after it. Know that this is an indication of the miraculous nature (of the Qur'an): it is as if He said, "In your reporting of these matters without presence, without witnessing, and without learning from its people, there is a clear proof of your prophethood," just as He said: ﴿Has there not come to them the clear evidence of what is in the earlier scriptures?﴾ [Ṭāhā: 133].

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 28, verse 45–46:

As for His saying, ﴿Nor were you a dweller among the people of Madyan﴾, the meaning is: you were not residing among them.

* * *

As for His saying, ﴿reciting to them Our verses﴾, there are two views concerning it:

The first: Muqatil said: It means, you did not witness the people of Madyan, so that you could recite to the people of Makkah their news. ﴿But We were sending messengers﴾, i.e., We sent you to the people of Makkah and revealed these reports to you; had it not been for that, you would not have known them.

The second: al-Dahhak said: It means, O Muhammad, you were not the messenger to the people of Madyan reciting the Book to them; rather it was someone other than you. ﴿But We were sending messengers﴾ in every age, a messenger; so We sent Shu'ayb to the people of Madyan, and We sent you to the Arabs so that you would be the seal of the Prophets.

As for His saying, ﴿Nor were you at the side of the Tur when We called﴾, it refers to God's calling out to Musa on the night of the intimate conversation (munajat) and His speaking to him. ﴿But it was a mercy from your Lord﴾, i.e., We taught you as a mercy. 'Isa ibn 'Umar read it in the nominative (raf'), meaning: it is a mercy. The exegetes mentioned other interpretations of His saying, ﴿when We called﴾:

One of them: "when We called" means, We said to Musa: ﴿My mercy encompasses all things﴾ [al-A'raf: 156] up to His saying: ﴿those are the successful﴾ [al-A'raf: 157].

The second: Ibn 'Abbas said: "when We called" means, when We called your community in the loins of their fathers: "O community of Muhammad, I answered you before you called upon Me, I gave you before you asked Me, and I forgave you before you sought forgiveness from Me." He said: God the Exalted only said that when He chose Musa, peace be upon him, seventy men for the appointed time of his Lord.

The third: Wahb said: "When God mentioned to Musa the virtue of the community of Muhammad ﷺ, he said: 'My Lord, show them to me.' He said: 'You will not reach them, but if You wish I will let you hear their voices.' He said: 'Yes, my Lord.' So He, glory be to Him, said: 'O community of Muhammad,' and they answered Him from the loins of their fathers. Then God the Exalted let him hear their voices, and then said: 'I answered you before you call upon Me'..." the hadith as mentioned by Ibn 'Abbas.

The fourth: Sahl ibn Sa'd narrated, he said: The Messenger of God ﷺ said regarding His saying, ﴿Nor were you at the side of the Tur when We called﴾, he said: "God wrote a Book two thousand years before He created the creation, then placed it upon the Throne, then called out: 'O community of Muhammad, indeed My mercy has preceded My wrath. I gave you before you asked Me, and I forgave you before you sought forgiveness from Me. Whoever meets Me among you, testifying that there is no god but God and that Muhammad is His servant and messenger, I will admit him into Paradise.'"

As for His saying, ﴿that you may warn a people to whom no warner had come before you﴾, warning (al-indhar) is the instilling of fear of punishment for disobedience. Know that when He, the Exalted, explained the story of Musa, peace be upon him, He said to His Messenger: ﴿Nor were you at the western side﴾, ﴿Nor were you a dweller among the people of Madyan﴾, ﴿Nor were you at the side of the Tur﴾. God combined all of these, because these three situations were the great states that befell Musa, peace be upon him; for by His saying, ﴿when We decreed to Musa the command﴾, is meant the sending down of the Torah until his religion was complete and his law was established; by His saying, ﴿Nor were you a dweller﴾ is meant the early part of his affair; and by "We called to him" is meant the middle of his affair, which was the night of intimate conversation. When God the Exalted had explained that he, peace be upon him, was not present during these situations, He explained that He had sent him and made him aware of these situations as a mercy to the worlds.

Some said: no warner from among them had been sent to them. Some said: the proof of the prophets had been established over them, but He had not sent anyone to renew that proof over them. Others said: it is not improbable that there was an interval (fatrah) in the obligations, so God the Exalted sent him to confirm the obligations and to remove that interval.
