Regarding His words, ﴿But had it not been that a calamity should befall them﴾ to the end of the verse. The author of *al-Kashshaf* said: The first *law* (لولا, "if not that") is *imtina'iyyah* (expressing the non-fulfilment of a condition due to the non-existence of its consequent), and its response (*jawab*) is omitted. The second *law* is *tahdiyyah* (expressing urging). The *fa'* in His words ﴿then they would say﴾ is for coordination (*'atf*), and the *fa'* in His words ﴿and we would follow﴾ is the response of *law*, because it has the force of a command, since a command prompts an action, and prompting and urging belong to the same category. The meaning is: "Had it not been that they would say, when they are punished for what they have sent ahead of shirk and sins, 'Why did You not send to us a messenger?', arguing against Us with that, We would not have sent a messenger to them." That is, We sent the messenger to remove this excuse. This is like His words: ﴿so that mankind will have no argument against Allah after the messengers﴾ and ﴿lest you say, "There came to us no bringer of good tidings and no warner"﴾ and ﴿Why did You not send to us a messenger, so that we might follow Your signs?﴾. Know that He, exalted is He, did not say, "Had it not been that they would make this excuse, We would not have sent," but rather He said, ﴿But had it not been that a calamity should befall them﴾ ﴿then they would say﴾ "This is the enemy," (and so forth) "We would not have sent." He only said that for a subtle reason, which is that if they were not punished, for example, while they had known the falsehood of their religion, they would not have said that. Rather, they only say that when punishment reaches them. This indicates that they did not mention this excuse out of regret for their disbelief, but because they could not bear it. It also alerts to the firmness and deep-rootedness of their disbelief, like His words: ﴿And if they were returned, they would return to what they were forbidden﴾ [al-An'am: 28].

* * *

In the verse there are issues:

**First issue:** Al-Jubba'i (al-Jubba'i) argued for the obligation of *lutf* (divine grace, meaning acts that move a person toward obedience). He said: If that were not obligatory, they would have no right to say, "Why did You not send to us a messenger so that we might follow Your signs?", since it would be permissible for Him not to send to them, even if they would not choose faith except by it, according to the view of the one who differs about the obligation of *lutf*, just as it has passed that what is possible, if it is known that were it created for him it would be impossible except that He would do that.

* * *

**Second issue:** Al-Ka'bi (al-Ka'bi) argued by it that God, exalted is He, accepts the argument of the servants, and the matter is not as Ahl al-Sunnah (the People of the Sunnah) say, that He, exalted is He, does not accept argument. It becomes clear from this that the meaning of His words ﴿He cannot be questioned about what He does﴾ [al-Anbiya': 23] is not what Ahl al-Sunnah suppose. And if it is established that He accepts argument, it is necessary that the act of the servant not be by the creation of God, exalted is He, for otherwise the disbeliever would have the greatest argument against God, exalted is He.

* * *

**Third issue:** The Qadi (al-Qadi) said: In it there is a refutation of the doctrine of *jabr* (compulsion, the view that human acts are wholly predetermined by God) from several aspects:

First: Their following and their faith depend on God creating that in them, whether He sends the messenger to them or not.

Second: If He creates the capacity for that in them, it is necessary, whether He sends the messenger or not.

Third: If He wills that, it is necessary, whether He sends the messenger to them or not. So what is the benefit in their saying this, if their acts were the creation of God, exalted is He?

It is said to the Qadi: Suppose you dispute about the creation and the will, but you agree about knowledge. So when He knows that they will disbelieve, is it necessary or not? If it is not necessary, then it would be possible for disbelief not to occur while knowledge of it is present, and that is a combining of two opposites. And if it is necessary, then what you raised against us binds you. Know that although the argument is strong and good, nevertheless, when it faces an objection (*naqd*) from which there is no escape, how can a reasonable person be content to rely upon it?

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 28, verses 48–55 (part 1 of 2)**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So when the truth came to them from Us, they said, "Why was he not given the like of what was given to Moses?" Did they not disbelieve in what was given to Moses before? They said, "Two kinds of magic supporting each other," and they said, "Indeed, we disbelieve in all of them."﴾ ﴿Say, "Then bring a Book from Allah that is better guidance than both of them, and I will follow it, if you are truthful."﴾ ﴿But if they do not respond to you, then know that they only follow their desires. And who is more astray than one who follows his desire without guidance from Allah? Indeed, Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people.﴾ ﴿And We have certainly conveyed to them the word, so that they may remember.﴾ ﴿Those to whom We gave the Book before it, they believe in it.﴾ ﴿And when it is recited to them, they say, "We believe in it. Indeed, it is the truth from our Lord. Indeed, we were Muslims [submitting] before it."﴾ ﴿Those will be given their reward twice, for what they patiently endured, and they repel evil with good, and from what We have provided them, they spend.﴾ ﴿And when they hear idle talk, they turn away from it and say, "To us are our deeds, and to you are your deeds. Peace be upon you. We do not seek the ignorant."﴾

Know that when He, exalted is He, related about them that when they feared, they said, "Why did You not send to us a messenger so that we might follow Your signs," He also explained that after the sending [of the Prophet] to the people of Makkah, they said, ﴿Why was he not given the like of what was given to Moses?﴾ So these people, before the mission, cling to a doubt, and after the mission, they cling to another. Thus it became clear that they have no aim except deviation and obstinacy.

As for His saying, ﴿So when the truth came to them from Us﴾, meaning: there came to them the Messenger confirming the Book, accompanied by the miraculous Book and all the other miracles. They said, "Why was he not given the like of what was given to Moses," of the Book revealed all at once, and of the other miracles, such as the staff turning into a serpent, the white hand, the splitting of the sea, the shading of the clouds, the water gushing from the rock, the manna and the quails, and that Allah spoke to him and wrote for him on the tablets, and other signs. So they came up with proposals based on obstinacy and enmity, as they said, ﴿Why has not a treasure been sent down to him, or why has an angel not come with him?﴾ and similar things.

Know that what they proposed is not necessary, because it is not required that the miracles of the prophets, peace be upon them, be a single one, nor that the books sent down to them be in one manner. Benefit may lie in sending them down collectively, as the Torah, or piecemeal, as the Qur'an.

They said, "Two kinds of magic supporting each other," and they said, "Indeed, we disbelieve in all of them."﴾ ﴿Say, "Then bring a Book from Allah that is better guidance than both of them, and I will follow it, if you are truthful."﴾ ﴿But if they do not respond to you, then know that they only follow their desires. And who is more astray than one who follows his desire without guidance from Allah? Indeed, Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people.﴾ ﴿And We have certainly conveyed to them the word, so that they may remember.﴾ ﴿Those to whom We gave the Book before it, they believe in it.﴾ ﴿And when it is recited to them, they say, "We believe in it. Indeed, it is the truth from our Lord. Indeed, we were Muslims [submitting] before it."﴾ ﴿Those will be given their reward twice, for what they patiently endured, and they repel evil with good, and from what We have provided them, they spend.﴾ ﴿And when they hear idle talk, they turn away from it and say, "To us are our deeds, and to you are your deeds. Peace be upon you. We do not seek the ignorant."﴾

Know that when He, exalted is He, related about them that when they feared, they said, "Why did You not send to us a messenger so that we might follow Your signs," He also explained that after the sending [of the Prophet] to the people of Makkah, they said, ﴿Why was he not given the like of what was given to Moses?﴾ So these people, before the mission, cling to a doubt, and after the mission, they cling to another. Thus it became clear that they have no aim except deviation and obstinacy.

As for His saying, ﴿So when the truth came to them from Us﴾, meaning: there came to them the Messenger confirming the Book, accompanied by the miraculous Book and all the other miracles. They said, "Why was he not given the like of what was given to Moses," of the Book revealed all at once, and of the other miracles, such as the staff turning into a serpent, the white hand, the splitting of the sea, the shading of the clouds, the water gushing from the rock, the manna and the quails, and that Allah spoke to him and wrote for him on the tablets, and other signs. So they came up with proposals based on obstinacy and enmity, as they said, ﴿Why has not a treasure been sent down to him, or why has an angel not come with him?﴾ and similar things.

Know that what they proposed is not necessary, because it is not required that the miracles of the prophets, peace be upon them, be a single one, nor that the books sent down to them be in one manner. Benefit may lie in sending them down collectively, as the Torah, or piecemeal, as the Qur'an.

Then He answered this doubt by His saying, ﴿Did they not disbelieve in what was given to Moses before?﴾ The scholars differed about whom the pronoun in His saying ﴿Did they not disbelieve﴾ refers to, and they mentioned several views:

The first: The Jews instructed the Quraysh to ask Muhammad to be given the like of what was given to Moses, peace be upon him. So He said, ﴿Did they not disbelieve in what was given to Moses?﴾ meaning: did you not disbelieve, O Jews, you who devised this question in regard to Moses, peace be upon him, despite those manifest signs?

The second: Those who raised this proposal were the disbelievers of Makkah, and those who disbelieved in Moses were those who lived at the time of Moses, peace be upon him. However, He placed them as a single entity, because in disbelief and obstinacy they are like a single thing.

The third: Al-Kalbi said: The polytheists of Makkah sent a delegation to the Jews of Madinah to ask them about Muhammad and his affair. They said, "We find him in the Torah with his description and attributes." When the delegation returned to them and informed them of the words of the Jews, they said, "He was a magician, just as Muhammad is a magician." So He, exalted is He, said, ﴿Did they not disbelieve in what was given to Moses?﴾

The fourth: Al-Hasan said: The Arabs had a root in the days of Moses, peace be upon him. So its meaning according to this is: did not their forefathers disbelieve when they said about Moses and Aaron, "Two magicians"?

The fifth: Qatadah said: Did not the Jews in the age of Muhammad disbelieve in what was given to Moses before, of the good tidings of Jesus and Muhammad, peace be upon them both? So they said, "Two magicians."

The sixth, which in my view is the most apparent: The disbelievers of the Quraysh and Makkah were deniers of all prophethood. Then when they asked the Messenger ﷺ for the miracles of Moses, peace be upon him, Allah, exalted is He, said, ﴿Did they not disbelieve in what was given to Moses before?﴾ Rather, [they disbelieved] in what was given to all the prophets before. So we know that you have no purpose in this proposal except obstinacy.

Then He, exalted is He, related the manner of their disbelief in what was given to Moses in two aspects:

The first: their saying, ﴿Two kinds of magic supporting each other.﴾ Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, and the people of Madinah read (sāḥirān, "two magicians") with an alif, while the people of Kufa read it without an alif. They mentioned several interpretations of "the two magicians":

One: The intended ones are Aaron and Moses, peace be upon them both, who "supported each other," i.e., cooperated. It was also read as (aẓẓāharā), with assimilation. "Siḥrān" means "two possessors of magic," and they described them as two magicians as an exaggeration of their description as magicians. Many exegetes interpreted His saying, ﴿Siḥrān,﴾ as meaning the Qur'an and the Torah. Abu 'Ubaydah preferred the reading with an alif, because "supporting one another" is more fitting for people and their actions than for books. The response to this: We have shown that His saying, ﴿siḥrān,﴾ can be taken to mean two men. Even if the intended meaning is two books, since each of the two books strengthens the other, it is not far-fetched to say, metaphorically, "they cooperated," as one says, "the reports supported one another." These interpretations are valid only if we take His saying, ﴿Did they not disbelieve in what was given to Moses,﴾ to refer either to the disbelievers of Makkah or to the disbelievers who lived at the time of Moses, peace be upon him. And there is no doubt that this is more suitable to the context of the verse.

The second: their saying, ﴿Indeed, we disbelieve in all of them.﴾ That is, in what was sent down to Muhammad, Moses, and all the other prophets, peace be upon them. It is known that this statement is fitting only for the polytheists and not for the Jews. This is an exaggeration that, despite the abundance of the signs of Moses, peace be upon him, they denied him. So what prevents such [denial] regarding Muhammad ﷺ, even if his proof is manifest?

When Allah answered their doubts, He mentioned the proof that indicates the truthfulness of Muhammad ﷺ, saying, ﴿Say, "Then bring a Book from Allah that is better guidance than both of them, and I will follow it.﴾ This is an alert to their inability to bring the like of it. Al-Zajjaj said: (attabi'hu, "I will follow it") is jussive as a conditional; whoever reads (attabi'uhu) with a raised vowel, the implied meaning is: "I will follow it."

Then He said, ﴿But if they do not respond to you.﴾ Ibn 'Abbas said: He means, if they do not believe in what you have brought of proofs. Muqatil said: If they are unable to bring a Book better than these two. This is more appropriate to the verse. If it is said: "Response" requires a call, so where is the call here? We say: His saying, ﴿Then bring a Book,﴾ is a command, and a command is a call to action.

Then He said, ﴿then know that they only follow their desires.﴾ That is: they have become bound, and nothing remains for them except following their desire. Then He refuted their way by His saying, ﴿And who is more astray than one who follows his desire without guidance from Allah?﴾ This is among the greatest proofs of the corruption of blind imitation (taqlid), and that there must be proof and reasoning. ﴿Indeed, Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people,﴾ which is general and includes the disbeliever, in accordance with His saying, ﴿Indeed, associating others with Allah is a great wrong﴾ (Luqman: 13). The Companions (al-Aṣḥāb, the Ash'arite scholars) used this verse to argue that Allah's guidance is specific to the believers.

The Mu'tazilah said: Among the acts of divine favour (lutf, divine grace enabling obedience), some are good to perform absolutely, and some are good only after faith. The evidence for this is His saying, ﴿And those who are guided, He increases them in guidance﴾ (Muhammad: 17). So His saying, ﴿Indeed, Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people,﴾ is to be understood as referring to the second category, and it is not permissible to understand it as referring to the first category. Because He, exalted is He, when He made clear in the previous verse that the non-sending of a messenger serves as an excuse for them, then the non-guidance being an excuse for them is more fitting. When He, exalted is He, established the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ by this evidence, He said, ﴿And We have certainly conveyed to them the word,﴾ and conveying the word is bringing explanation after explanation, from "wasala al-ba'ḍ bi-al-ba'ḍ" (joined one part to another). This conveyed word may mean: We sent down the Qur'an in installments, piece by piece, its parts connected to one another, so that this would be closer to reminder and alertness, for each day they come to know another wisdom and an additional benefit, and thus they become closer to remembering. According to this interpretation, this is an answer to their statement: "Why was Muhammad not given his Book all at once, as Moses was given his Book in the same way?" It may also mean: We conveyed the reports of the prophets, some connected to others, and the reports of the disbelievers regarding how they were destroyed, multiplying occasions for admonition and restraint. It may also mean: We made clear the evidence that this Qur'an is miraculous, time after time, so that they may remember.

Then, when He, exalted is He, established the evidence for prophethood, He affirmed it by saying, ﴿Those to whom We gave the Book before it,﴾ that is, before the Qur'an, they embraced Islam with Muhammad. Whoever does not know the Books is even more deserving of this. The scholars differed about the meaning of His saying, ﴿Those to whom We gave the Book,﴾ and they mentioned several views:

The first: Qatadah said: It was revealed concerning some people from the People of the Book who were upon a true law which they held fast to. When Allah sent Muhammad, they believed in him, among them Salman and 'Abdullah ibn Salam.

The second: Muqatil said: It was revealed concerning forty men from the People of the Gospel, who were the people of the ship, who came from Abyssinia with Ja'far.

The third: Rifa'ah ibn Qarazah said: It was revealed concerning ten men, and I am one of them.

You know that the lesson is in the generality of the wording and not in the specificity of the occasion of revelation. So whoever has that attribute is included in the verse. Then He related of them what indicates the affirmation of their faith, which is their saying, ﴿We believe in it. Indeed, it is the truth from our Lord. Indeed, we were Muslims [submitting] before it.﴾ His saying, ﴿Indeed, it is the truth from our Lord,﴾ indicates causation, meaning that its being true from Allah necessitates belief in it. His saying, ﴿Indeed, we were Muslims [submitting] before it,﴾ explains His saying, ﴿We believe in it,﴾ because it may be a faith of recent or of long standing. So they informed that their faith in it was long established, due to what they found in the books of the earlier prophets, peace be upon them, of the good tidings of its coming.

Then, when He, exalted is He, praised them with this great praise, He said, ﴿Those will be given their reward twice, for what they patiently endured.﴾ The scholars mentioned several views concerning this:

The first: They will be given their reward twice for their faith in Muhammad ﷺ, before his mission and after his mission. This is the closest view, because when He, exalted is He, explained that they believed in him after the mission, and also explained that they were believers in him before the mission, then He established the reward as twice, and it is necessary to interpret it accordingly.

The second: They will be given the reward twice: once for their faith in the prophets who came before Muhammad ﷺ, and once for their faith in Muhammad ﷺ.

The third: Muqatil said: When these people believed in Muhammad ﷺ, the polytheists reviled them, and they forgave them. So they have two rewards: a reward for forgiveness and a reward for faith. It is related that when they embraced Islam, Abu Jahl cursed them, and they remained silent toward him. Al-Suddi said: The Jews blamed 'Abdullah ibn Salam and reviled him, while he would say, "Peace be upon you."

Then He said, ﴿and they repel evil with good.﴾ The meaning is that they repel a previous disobedience with obedience. It may also mean that they repel harm by pardon and forgiveness. It may also mean by "good" their abstention from sins, since abstention itself is a good deed, and by it they repel what would otherwise be an evil. It may also include repentance, turning back, and steadfastness upon it. Then He said, ﴿and from what We have provided them, they spend.﴾

Know that He, exalted is He, first praised them for faith, then for bodily acts of obedience in His saying, ﴿and they repel evil with good,﴾ then

with the financial acts of obedience, in His saying: ﴿And from what We have provided them, they spend.﴾ The judge (al-Qadi) said: This praise indicates that what is unlawful cannot be provision (rizq). The answer to this: the word "min" (from) is for partition (lil-tab'id), so it indicates that they deserved praise for spending some of what was provision, and according to this interpretation his argument falls apart. Then, when He explained how they occupied themselves with acts of obedience and good deeds, He explained how they turned away from the ignorant, so He said: ﴿And when they hear idle talk, they turn away from it.﴾ Al-laghw is that which ought to be disregarded and left aside, such as frivolity and other things. They would hear such things and not engage in them, but rather turn away from them in a graceful manner. Therefore God the Exalted said: ﴿To us our deeds, and to you your deeds; peace be upon you.﴾ How excellent is what al-Hasan (may God have mercy on him) said, that this word is a greeting among the believers and a sign of forbearance toward the ignorant. A parallel to this verse is His saying: ﴿And the servants of the Most Merciful are those who walk upon the earth in humility, and when the ignorant address them, they say, "Peace"﴾ (al-Furqan: 63). Then God the Exalted confirmed this with His saying, relating it from them: ﴿We do not seek the ignorant.﴾ The meaning is: we do not repay their falsehood with falsehood. Some people said: this was abrogated (naskh) by the command to fight, but this is far-fetched, because abandoning vulgar abuse (al-musafaha) is recommended (mandub), even if fighting is obligatory.

A parallel to this verse is His saying: ﴿And the servants of the Most Merciful are those who walk upon the earth in humility, and when the ignorant address them, they say, "Peace"﴾ (al-Furqan: 63). Then God the Exalted confirmed this with His saying, relating it from them: ﴿We do not seek the ignorant.﴾ The meaning is: we do not repay their falsehood with falsehood. Some people said: this was abrogated (naskh) by the command to fight, but this is far-fetched, because abandoning vulgar abuse (al-musafaha) is recommended (mandub), even if fighting is obligatory.

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

God, exalted is He, says: ﴿Indeed, you do not guide whom you love, but God guides whom He wills, and He knows best those who are guided.﴾ ﴿And they say, "If we follow the guidance with you, we will be snatched from our land." Have We not established for them a secure sanctuary to which the fruits of every thing are brought as provision from Us? But most of them do not know.﴾

Know that in His words, exalted is He, ﴿Indeed, you do not guide whom you love, but God guides whom He wills﴾, there are several issues:

The first issue: This verse contains no indication in its apparent meaning that Abu Talib was a disbeliever. Then al-Zajjaj (grammarian and exegete) said: The Muslims have agreed that it was revealed concerning Abu Talib, because "Abu Talib said at the time of his death: O assembly of the Banu Abd Manaf, obey Muhammad and affirm him, and you will prosper and be rightly guided. The Prophet, peace be upon him, said: 'O uncle, you command them to advise their own selves while you abandon it for yourself!' He said: 'What do you want, O son of my brother?' He said: 'I want from you one word, for at the last day of the days of this world you will say: There is no god but God, and I will testify for you with it before God, exalted is He.' He said: 'O my brother, I know that you are truthful, but I dislike that it be said that he panicked at the time of death. Had it not been that there would be shame and reproach upon you and upon the sons of your father after me, I would have said it, and I would have brought comfort to your eye at the parting, because of what I see of your intense grief and sincere advice. But I will die upon the religion of the elders: Abd al-Muttalib, Hashim, and Abd Manaf.'"

* * *

The second issue: In this verse He, exalted is He, said ﴿Indeed, you do not guide whom you love﴾, and in another verse He said ﴿And indeed, you guide to a straight path﴾ (al-Shura: 52). There is no contradiction between them, for what He affirmed and attributed to him is the calling (da'wah, invitation) and the clarification (bayan), while what He negated from him is the guidance of success (hidayat al-tawfiq) and the expansion of the breast (sharh al-sadr). That guidance is a light cast into the heart, by which the heart comes to life, as He, glorified is He, said: ﴿Is one who was dead and We gave him life and made for him a light﴾ (al-An'am: 122), and the verse continues.

[p. 4]

**The third issue:** The Ash'aris (al-Ashab) cited this verse in the question of guidance and misguidance. They said: His saying, ﴿Indeed, you do not guide whom you love, but Allah guides whom He wills﴾, requires that "guidance" carry one and the same meaning in both places. For if "guidance" meant one thing in ﴿Indeed, you do not guide﴾ and another in ﴿but Allah guides whom He wills﴾, the composition would be disrupted. Then the meaning of guidance is either: (a) showing the proof (bayan al-dalalah), (b) calling to Paradise (al-da'wah ila al-Jannah), (c) making the path to Paradise known (ta'rif tariq al-Jannah), (d) creating knowledge in the hearts by way of compulsion (al-ilja'), or (e) creating knowledge in the hearts not by way of compulsion.

It is not permissible that the meaning be showing the proofs, because he, peace be upon him, guided everyone in this sense, so it is other than the guidance whose generality Allah negated. The same applies to guidance in the sense of calling to Paradise. As for guidance in the sense of making known the path to Paradise, it too is not what is meant by the verse, because God made this guidance contingent upon His will, whereas making known the path to Paradise is not contingent upon His will, since it is obligatory upon God, and what is obligatory cannot be contingent upon will. Whoever is obligated to pay ten dinars may not say, "I will pay ten dinars if I wish."

As for guidance in the sense of compulsion and coercion, it is impermissible, because that is, in their view, an ugliness (qabih) on the part of God toward the accountable person, and doing what is ugly entails ignorance or need, both of which are impossible, and what entails the impossible is impossible. Thus that would be impossible on God's part, and the impossible cannot be made contingent upon will. Since the divisions have been refuted, nothing remains except that what is meant is that He specifies some with the creation of guidance and knowledge and withholds them from others, and "He is not questioned about what He does." When you present the discourse in this manner, everything that al-Qadi raised as an objection to this is dispelled.

As for His saying, ﴿and He knows best those who are guided﴾, the meaning is that He alone has exclusive knowledge of the unseen, so He knows who will be guided later and who will not be guided.

Then, after He (glorified be He) had mentioned their doubts and answered them with clear replies, He explained that the clarity of the proofs is not sufficient unless God's guidance is joined to it. He then related another doubt of theirs, concerning the affairs of this world, namely their saying: ﴿If we follow the guidance with you, we will be snatched away from our land.﴾

Al-Mubarrad said: al-khatf is seizing swiftly. It is narrated that al-Harith ibn 'Amir ibn Nawfal ibn 'Abd Manaf said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "We indeed know that what you say is true, but what prevents us from it is that we will be snatched away from our land," meaning that they would gather together to fight us and expel us from our land. Allah (glorified and exalted be He) answered this from several aspects.

The first: His saying, ﴿Did We not establish for them a secure sanctuary?﴾ That is: We gave you a dwelling in which there is no fear for you. This is either because the Arabs used to revere the sanctuary and never at all molested its inhabitants, for it is related that the Arabs outside the sanctuary were occupied with plundering and raiding, yet never at all molested the people of the sanctuary; or it refers to His saying, ﴿and whoever enters it is safe﴾ (Al 'Imran: 97).

As for His saying, ﴿to which the fruits of all things are brought﴾, just as He (exalted be He) explained that this place was free of fears and calamities, He also explained the abundance of blessings in it. The meaning of ﴿yujba﴾ is "is gathered," from the expression "I gathered the water in the basin" (jabaytu al-ma'a fi al-hawd) when I collected it. The people of Madinah read tujba with the letter ta', while the people of Kufah and Abu 'Amr read yujba with the letter ya', because the feminine marking of al-thamarat (fruits) is a feminine of a plural, not a true feminine; so it is permissible to make it feminine according to the wording and masculine according to the meaning. The meaning of "all" (kulliyyah) is abundance, as in His saying, ﴿and she has been given of everything﴾ (al-Naml: 23).

The summary of the reply: When He made the sanctuary secure and multiplied provision in it, while they were turning away from the worship of Allah and devoting themselves to idol-worship, then if they believed, the continuation of this state would be more fitting. Al-Qadi said: If the Messenger had said to them, "What you have mentioned of being snatched away, if it were true, would not be an excuse for you not to believe, and the proof has become manifest," they would have been silenced. Or if he had said to them, "Their snatching you away by killing and otherwise, when you have believed, is like martyrdom for you, and so it is a benefit returning to you," they would also have been silenced. Or if he had said to them, "What is the magnitude of the harm of being snatched away compared to the everlasting punishment with which I warn you if you remain upon your disbelief?" they would have been silenced. But He (exalted be He) argued with what is stronger, since He demonstrated the falsity of their claim that they would be snatched away, by pointing to what they knew from the customary state of that locality, that this would not happen if they believed. Whatever can be made clear to the opponent in this way is better than all the other things we have mentioned, and for this reason God (exalted be He) put it first.

[p. 5]

The verse indicates the soundness of the argument by which one reaches the removal of the doubt of the falsifiers. Two discussions remain here:

**The first:** The author of *al-Kashshaf* said concerning the accusative of ﴿rizqan﴾: if you take it as a verbal noun (masdar), it may be governed by the meaning of what precedes it, because the meaning of ﴿to which the fruits of all things are brought﴾ and "the fruits of all things are provided" is one and the same. It may also be an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu). If you take it in the sense of "provided" (marzuq), it is a circumstantial accusative (hal) from "the fruits," because it is specified by the genitive construction, just as an indefinite noun specified by a qualifier takes the accusative.

**The second:** The Ash'aris cited His saying, ﴿a provision from Us﴾, to establish that the act of the servant is the creation of Allah (exalted be He). Its explanation: those provisions only reached them because people carried them to them. Had the act of the servant not been the creation of Allah (exalted be He), that attribution would not be valid. If it is said that the cause of that attribution is that God is the one who cast those motives into the hearts of those who brought those provisions to them, we reply: if those motives entail preponderance (rujhan), we have shown in more than one place that whenever preponderance occurs, obligation occurs, and then the aim is achieved. And if preponderance does not occur, the attribution is cut off entirely.

Know that He (exalted be He) only explained that those provisions did not reach them except from Allah (exalted be He) so that, when they know this, they will be in a state where they fear no one besides Allah (exalted be He) and hope in no one other than Allah (exalted be He). Then their gaze remains detached from creation and attached to the Creator. This necessitates the perfection of faith, the complete turning away from other than Allah (exalted be He), and the complete turning toward obedience to Allah (exalted be He).

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 28, verses 58–60:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿How many a town have We destroyed which exulted in its livelihood! Those are their dwellings, not inhabited after them except a little. And We are the inheritors.﴾ ﴿Your Lord would never destroy the towns until He sends in their mother [town] a messenger reciting to them Our verses. And We would never destroy the towns unless their people were wrongdoers.﴾

Know that this is the second answer to that doubt. This is because, when He, may He be exalted, explained to the people of Makkah the blessings with which they had been favoured, He followed it with what God, may He be exalted, sent down upon the earlier nations who were in the blessings of this world. When they denied the messengers, God removed those blessings from them. The purpose is that when the unbelievers said, "We will not believe, out of fear of the loss of the blessings of this world," God, may He be exalted, explained to them that persistence in refusing to accept faith is what removes these blessings, not the act of embracing faith.

The author of *al-Kashshaf* said: *al-baṭar* (exultation, insolence) is poor handling of wealth, which is not to observe God's right concerning it. The word ﴿maʿīshatahā﴾ (its livelihood) is in the accusative either by the omission of the preposition so that the verb reaches it directly, as in His saying: ﴿And Moses chose his people﴾ (al-Aʿrāf 7:155), or by assuming the omission of a temporal noun that is in construct, the original being "exulted during the days of its livelihood." Or *baṭirat* is taken to include the meaning of *kafarat* (was ungrateful).

As for His saying: ﴿Those are their dwellings, not inhabited after them except a little﴾, there are several views concerning this exception:

First: Ibn ʿAbbās, may God be pleased with him and his father, said: "Only a traveller or a passer-by on the road stayed in it, for a day or an hour."

Second: It is possible that the evil consequence of the sins of the destroyed people remained in their dwellings, so that whoever lived there from their descendants did not remain in it except a little. "And We are the inheritors" of it after the destruction of its people. When a thing no longer has a specific owner, it is said to be the inheritance of God, because He is the one who remains after the perishing of His creation.

Then, when He, glory be to Him, mentioned that He destroyed those towns because of the exultation of their people, it was as if a questioner raised the question from two aspects.

The first: Why did God not destroy the unbelievers before Muhammad (ﷺ), although they were immersed in unbelief and obstinacy?

The second: Why did He not destroy them after the mission of Muhammad (ﷺ), although the people persisted in unbelief in God, may He be exalted, and in denying Muhammad (ﷺ)?

He answered the first question with His saying: ﴿Your Lord would never destroy the towns until He sends in their mother [town] a messenger reciting to them Our verses﴾. The essential answer is that He, may He be exalted, first showed that the non-sending of a messenger serves as an excuse for the people, so it was not permissible to destroy them except after the sending of a messenger. Then the commentators mentioned two views.

One of them: ﴿Your Lord would never destroy the towns until He sends in their mother [town] a messenger﴾, that is, in the town which is their mother, their origin and their metropolis, whose affairs and dependencies they are, a messenger, in order to establish the proof and cut off all excuse.

The second: "Your Lord would never destroy the towns that are on the earth until He sends in the mother of the towns, meaning Makkah, a messenger, who is Muhammad (ﷺ), the seal of the prophets." The meaning of ﴿reciting to them Our verses﴾ is "conveying and delivering."

He answered the second question with His saying: ﴿And We would never destroy the towns unless their people were wrongdoers﴾, meaning wrongdoers toward themselves through polytheism. The people of Makkah are not like this, for some of them have believed, and some of them are those whom God knew would believe, and others, whom God knew would not believe, yet from their offspring there would come one who would be a believer.

The commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 28, verses 61–63:

The exegesis of His words, may He be exalted: ﴿And whatever you have been given is but the enjoyment of worldly life and its adornment, while what is with God is better and more lasting. Will you not reason?﴾ ﴿Is one to whom We have made a good promise, and who will meet it, like one whom We have given the enjoyment of worldly life and then on the Day of Resurrection he will be among those brought forth [to punishment]?﴾

Know that this is the third answer to that doubt, because the essence of their doubt was that they said: "We have abandoned the religion so that the world will not escape us." So God, may He be exalted, made clear that this is a great error, because what is with God is better and more lasting. As for its being better, that is for two reasons.

The first: the benefits there are greater.

The second: they are pure, free of impurities, whereas the benefits of this world are mixed with harms, indeed the harms in it are more numerous. As for its being more lasting, that is because it is everlasting and not cut off, whereas the benefits of this world are cut off. Whenever the finite is compared with the infinite, it amounts to nothing. How much more so when each person's share, compared with all the benefits of this world, is like a speck compared with the sea? From this it becomes clear that the benefits of this world have no ratio at all to the benefits of the Hereafter. So it is a great ignorance to abandon the benefits of the Hereafter to preserve the benefits of this world. When He, glorified be He, drew attention to this, He said: ﴿Will you not reason?﴾, meaning that whoever does not prefer the benefits of the Hereafter over the benefits of this world is, as it were, outside the bounds of reason. May God have mercy on al-Shafi'i, when he said: "If someone bequeaths a third of his wealth to the most intelligent of people, that third is to be given to those occupied with obedience to God, the Exalted, because the most intelligent of people is one who gives little and takes much, and they are none other than those occupied with obedience." It is as if he, may God have mercy on him, took this from this verse.

Then, He, may He be exalted, reinforced this preference from another aspect, which is that if we suppose that God's blessings were to end in cessation and extinction, and were not connected to everlasting punishment, sound reason would still require the preference of the blessings of the Hereafter over the blessings of this world. How much more so when the blessings of this world are connected to the punishment of the Hereafter? What reason, then, could doubt that the blessings of the Hereafter outweigh them?

This is what is meant by His words: ﴿Is one to whom We have made a good promise, and who will meet it, like one whom We have given the enjoyment of worldly life﴾. Such a one is like someone to whom God has given a small measure of the enjoyment of this world, and then in the Hereafter he will be among those brought forth for punishment. The point is that when they said, "We have abandoned the religion for the sake of this world," God said to them: Even if the painful consequence of punishment did not follow your worldly life, reason would still require preferring the benefits of the Hereafter over the benefits of this world. How much more so when, after this world, there is everlasting punishment. He expressed this statement in the form of a question, so that it would be more emphatic in acknowledging the preference. As for restricting the word "brought forth" (al-muhdarin) to those who are brought forth for punishment, this is something known from the Qur'an. God, the Exalted, said: ﴿you would have been among those brought forth﴾ (al-Saffat: 57), and ﴿indeed they will be brought forth﴾ (al-Saffat: 127). In the word itself there is an indication of this, because "bringing forth" (al-ihdar) implies obligation and compulsion, and that does not befit places of pleasure; it befits only places of harm and hardship.

The second: they are pure, free of impurities, whereas the benefits of this world are mixed with harms, indeed the harms in it are more numerous. As for its being more lasting, that is because it is everlasting and not cut off, whereas the benefits of this world are cut off. [p. 8]

Know that Allah, glory be to Him, mentions in this verse that on the Day of Resurrection He will question the disbelievers about three things.

Where is it, so that it may help you and rescue you from this which has befallen you?"

Then Allah explains what those against whom the word has been justified will say. The "word" meant here is His saying: ﴿"I will surely fill Hell with jinn and humankind all together."﴾ (As-Sajdah 13). The meaning of "the word has been justified against them" is that its requirement has been justified against them. Scholars differed over who these people are against whom this word has been justified. Some said they are the leaders who call to misguidance, and others said they are the devils (*shayatin*).

His saying: ﴿"Our Lord, these are the ones whom we led astray"﴾. "These" (*hā'ulā'*) is a subject (*mubtada'*), "whom we led astray" (*alladhina aghwaynā*) is its qualifier (*sifah*), the returning pronoun to the qualified noun is omitted, and "we led them astray" (*aghwaynāhum*) is the predicate (*khabar*). The *kāf* in ﴿as we ourselves were astray﴾ is an adjective of an omitted verbal noun (*masdar*), whose implied sense is: "We led them astray, so they went astray with a going astray like ours." The meaning is that just as our going astray was by our own choice, so their going astray was by their own choice. That is, our leading them astray did not compel them into error; rather they were choosing to adopt those beliefs and actions. This is the meaning of what Allah relates from the Satan, that he said:

[p. 8 continued] ﴿"Indeed, Allah promised you the promise of truth, and I promised you, but I broke it to you. I had no authority over you except that I called you, and you responded to me. So do not blame me; blame yourselves."﴾ (Ibrahim 22). Allah also said to Iblis: ﴿"Indeed, My servants, you have no authority over them, except those who follow you among the misguided."﴾ (Al-Hijr 42). His saying ﴿"except those who follow you"﴾ (Al-Hijr 42) indicates that this following was from their own side, not from the compulsion of the Satan toward it. Then they said: "We disown them and their beliefs and actions" ﴿"it was not us they worshipped"﴾, "they were only worshipping their own desires." The upshot is that they disown them, as Allah said: ﴿"When those who were followed disown those who followed."﴾ (Al-Baqarah 166).

Also, there is no impediment to interpreting His saying ﴿"Where are My partners"﴾ as referring to these leaders and devils. Since they obeyed them, they made them, by virtue of that obedience, occupy the position of partners with Allah, the Exalted. If the speech is understood in this way, their answer would be that they say: "Our God, these did not worship us; they only worshipped their corrupt desires."

The second is His saying: ﴿"And it will be said, 'Call upon your partners,' and they will call upon them, but they will not answer them."﴾ The closer view is that this is by way of affirmation (*taqrir*), because they know there is no benefit in calling upon them. The meaning is that if they called upon them, no response of help would come from them, and the punishment is established upon them. All of this is by way of reproach, and mentioning it carries a deterrent and a warning in the life of this world. As for His saying ﴿"If only they had been guided!"﴾, many exegetes claimed that the answer to *law* (if only) is omitted, and they mentioned several views about it:

First: al-Dahhak and Muqatil said: the meaning is that the followed and the followers see the punishment, and if they had been guided in this world, they would not have seen it in the Hereafter.

Second: If they had been guided in this world, they would have known that the punishment is true.

Third: When they saw the punishment, they wished that they had been guided in the world.

Fourth: If they had been guided to some way of stratagems, they would have averted the punishment by it.

Fifth: It is time for them to be guided; if they had been guided, when they see the punishment... and this is confirmed by His saying: ﴿"They will not believe in it until they see the painful punishment."﴾ (Ash-Shu'ara' 201).

In my view, the answer is not omitted, and there are views for its explanation:

First: When Allah addresses them with His saying ﴿"Call upon your partners"﴾, at that point fear intensifies upon them, and something like intoxication and dizziness overtakes them, so that they cannot see anything. Then Allah said ﴿"and they see the punishment, if only they had been guided"﴾ — meaning they see nothing. Since, from the intensity of fear, they become such that they see nothing, they therefore do not see the punishment.

Second: When Allah mentioned about the partners, which are the idols, that they do not answer those who called upon them, He said concerning them ﴿"and they see the punishment, if only they had been guided"﴾, meaning: these idols, had they been living and guided, would have been witnessing the punishment; but they are not like that, so they did not see the punishment. If it is said: the pronoun in ﴿"and they see the punishment"﴾ is one that befits only rational beings, so how can it refer to idols? We say: this is like His saying ﴿"then they called upon them, but they did not respond to them"﴾, and it came in accordance with the belief of the people, so likewise here.

Third: The "seeing" may be intended as seeing of the heart, meaning that the disbelievers knew the reality of this punishment in the world, had they been guided. These views are, in my opinion, better than the views based on the claim that the answer to *law* is omitted, because that requires disjointing the composition of the verse.

The third of the matters about which Allah questions the disbelievers is His saying: ﴿"And the day He calls to them and says, 'What answer did you give the messengers?'"﴾ ﴿"Then the news will be blinded to them."﴾ That is, the news becomes like blindness to them all; it does not reach them. ﴿"And they will not question one another"﴾: they do not ask one another as people ask one another about difficult matters, because they are all equal in the blinding of news to them and in their inability to answer. It is also read as ﴿"fa-'amiyat"﴾ (with a different vowelling). And when even the prophets, because of the terror of that situation, stammer in answering such a question, and they entrust the matter to the knowledge of Allah, the Exalted, this is His saying: ﴿"On the day when Allah gathers the messengers and says, 'What answer were you given?' They will say, 'We have no knowledge; indeed You are the Knower of the unseen.'"﴾ (Al-Ma'idah 109). So what do you think about these misguided ones?

[p. 9] Al-Qadi said: This verse indicates the invalidity of the doctrine of compulsion (*jabr*, the view that human acts are determined without real choice). For if their deed were a creation from Allah, the Exalted, and its occurrence were necessary through power and will, then the news would not have been blinded to them, and they would have said: "We came to deny the messengers from Your creating in us this denial and the power that necessitates it." Then their argument against Allah, the Exalted, would be evident. The same is the case regarding what preceded, because the Satan could have said: "I only went astray through Your creating misguidance in me, and whoever answered my call did so for a similar reason." Thus their argument in that would be strong and their excuse evident.

The answer: The Qadi does not leave any verse containing praise and blame, reward and punishment, without repeating his argument from it. Just as the basis of his argument in all of them is this one point, so the basis of our answer is one point: that Allah's knowledge of the non-occurrence of faith and the occurrence of faith are mutually exclusive by their very natures. So, with the knowledge that faith will not occur, if He commands the bringing of faith into existence, He has commanded the combining of two opposites. The principle on which al-Qadi relied in answering this point in his theological books is his saying: "The view of the one who says it is possible is wrong, and the view of the one who says it is impossible is wrong; rather, the obligation is silence. And if the disbeliever were to raise this question to his Lord, his Lord would have no answer to it except silence; thus the disbeliever's argument would be strong and his excuse evident." Thus it is established that the problem is shared. And Allah knows best.

Know that Allah, glory be to Him, mentions in this verse that on the Day of Resurrection He will question the disbelievers about three things.

The first is His saying: ﴿And the day He calls to them and says, "Where are My partners whom you used to claim?"﴾ Since it is established that on the Day of Resurrection the disbelievers will know by necessity (*darurah*) the falsehood of what they used to hold and the truth of divine oneness (*tawhid*) and prophethood (*nubuwwah*), He will say to them: "Where is that which you used to worship, which you made a partner in worship, and which you claimed would intercede? Where is it, so that it may help you and rescue you from this which has befallen you?"

Then Allah explains what those against whom the word has been justified will say. The "word" meant here is His saying: ﴿"I will surely fill Hell with jinn and humankind all together."﴾ (As-Sajdah 13). The meaning of "the word has been justified against them" is that its requirement has been justified against them. Scholars differed over who these people are against whom this word has been justified. Some said they are the leaders who call to misguidance, and others said they are the devils (*shayatin*).

His saying: ﴿"Our Lord, these are the ones whom we led astray"﴾. "These" (*hā'ulā'*) is a subject (*mubtada'*), "whom we led astray" (*alladhina aghwaynā*) is its qualifier (*sifah*), the returning pronoun to the qualified noun is omitted, and "we led them astray" (*aghwaynāhum*) is the predicate (*khabar*). The *kāf* in ﴿as we ourselves were astray﴾ is an adjective of an omitted verbal noun (*masdar*), whose implied sense is: "We led them astray, so they went astray with a going astray like ours." The meaning is that just as our going astray was by our own choice, so their going astray was by their own choice. That is, our leading them astray did not compel them into error; rather they were choosing to adopt those beliefs and actions. This is the meaning of what Allah relates from the Satan, that he said:

[p. 8 continued] ﴿"Indeed, Allah promised you the promise of truth, and I promised you, but I broke it to you. I had no authority over you except that I called you, and you responded to me. So do not blame me; blame yourselves."﴾ (Ibrahim 22). Allah also said to Iblis: ﴿"Indeed, My servants, you have no authority over them, except those who follow you among the misguided."﴾ (Al-Hijr 42). His saying ﴿"except those who follow you"﴾ (Al-Hijr 42) indicates that this following was from their own side, not from the compulsion of the Satan toward it. Then they said: "We disown them and their beliefs and actions" ﴿"it was not us they worshipped"﴾, "they were only worshipping their own desires." The upshot is that they disown them, as Allah said: ﴿"When those who were followed disown those who followed."﴾ (Al-Baqarah 166).

Also, there is no impediment to interpreting His saying ﴿"Where are My partners"﴾ as referring to these leaders and devils. Since they obeyed them, they made them, by virtue of that obedience, occupy the position of partners with Allah, the Exalted. If the speech is understood in this way, their answer would be that they say: "Our God, these did not worship us; they only worshipped their corrupt desires."

The second is His saying: ﴿"And it will be said, 'Call upon your partners,' and they will call upon them, but they will not answer them."﴾ The closer view is that this is by way of affirmation (*taqrir*), because they know there is no benefit in calling upon them. The meaning is that if they called upon them, no response of help would come from them, and the punishment is established upon them. All of this is by way of reproach, and mentioning it carries a deterrent and a warning in the life of this world. As for His saying ﴿"If only they had been guided!"﴾, many exegetes claimed that the answer to *law* (if only) is omitted, and they mentioned several views about it:

First: al-Dahhak and Muqatil said: the meaning is that the followed and the followers see the punishment, and if they had been guided in this world, they would not have seen it in the Hereafter.

Second: If they had been guided in this world, they would have known that the punishment is true.

Third: When they saw the punishment, they wished that they had been guided in the world.

Fourth: If they had been guided to some way of stratagems, they would have averted the punishment by it.

Fifth: It is time for them to be guided; if they had been guided, when they see the punishment... and this is confirmed by His saying: ﴿"They will not believe in it until they see the painful punishment."﴾ (Ash-Shu'ara' 201).

In my view, the answer is not omitted, and there are views for its explanation:

First: When Allah addresses them with His saying ﴿"Call upon your partners"﴾, at that point fear intensifies upon them, and something like intoxication and dizziness overtakes them, so that they cannot see anything. Then Allah said ﴿"and they see the punishment, if only they had been guided"﴾ — meaning they see nothing. Since, from the intensity of fear, they become such that they see nothing, they therefore do not see the punishment.

Second: When Allah mentioned about the partners, which are the idols, that they do not answer those who called upon them, He said concerning them ﴿"and they see the punishment, if only they had been guided"﴾, meaning: these idols, had they been living and guided, would have been witnessing the punishment; but they are not like that, so they did not see the punishment. If it is said: the pronoun in ﴿"and they see the punishment"﴾ is one that befits only rational beings, so how can it refer to idols? We say: this is like His saying ﴿"then they called upon them, but they did not respond to them"﴾, and it came in accordance with the belief of the people, so likewise here.

Third: The "seeing" may be intended as seeing of the heart, meaning that the disbelievers knew the reality of this punishment in the world, had they been guided. These views are, in my opinion, better than the views based on the claim that the answer to *law* is omitted, because that requires disjointing the composition of the verse.

The third of the matters about which Allah questions the disbelievers is His saying: ﴿"And the day He calls to them and says, 'What answer did you give the messengers?'"﴾ ﴿"Then the news will be blinded to them."﴾ That is, the news becomes like blindness to them all; it does not reach them. ﴿"And they will not question one another"﴾: they do not ask one another as people ask one another about difficult matters, because they are all equal in the blinding of news to them and in their inability to answer. It is also read as ﴿"fa-'amiyat"﴾ (with a different vowelling). And when even the prophets, because of the terror of that situation, stammer in answering such a question, and they entrust the matter to the knowledge of Allah, the Exalted, this is His saying: ﴿"On the day when Allah gathers the messengers and says, 'What answer were you given?' They will say, 'We have no knowledge; indeed You are the Knower of the unseen.'"﴾ (Al-Ma'idah 109). So what do you think about these misguided ones?

[p. 9] Al-Qadi said: This verse indicates the invalidity of the doctrine of compulsion (*jabr*, the view that human acts are determined without real choice). For if their deed were a creation from Allah, the Exalted, and its occurrence were necessary through power and will, then the news would not have been blinded to them, and they would have said: "We came to deny the messengers from Your creating in us this denial and the power that necessitates it." Then their argument against Allah, the Exalted, would be evident. The same is the case regarding what preceded, because the Satan could have said: "I only went astray through Your creating misguidance in me, and whoever answered my call did so for a similar reason." Thus their argument in that would be strong and their excuse evident.

The answer: The Qadi does not leave any verse containing praise and blame, reward and punishment, without repeating his argument from it. Just as the basis of his argument in all of them is this one point, so the basis of our answer is one point: that Allah's knowledge of the non-occurrence of faith and the occurrence of faith are mutually exclusive by their very natures. So, with the knowledge that faith will not occur, if He commands the bringing of faith into existence, He has commanded the combining of two opposites. The principle on which al-Qadi relied in answering this point in his theological books is his saying: "The view of the one who says it is possible is wrong, and the view of the one who says it is impossible is wrong; rather, the obligation is silence. And if the disbeliever were to raise this question to his Lord, his Lord would have no answer to it except silence; thus the disbeliever's argument would be strong and his excuse evident." Thus it is established that the problem is shared. And Allah knows best.

He, exalted is He, when He had explained the state of the disbelievers who are punished and the rebuke that befalls them, followed it with mention of those among them who repent in this world, as an encouragement to repentance and a deterrent from persisting in disbelief. So He said: ﴿But as for one who repents and believes and does righteousness, it is expected that he will be among the successful.﴾ There are several points concerning *'asā* (it is expected):

First: that it comes from the Generous, and it is a confirmation, since God is the Most Generous of the generous.

Second: that it expresses the penitent's hope and longing, as if He had said: let him hope for success.

Third: it is expected that they will be that way if they persist in repentance and faith, given the possibility that they may not persist. Know that the people used to raise another doubt and say: ﴿Why was this Qur'an not sent down upon a great man of the two cities?﴾ (az-Zukhruf: 31), meaning al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah or Abu Mas'ud ath-Thaqafi. God answered them with His words: ﴿And your Lord creates what He wills and chooses.﴾ The meaning is that He is the absolute Owner, transcendent above benefit and harm, so He may single out whomever He wills with whatever He wills, and there is absolutely no objection to Him. According to the method of the Mu'tazilah (the rationalist theological school), since it is established that He is absolutely Wise, it is known that whatever He does is wisdom and rightness, so no one has the right to object to Him. His words ﴿They have no choice﴾: *al-khiyarah* is a noun derived from *al-ikhtiyar* (choosing), functioning in the place of the verbal noun, and *al-khiyarah* is also a noun for the chosen one; it is said: Muhammad is God's chosen one (*khiyarah*) among His creation. Having understood this, we say that there are two readings of the verse:

The first, which is the better: the pause is complete at His words ﴿and chooses﴾, and *mā* is a negation, and the meaning is: ﴿your Lord creates what He wills and chooses﴾; they have no choice, since it is not for them to choose over God what He should do.

The second: that *mā* means "that which," so the pause falls at His words ﴿your Lord creates what He wills﴾, then He says ﴿and chooses﴾ that which they have no choice in. Abu al-Qasim al-Ansari said: This is the Mu'tazilah's argument for making *al-salah* and *al-aslah* (what is best for the servant) obligatory upon God. What benefit is there in obligating one whom He knows will not believe? Had He not obligated him, would he not have deserved Paradise and bliss by God's grace? If it is said: once He obligated him, He became bound to do what is best, since the one who deserves something is superior to the one who is granted it as a favour, we reply: when He knows with certainty that this best will not be attained, then casting him into everlasting punishment is not a consideration of what is good. Moreover, their saying that the one who deserves is better than the one who is favoured is ignorance, because that disparity arises only regarding one who disdains receiving favour; but as for the One who did not bring about the essence and attributes except by His creation, His grace and His beneficence, how could He disdain bestowing His favour? Then He said: ﴿Glory be to God, and exalted is He above what they associate.﴾ The purpose is to make known that creation, choice, honouring and humbling are entrusted to Him alone; no one has any partnership or contention in them. Then He confirmed this by saying that He knows what their breasts conceal of enmity towards the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and what they openly express of their slander against him and their saying: "Why was someone else not chosen for prophethood?" When He had made clear His knowledge of what they harbour of rancour, envy and foolishness, He said: ﴿He is God; there is no god but He.﴾ In this is an alert to His being capable of all possibilities, knowing all knowables, exempt from deficiencies and calamities, who rewards the righteous for their obedience and punishes the disobedient for their disobedience. In it is the utmost deterrence and restraint for the disobedient and the utmost strengthening of the heart for the obedient. It is also possible that, since He had clarified the corruption of the way of the polytheists from His words ﴿And the day He calls to them﴾, saying ﴿Where are My partners?﴾, He concluded the discourse on that by manifesting this tawhid (oneness of God) and clarifying that praise and commendation befit none but Him.

As for His words ﴿To Him belongs praise in the first and the last﴾, it is clear according to our view, since reward is not obligatory upon Him; rather He, glory be to Him, gives it as bounty and beneficence, so to Him belongs praise in this world and the next. This is confirmed by the saying of the people of Paradise: ﴿Praise be to God who has removed from us grief﴾ (Fatir: 34), ﴿Praise be to God who has fulfilled His promise to us﴾ (az-Zumar: 74), and ﴿Their final call will be: "Praise be to God, Lord of the worlds"﴾ (Yunus: 10). As for the Mu'tazilah, reward is owed to them, so the people of Paradise do not deserve praise for their deed; and as for the people of Hellfire, He did not bestow any favour upon them that would merit praise from them. The Qadi (al-Qadi, i.e., 'Abd al-Jabbar) said: He deserves praise and thanks from the people of the Fire as well, for what He did for them in this world of empowerment, facilitation, kindnesses and all other blessings; for by their wrongdoing the blessings God bestowed upon them do not cease to require gratitude. This requires examination, because the people of the Hereafter are compelled to know the truth; so when they know by necessity that repentance from vices is binding upon God to accept, and they know by necessity that occupying themselves with the obligatory gratitude makes it binding upon God to grant reward, and they are able to do that and know that it will save them from torment and bring them into entitlement to reward, do you think a person, knowing this and having the power to do it, would forgo this repentance? No indeed! Rather they must repent and occupy themselves with gratitude, and once they do that, punishment is nullified.

As for His words ﴿And to Him belongs judgment﴾, it is either in this world or in the Hereafter. In this world, the judgment of everyone other than Him is only executed by His judgment: were it not for His judgment, the judgment of a master would not be enforced upon a slave, nor the judgment of a husband upon a wife, nor the judgment of a father upon a son, nor the judgment of rulers upon their subjects, nor the judgment of the Messenger upon the community. He is the true Judge. In the Hereafter, there is no doubt that He is the Judge, for He is the One who undertakes judgment among the servants in the Hereafter, granting the oppressed justice against the oppressors.

As for His words ﴿And to Him you will be returned﴾, the meaning is: to the place of His judgment and decree you will be returned, for the word *ilā* ("to") indicates the endpoint, and He, exalted is He, is exempt from place and direction.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 28, verses 71–73:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: Have you considered, if Allah made the night perpetual over you until the Day of Resurrection, who is a god other than Allah who could bring you light? Will you not then listen?﴾ ﴿Say: Have you considered, if Allah made the day perpetual over you until the Day of Resurrection, who is a god other than Allah who could bring you a night in which you rest? Will you not then see?﴾ ﴿And out of His mercy He made for you the night and the day, that you may rest therein and that you may seek of His bounty, and that you may be grateful.﴾

Know that when He, exalted is He, had previously shown in general terms that He deserves praise, with His saying: ﴿And He is Allah; there is no god but He. To Him is praise in the first and the last, and to Him is the judgment, and to Him you will be returned﴾, He then elaborated, after that, on some of the things for which He ought to be praised, which none other than Him can do. So He said to His Messenger: ﴿Say: Have you considered, if Allah made the night perpetual over you until the Day of Resurrection...﴾. He thereby drew attention to the reason why night and day are two blessings that alternate over time: a person in this world, in the state of being responsible (taklif), is driven to toil in order to obtain what he needs, and this cannot be completed without the light of day. For this reason gathering together occurs and dealings become possible. It is known that this cannot be completed without rest and tranquility at night, so both are necessary in this state. As for in Paradise, there is no fatigue or toil, so they have no need for night; therefore light and pleasures endure for them. Thus He, exalted is He, made clear that none is able to do that except Allah, exalted is He. He said: ﴿Will you not then listen?﴾ and ﴿Will you not then see?﴾ because the purpose of these is benefit from what they hear and see by way of reflection (tadabbur). When they did not benefit, they were placed in the position of those who neither hear nor see.

Al-Kalbi said: His saying ﴿Will you not then listen?﴾ means: will you not then obey Him who does that? And His saying ﴿Will you not then see?﴾ means: will you not see the error and misguidance you are upon?

The author of al-Kashshaf said: al-sarmad (perpetual) is that which is continuous and unbroken, from al-sard (succession), which is consecutiveness. From it comes the saying: in the sacred months there are three in succession (sard) and one single (fard).

If it is asked: why did He not say "by day in which you move about freely (tatasarrafun)," just as He said "by night in which you rest"? We say: He mentioned light, which is the light of the sun, because the benefits connected with it are numerous; it is not merely for the sake of livelihood, and darkness does not hold that rank. He paired light with ﴿Will you not then listen?﴾ because hearing perceives what sight does not perceive of the grasp of its benefits and the description of its advantages. And He paired night with ﴿Will you not then see?﴾ because another person perceives from the benefit of darkness what you perceive of tranquility and the like.

And out of His mercy He paired night and day for three purposes: that you may rest in one of them, which is the night; that you may seek of His bounty in the other, which is the day; and for rendering thanks for both benefits together.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 28, verses 74–75:

Page 12

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And on the Day when He calls to them, He will say, "Where are My partners, those you used to claim?"﴾ ﴿And We will extract from every nation a witness, and We will say, "Bring your proof." Then they will know that the truth belongs to Allah, and what they used to invent will have vanished from them.﴾

Know that when He, glorified is He, first censured the way of the polytheists, then mentioned the Oneness (tawhid) and its proofs (dala'il) secondly, He returned once more to censuring their way and explained their state in the Hereafter, so He said: ﴿And on the Day when He calls to them﴾, that is, the Day of Resurrection, ﴿He will say: "Where are My partners, those you used to claim?"﴾ The meaning is: where are those whose divinity you claimed in order to be saved, or where is your saying, "They bring us near to Allah in nearness"? Yet they knew that there is no god but Allah. This will add to their distress when they are addressed with this statement.

As for His saying: ﴿And We will extract from every nation a witness﴾, the meaning is that We will single out one (witness) from each to bear witness against them. Then some said: they are the prophets, who will bear witness that they conveyed the proofs to their people and exerted every effort in clarifying them, so that it becomes known that the shortcoming came from them, and this will add to their distress. Others said: rather, they are the martyrs (shuhada') who bear witness over people in every age, and the prophets are included among them. This is closer to the truth, because He, exalted is He, made it general for every nation and every community, by extracting from them a witness, so that it includes the circumstances in which no prophet existed, namely the periods of interruption (al-fatarat), and the times that occurred after Muhammad ﷺ. ﴿Then they will know at that time that the truth belongs to Allah and to His messengers.﴾ ﴿And what they used to invent will have vanished from them﴾, that is, it went missing from them as a lost thing goes missing, ﴿of falsehood and lies﴾.
