Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 28, verses 76–78 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, Qarun was of the people of Musa, but he oppressed them. And We had given him of treasures whose keys would indeed weigh down a group of strong men. When his people said to him, "Do not exult. Indeed, Allah does not love the exultant."﴾ ﴿But seek, through that which Allah has given you, the Hereafter, and do not forget your share of the world. And do good as Allah has done good to you, and seek not corruption in the land. Indeed, Allah does not love the corrupters.﴾ ﴿He said, "I was only given it on knowledge I have." Did he not know that Allah had destroyed before him of generations those who were greater than him in strength and more abundant in accumulation? But the criminals will not be asked about their sins.﴾

Know that the explicit text of the Qur'an indicates that Qarun was of the people of Musa (peace be upon him), and the apparent meaning indicates that he was among those who believed in him. It is also not far-fetched to take it as a matter of kinship. Al-Kalbi said: he was the cousin (ibn 'amm) of Musa (peace be upon him), for Qarun was the son of Yashar ibn Qahith ibn Lawi, and Musa was the son of 'Imran ibn Qahith ibn Lawi. Muhammad ibn Ishaq said: he was the paternal uncle ('amm) of Musa (peace be upon him), since Musa ibn 'Imran ibn Yashar ibn Qahith and Qarun ibn Yashar ibn Qahith.

And from Ibn
page 13
'Abbas, that he was the son of his maternal aunt. Then it was said: he was called al-Munawwar (the Illuminated) for the beauty of his appearance, and he was the most learned of the Children of Israel in the Torah, except that he became a hypocrite just as the Samiri became one.

As for His saying: ﴿so he oppressed them﴾ (al-Qasas: 76), there are several views concerning it:

First: he oppressed them because of his wealth, and his oppression was that he belittled the poor, did not respect their right of faith, and did not honor them despite the abundance of his wealth.

Second: it is from injustice (zulm). It was said: Pharaoh made him ruler over the Children of Israel, and he wronged them.

Third: al-Qaffal said: "he oppressed them," that is, he sought superiority over them and that they be under his hand.

Fourth: al-Dahhak said: he transgressed against them and exalted himself over them, so he did not grant them success in any matter.

Fifth: Ibn 'Abbas said: he acted arrogantly and proudly over them and was wrathful toward them.

Sixth: Shahr ibn Hawshab said: his oppression of them was that he lengthened his garments over theirs by a span, and this returns to arrogance.

Seventh: al-Kalbi said: his oppression of them was that he envied Harun for the priesthood (al-Hubburah). It is narrated that when Musa (peace be upon him) crossed the sea and Allah the Exalted drowned Pharaoh, Musa made the priesthood (al-Hubburah) for Harun, so prophethood and the priesthood came to him, and he was the one in charge of the offering and the altar, while the messengership belonged to Musa. Qarun found this in his soul and said: "O Musa, to you is the messengership, and to Harun the priesthood. I am nothing and I cannot bear this." Musa (peace be upon him) said: "By Allah, I did not do that for Harun, but Allah made it for him." He said: "By Allah, I will never believe you until you bring me a sign by which I may know that Allah made that for Harun." He said: So Musa (peace be upon him) commanded the leaders of the Children of Israel that each man should bring his staff, and they brought them. Musa (peace be upon him) placed them in a tent of his, and that was by the command of Allah the Exalted. He then prayed to his Lord that He show them the evidence of that. They spent the night guarding their staffs, and in the morning the staff of Harun was stirring and bore green leaves, and it was of almond wood. Musa said: "O Qarun, do you not see what Allah has done for Harun!" He said: "By Allah, this is no more wondrous than what you do of sorcery." So Qarun withdrew, and with him many people, while Harun took charge of the priesthood, the altar and the offering. The Children of Israel would bring their gifts to Harun, and he would place them on the altar, and fire would descend from the sky and consume them. Qarun withdrew with his followers, and he had much wealth and a retinue from the Children of Israel. He would not come to Musa (peace be upon him) nor sit with him. Abu Umamah al-Bahili narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Qarun was among the chosen seventy who heard the speech of Allah the Exalted."

As for His saying: ﴿And We had given him of treasures whose keys would indeed weigh down a group of strong men﴾, there are discussions concerning it:

The first discussion: al-Ka'bi said: Do you not say that Allah does not give what is unlawful? How then does Allah attribute Qarun's wealth to Himself by saying "And We had given him"? He answered: there is no proof that it was unlawful; it is possible that earlier kings gathered and hoarded, and Qarun came upon that by way of inheritance, or he obtained it from various sources, and then by earning through profit-sharing (mudaraba) and other means, and all of this is possible.

The second discussion: al-Mafatih (the keys) is the plural of miftah, with a kasra on the mim, which is that by which something is opened. It was said: they are the treasuries, and the analogical singular of it is maftah with a fatha on the mim. It is said: "na'a bihi al-himl" when the load weighed on him until it inclined him. Al-'Usbah is the large group, and al-'Usabah is like it. Ten is an 'usbah, by the evidence of the saying of Allah the Exalted concerning the brothers of Yusuf (peace be upon him): ﴿while we are a group (usbah)﴾ (Yusuf: 8), and they were ten, because Yusuf and his brother were not with them.

Once you know the meanings of the words, we say: here there are two views:

One: that what is meant by al-mafatih is the keys, with which doors are opened. They said: his keys were made of camel hide, and each key was like a finger, and for each storeroom there was a key. When Qarun rode, the keys were loaded upon sixty mules.

page 14
Some people have criticized this view on two grounds:

The first: the wealth of one man does not reach this amount. Even if we assume a town filled with gold and jewels, a few keys would suffice for it, so what need is there for so many keys?

The second: treasures are wealth stored in the earth, so it is not permissible that they have keys. The answer to the first: if the wealth is of the kind of goods ( 'urud) and not of the kind of coinage, it is possible for it to reach such abundance. Also, what is said, that those keys reached sixty loads, is not mentioned in the Qur'an, so this narration is not accepted. The tafsir of the Qur'an is that those keys were numerous, and each one was specific to something else, so that it would be burdensome for the group to keep and know them because of their number; on this view the improbability disappears. The answer to the second: although the ordinary sense of "treasure" is what they said, it may apply to gathered wealth in places that have locks.

The second view, which is the choice of Ibn 'Abbas and al-Hasan, is that the keys are to be taken as the wealth itself, and this is clearer and further from doubt. Ibn 'Abbas said: his treasuries were carried by forty strong men, and his treasuries were four hundred thousand, so each man carried ten thousand.

The third view, which is the choice of Abu Muslim: what is meant by the keys is knowledge and comprehension, as in His saying: ﴿and with Him are the keys of the unseen﴾ (al-An'am: 59). The meaning is: We gave him of treasures whose guarding and oversight would indeed weigh heavily upon the group of strong and guided men, that is, these treasures, because of their abundance and variety of kinds, would tire their guardians and those in charge of them who must preserve them. Then Allah the Exalted explained that among his people there was one who admonished him with several matters.

The first of them: His saying: ﴿Do not exult. Indeed, Allah does not love the exultant﴾. What is meant is that there should not befall him, from insolence and clinging to the world, anything that diverts him from the matter of the Hereafter at all. Some of them said: one does not exult in the world except one who is content with it and at rest in it; as for one who knows that he will leave the world soon, he does not exult in it. How excellent is what al-Mutanabbi said:

"The greatest grief to me is in a joy whose possessor is certain he will depart from it."

Even more excellent and concise than this is what Allah said: ﴿so that you do not despair over what has escaped you, nor exult over what He has given you﴾ (al-Hadid: 23). Ibn 'Abbas said: his exultation in that was shirk, for he did not fear, along with it, the punishment of Allah the Exalted.

The second: His saying: ﴿But seek, through that which Allah has given you, the Hereafter﴾. The apparent meaning is that he was acknowledging the Hereafter, and what is meant is that he should direct the wealth toward what leads him to Paradise, and follow the path of humility.

The third: His saying: ﴿and do not forget your share of the world﴾, and in it there are views:

First: perhaps he was absorbed in seeking the world, so for that reason he did not make time for enjoyment and pleasure, and the admonisher forbade him from that.

Second: when the admonisher commanded him to spend his wealth on the Hereafter, he explained to him through this statement that there is no harm in enjoying permissible things.

Third: what is meant by it is spending in obedience to Allah, for that is a person's share of the world, not what he eats and drinks. He (peace be upon him) said: "Let the servant take from himself for himself, and from his worldly life for his Hereafter, and from youth before old age, and from life before death. By Him in whose hand is the soul of Muhammad, there is no return to repentance after death, nor after the world is there any abode except Paradise or Hellfire."

The fourth: His saying: ﴿And do good as Allah has done good to you﴾. Since He commanded him to do good with wealth, He commanded him to do good in general, and it includes assistance with wealth and status, cheerfulness of face, good meeting, and good remembrance. He said: ﴿as Allah has done good to you﴾ as an alert to His saying: ﴿If you are grateful, I will surely increase you﴾ (Ibrahim: 7).

The fifth: His saying: ﴿and seek not corruption in the land﴾. What is meant is the injustice and oppression he was upon. It was said: this speaker was Musa (peace be upon him); others said: rather, it was the believers of his people. However it was, this admonition gathered what, had he accepted it, nothing more would have been required of him. But he refused to accept it, and instead added to it the denial of blessing, so he said: ﴿I was only given it on knowledge I have﴾. In this there are several views:

First: Qatadah, Muqatil and al-Kalbi said: Qarun was the most learned of the Children of Israel in the Torah, and he said: I was only given it for the excellence of my knowledge and my deserving of it.

Second: Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib and al-Dahhak said: Musa (peace be upon him) had been sent down from heaven the knowledge of alchemy, and he taught Qarun a third of the knowledge, Yusha' a third, and Kalib a third. Qarun deceived the other two until he added their knowledge to his own, and he would take lead and make it silver, and copper and make it gold.

Third: he meant by it his knowledge of the ways of gain and trade.

Fourth: his saying: ﴿I was only given it on knowledge I have﴾ may mean: Allah gave me that while He knows me and my circumstances; had it not been a benefit, He would not have done it. And his saying: ﴿on knowledge I have﴾ means: in my view the matter is so, as a jurist says, "in my view the matter is thus," that is, my opinion and belief is that. Then Allah the Exalted answered his statement with His saying: ﴿Did he not know that Allah had destroyed before him of generations those who were greater than him in strength and more abundant in accumulation?﴾ In this there are two views:

The first: this may be an affirmation of his knowledge that Allah the Exalted had destroyed before him of generations those who were stronger than him and wealthier; for he had read of it in the Torah, Musa (peace be upon him) had informed him of it, and he had heard it from the keepers of histories. It is as if it were said to him: did he not know, among what he had of knowledge, this, so that he would not be deceived by the abundance of his wealth and his strength?

The second: this may be a negation of his knowledge of that, as if, when he said "I was only given it on knowledge I have," he boasted of knowledge and magnified himself by it, it was said: does he possess the like of that knowledge which he claimed, and did he see himself deserving of every blessing because of it, and did he not know this beneficial knowledge by which he could protect himself from the fate of the ruined?

As for His saying: ﴿and more abundant in accumulation﴾, the meaning is more abundant in accumulation of wealth, or more abundant in company and number. The conclusion of the answer is that his being deceived by his wealth, his strength and his gatherings is a great error, and that if Allah wills to destroy him, that will not benefit him, nor anything that multiplies it many times over.

Regarding His saying, ﴿And the criminals will not be asked about their sins﴾, the meaning is that when God Most High punishes the criminals, there is no need for Him to ask them about the manner and quantity of their sins, because He, Most High, knows all that is known, so He has no need to ask. If it is said: how is this reconciled with His saying, ﴿So by your Lord, We will surely question them all﴾ (al-Hijr: 92)? We say: that is to be understood as applying to two different times, as we have established. Abu Muslim mentioned another explanation, saying: questioning may be for reckoning, may be for reproach and rebuke, and may be for seeking to make amends (isti'tab). The most fitting interpretation for this verse is the seeking of amends, because of His saying: ﴿Then they will not be given leave, nor will they be asked to make amends﴾ (al-Nahl: 84), and ﴿This is a day when they will not speak﴾, and ﴿Nor will they be given leave so that they may make excuses﴾ (al-Mursalat: 35).

Some people have criticized this view on two grounds:

The first: the wealth of one man does not reach this amount. Even if we assume a town filled with gold and jewels, a few keys would suffice for it, so what need is there for so many keys?

The second: treasures are wealth stored in the earth, so it is not permissible that they have keys. The answer to the first: if the wealth is of the kind of goods ( 'urud) and not of the kind of coinage, it is possible for it to reach such abundance. Also, what is said, that those keys reached sixty loads, is not mentioned in the Qur'an, so this narration is not accepted. The tafsir of the Qur'an is that those keys were numerous, and each one was specific to something else, so that it would be burdensome for the group to keep and know them because of their number; on this view the improbability disappears. The answer to the second: although the ordinary sense of "treasure" is what they said, it may apply to gathered wealth in places that have locks.

The second view, which is the choice of Ibn 'Abbas and al-Hasan, is that the keys are to be taken as the wealth itself, and this is clearer and further from doubt. Ibn 'Abbas said: his treasuries were carried by forty strong men, and his treasuries were four hundred thousand, so each man carried ten thousand.

The third view, which is the choice of Abu Muslim: what is meant by the keys is knowledge and comprehension, as in His saying: ﴿and with Him are the keys of the unseen﴾ (al-An'am: 59). The meaning is: We gave him of treasures whose guarding and oversight would indeed weigh heavily upon the group of strong and guided men, that is, these treasures, because of their abundance and variety of kinds, would tire their guardians and those in charge of them who must preserve them. Then Allah the Exalted explained that among his people there was one who admonished him with several matters.

The first of them: His saying: ﴿Do not exult. Indeed, Allah does not love the exultant﴾. What is meant is that there should not befall him, from insolence and clinging to the world, anything that diverts him from the matter of the Hereafter at all. Some of them said: one does not exult in the world except one who is content with it and at rest in it; as for one who knows that he will leave the world soon, he does not exult in it. How excellent is what al-Mutanabbi said:

"The greatest grief to me is in a joy whose possessor is certain he will depart from it."

Even more excellent and concise than this is what Allah said: ﴿so that you do not despair over what has escaped you, nor exult over what He has given you﴾ (al-Hadid: 23). Ibn 'Abbas said: his exultation in that was shirk, for he did not fear, along with it, the punishment of Allah the Exalted.

The second: His saying: ﴿But seek, through that which Allah has given you, the Hereafter﴾. The apparent meaning is that he was acknowledging the Hereafter, and what is meant is that he should direct the wealth toward what leads him to Paradise, and follow the path of humility.

The third: His saying: ﴿and do not forget your share of the world﴾, and in it there are views:

First: perhaps he was absorbed in seeking the world, so for that reason he did not make time for enjoyment and pleasure, and the admonisher forbade him from that.

Second: when the admonisher commanded him to spend his wealth on the Hereafter, he explained to him through this statement that there is no harm in enjoying permissible things.

Third: what is meant by it is spending in obedience to Allah, for that is a person's share of the world, not what he eats and drinks. He (peace be upon him) said: "Let the servant take from himself for himself, and from his worldly life for his Hereafter, and from youth before old age, and from life before death. By Him in whose hand is the soul of Muhammad, there is no return to repentance after death, nor after the world is there any abode except Paradise or Hellfire."

The fourth: His saying: ﴿And do good as Allah has done good to you﴾. Since He commanded him to do good with wealth, He commanded him to do good in general, and it includes assistance with wealth and status, cheerfulness of face, good meeting, and good remembrance. He said: ﴿as Allah has done good to you﴾ as an alert to His saying: ﴿If you are grateful, I will surely increase you﴾ (Ibrahim: 7).

The fifth: His saying: ﴿and seek not corruption in the land﴾. What is meant is the injustice and oppression he was upon. It was said: this speaker was Musa (peace be upon him); others said: rather, it was the believers of his people. However it was, this admonition gathered what, had he accepted it, nothing more would have been required of him. But he refused to accept it, and instead added to it the denial of blessing, so he said: ﴿I was only given it on knowledge I have﴾. In this there are several views:

First: Qatadah, Muqatil and al-Kalbi said: Qarun was the most learned of the Children of Israel in the Torah, and he said: I was only given it for the excellence of my knowledge and my deserving of it.

Second: Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib and al-Dahhak said: Musa (peace be upon him) had been sent down from heaven the knowledge of alchemy, and he taught Qarun a third of the knowledge, Yusha' a third, and Kalib a third. Qarun deceived the other two until he added their knowledge to his own, and he would take lead and make it silver, and copper and make it gold.

Third: he meant by it his knowledge of the ways of gain and trade.

Fourth: his saying: ﴿I was only given it on knowledge I have﴾ may mean: Allah gave me that while He knows me and my circumstances; had it not been a benefit, He would not have done it. And his saying: ﴿on knowledge I have﴾ means: in my view the matter is so, as a jurist says, "in my view the matter is thus," that is, my opinion and belief is that. Then Allah the Exalted answered his statement with His saying: ﴿Did he not know that Allah had destroyed before him of generations those who were greater than him in strength and more abundant in accumulation?﴾ In this there are two views:

The first: this may be an affirmation of his knowledge that Allah the Exalted had destroyed before him of generations those who were stronger than him and wealthier; for he had read of it in the Torah, Musa (peace be upon him) had informed him of it, and he had heard it from the keepers of histories. It is as if it were said to him: did he not know, among what he had of knowledge, this, so that he would not be deceived by the abundance of his wealth and his strength?

As for His saying: ﴿and more abundant in accumulation﴾, the meaning is more abundant in accumulation of wealth, or more abundant in company and number. The conclusion of the answer is that his being deceived by his wealth, his strength and his gatherings is a great error, and that if Allah wills to destroy him, that will not benefit him, nor anything that multiplies it many times over.

Regarding His saying, ﴿And the criminals will not be asked about their sins﴾, the meaning is that when God Most High punishes the criminals, there is no need for Him to ask them about the manner and quantity of their sins, because He, Most High, knows all that is known, so He has no need to ask. If it is said: how is this reconciled with His saying, ﴿So by your Lord, We will surely question them all﴾ (al-Hijr: 92)? We say: that is to be understood as applying to two different times, as we have established. Abu Muslim mentioned another explanation, saying: questioning may be for reckoning, may be for reproach and rebuke, and may be for seeking to make amends (isti'tab). The most fitting interpretation for this verse is the seeking of amends, because of His saying: ﴿Then they will not be given leave, nor will they be asked to make amends﴾ (al-Nahl: 84), and ﴿This is a day when they will not speak﴾, and ﴿Nor will they be given leave so that they may make excuses﴾ (al-Mursalat: 35).

The Exalted's saying: ﴿So he went out before his people in his finery. Those who desired the life of this world said, "Would that we had the like of what Qarun has been given! Indeed, he is truly possessed of a great fortune." And those who had been given knowledge said, "Woe to you! The reward of Allah is better for one who believes and does righteous deeds, and none receives it except the patient."﴾ ﴿So We caused the earth to swallow him and his home. He had no company to help him against Allah, nor was he among those who could defend themselves.﴾

As for His saying, ﴿So he went out before his people in his finery﴾, it indicates that he went out in the most conspicuous and most complete of adornments. The Qur'an mentions nothing beyond this, but people have offered various descriptions of the manner of that finery. Muqatil said: he went out on a white mule with a saddle of gold, accompanied by four thousand horsemen on horses, wearing purple garments, and with him three hundred fair-skinned slave girls adorned with jewelry and wearing red garments, riding white mules. Others said: rather, he went out with ninety thousand, in this manner. And others said: rather, with three hundred.

The better course is to leave these reports aside, because they contradict one another. Then, when the people saw that finery upon him, those among them who were inclined to the world said: ﴿Would that we had the like of what Qarun has been given﴾ of these things and wealth. Those who desired it may have been among the disbelievers, or among the Muslims who love the world. As for the scholars and the people of religion, they said to those who wished for this: ﴿Woe to you! The reward of Allah is better﴾ than these blessings, because the reward has great benefits that are pure, free from the blemishes of harm, and lasting, whereas these immediate blessings are the opposite of these three qualities. The author of al-Kashshaf said: "Woe to you" (waylaka) originally is a supplication for destruction, then it came to be used for rebuke, deterrence, and urging to abandon what is not approved.

As for His saying, ﴿and none receives it except the patient﴾, the exegetes said: none is granted success in it. The pronoun in ﴿yulaqqaha﴾ (receives it) refers to what? There are two views on this:

One: it refers to what is indicated by His saying ﴿believes and does righteous deeds﴾, meaning: none is given these deeds except the patient.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 28, verses 82–83:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And those who had wished to be in his place the day before began to say, "Ah, it is as if Allah extends provision to whom He wills of His servants and restricts it. Had Allah not been gracious to us, He would have caused the earth to swallow us. Ah, it is as if the disbelievers will not succeed."﴾ ﴿That is the Hereafter abode; We grant it to those who do not desire haughtiness upon the earth or corruption, and the [best] outcome is for the righteous.﴾

Know that the people who had witnessed Qarun in his adornment, when they witnessed what befell him of the sinking into the earth, that became a deterrent for them from love of this world and from opposing Musa, peace be upon him, and a call to be content with Allah's decree and apportionment, and to display obedience and submission to the prophets and messengers of Allah.

As for His saying, ﴿Ah, it is as if Allah﴾, know that "ويْ" (way) is a word separated from "كَأنَّ" (ka'anna), and it is a word used upon becoming alert to an error and expressing regret. When they had said, ﴿Would that we had the like of what Qarun was given﴾, and then witnessed the sinking, they became alert to their error and said, "ويْ," then said, "It is as if Allah extends provision to whom He wills of His servants according to His will and wisdom, not because of his honor with Him, and restricts it for whom He wills, not because of the humiliation of the one He restricts, but rather for His wisdom and decree, as a trial and a test."

Sibawayh said: I asked al-Khalil about this particle, and he said: "ويْ" is separated from "كَأنَّ," and the people became alert and said, regretful of what had passed from them, "ويْ."

Al-Farra' mentioned two aspects:

The first: the meaning is "ويْلَكَ" (waylaka), so he dropped the lam, and such omission is permissible because of its frequency in speech, and he made "أنَّ" (anna) open by a hidden verb, as if he said: "Woe to you, know that Allah..." This is the view of Qutrub, which he related from Yunus.

The second: "ويْ" is separated from "كَأنَّ," and it is for wonder. A man says to another, "Wai, do you not see what is before you?" Then Allah said, "ويْ," then resumed, "It is as if Allah extends..." So Allah mentioned it only to make His creation marvel. Al-Wahidi said: this is a sound view, except that the Arabs did not write it separated, and if it were as they claimed, they would have written it separated.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 28, verses 84–88 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Whoever brings a good deed, for him there is better than it; and whoever brings an evil deed, those who did evil deeds will not be recompensed except according to what they used to do.﴾ ﴿Indeed, He who has imposed upon you the Qur'an will surely bring you back to a place of return. Say, "My Lord knows best who has come with guidance and who is in manifest error."﴾ ﴿And you did not expect that the Book would be bestowed upon you, but it was a mercy from your Lord, so never be a supporter of the disbelievers.﴾ ﴿And let them not avert you from the verses of Allah after they have been revealed to you. And invite to your Lord, and never be among the polytheists.﴾ ﴿And do not invoke with Allah another god. There is no deity except Him. Everything is perishing except His Face. To Him belongs the judgment, and to Him you will be returned.﴾

Know that when Allah, exalted is He, explained that the Final Abode is not for those who desire elevation in the earth or corruption, but rather it is for the God-conscious (al-muttaqun), He then explained what they will attain, saying: ﴿Whoever brings a good deed, for him there is better than it﴾, and in this there are several interpretations.

The first: the meaning is that whoever brings a good deed, he obtains from that word something better.

The second: he obtains something better than that good deed; its meaning is that they will be given increase upon their reward. Its explanation has already passed at the end of al-Naml. As for His saying: ﴿and whoever brings an evil deed, those who did evil deeds will not be recompensed except according to what they used to do﴾, its apparent meaning is that they will not be given increase beyond what they deserve.

If that is valid regarding evil deeds, it indicates that what is meant regarding good deeds by "better than it" is the abundant bounty over the reward that we have mentioned. The author of al-Kashshaf said: the structure of the verse is: "and whoever brings an evil deed, they will not be recompensed except according to what they used to do," but He repeated it, because attributing the doing of evil deeds to them repeatedly carries the sense of disparaging their condition and increasing the hatefulness of evil deeds in the hearts of the listeners. And from His great bounty is that He does not recompense an evil deed except with its like, and recompenses a good deed with ten times its like. Here there are two questions:

Then He said: ﴿Everything is perishing except His Face﴾, and in this there are issues:

First issue: They differed regarding His saying: ﴿Everything is perishing﴾. Among people, some explained "perishing" as non-existence, meaning that Allah, exalted is He, annihilates everything other than Him. Among them, some explained perishing as removing a thing from being beneficial, either by causing it to die or by dispersing its parts, even if its parts remain, for it is said "the garment perished" and "the goods perished," and they do not mean by it the annihilation of its parts, but its removal from being beneficial. Among them, some said: the meaning of its being perishing is its being capable of perishing in its essence, for everything other than Him is possible in existence by its essence, and whatever is possible in existence is capable of non-existence, so it is capable of perishing; so the name perishing is applied to it considering this aspect.

Know that when the theologians wished to establish the proof that everything other than Allah, exalted is He, accepts non-existence and perishing, they said: it is established that the world is originated, and whatever is originated, its reality is capable of existence and non-existence, and whatever is like that must remain in this state forever, because possibility is a necessary property of quiddity, and the necessary property of quiddity never ceases. However, when we examined this proof, we did not find it adequate for this purpose; for they only established the proof for the origination of bodies and accidents. If they were able to establish the proof that whatever is other than Allah, exalted is He, is either a spatially located entity or subsisting in a spatially located entity, their aim would have been achieved. But the opponent affirms existents that are neither spatially located nor subsisting in what is spatially located. So the proof that demonstrates the origination of the spatially located and what subsists in the spatially located does not demonstrate the origination of everything other than Allah, exalted is He, except after establishing the proof negating that third category. For them, in negating this third category, there are two methods:

One: their saying, "there is no proof for it, so it must be negated." This is a feeble method, whose invalidity we have explained in the theological books.

The second: their saying, "If such an existent were found, it would share with Allah, exalted is He, in negating place, time, and possibility; and if that were so, it would become a like of Allah, exalted is He," and this is weak; because it may be said: although they share in this negation, each of them is distinguished from the other by a quiddity and reality. Given this, it is clear that their rational proof does not suffice to establish that everything perishes except His Face. What is relied upon in this matter is that we say: it is established that the Creator of the world is necessarily existent in His essence, so the existence of another existent necessary in its essence is impossible; otherwise both would share in necessity and each would be distinguished from the other by its particularity, and what makes them share is other than what makes them distinct, so each of them would be composed of what makes them share and what makes them distinct; and every composite is possible and needs its parts. Then, if both parts were necessary, they would share in necessity and be distinguished by another aspect, so each of them would also be composite, and this entails infinite regress, which is impossible. And if they were not both necessary, then what is composed of them and needs them is even more deserving of not being necessary. Thus it is established that the necessary existent is one, and that everything other than Him is possible; and every possible thing must have a determinant, and its need for a determinant is either in the state of its non-existence or in the state of its existence. If it is the first

It has been established that it (the contingent existent) is originated (muhdath). If it is the second case, then the existent's need for an effecting agent (mu'aththir) is either at the moment of its origination or at the moment of its continuance. The second is false, because it would necessitate the bringing into existence of something already existent, and that is impossible. Thus it is established that the need arises only at the moment of origination. It is also established that everything other than God Most High is originated, whether it is a spatial entity (mutahayyiz), or subsists in a spatial entity, or is neither a spatial entity nor subsists in one.

If you object to this proof by pointing to the essence of God and His attributes, know that there is a strong difference. Once it is established that everything other than Him is originated, and that everything originated is capable of non-existence, this compelling proof establishes that everything is perishing except His Face, meaning that it is capable of perishing and non-existence.

Then, those who interpreted the verse in this way said: this is preferable, because He, glorified is He, has judged them to be perishing at present. According to our view, they are perishing at present. According to what you say, that they will perish, not that they are perishing at present, our statement is preferable.

Furthermore, the possible (mumkin), when it exists, considered in itself, is not entitled either to existence or to non-existence by its own essence. This entitlement is what is due to it from its essence. As for existence, it comes to it from outside. So existence is for it like a borrowed garment. And considered in itself, it is like the poor man who borrowed a garment from a wealthy man: the poor man does not, by this means, cease to be poor. Likewise, the possibles are devoid of existence considered in themselves, and existence is only a garment that they acquired by loan. Therefore it is correct that they are always perishing considered in themselves.

As for those who understood it to mean that they will be annihilated, they argued by saying: "Perishing (al-halak) in the language has two meanings:

First: the thing's going out of being benefited by.

Second: passing away and non-existence."

It is not permissible to take the word in the first sense, because their perishing in the sense of going out of the limit of benefit is impossible; for even if their parts are dispersed, they are still beneficial, because the intended benefit is that they are such that one can infer from them the existence of the eternal Creator. This benefit remains, whether they remain dispersed or assembled, and whether they remain existent or become non-existent. When it is impossible to take perishing in this sense, it is necessary to take it in the sense of passing away.

Those who took perishing to mean dispersal responded: the perishing of a thing is its going out of the benefit for which the thing is desired. So when a human dies, it is said he has perished, because the desired attribute of him is his life and his intellect. And when a garment is torn, it is said to have perished, because its purpose is its suitability for wear. Thus when the parts of the world are dispersed, the heavens, the stars, the mountains, and the seas go out of their attributes for which they were beneficial in a particular way. Therefore it is rightly said of them that they have perished. As for the correctness of inferring the Creator, glorified is He, from them, this benefit is not a benefit specific to the sun as sun, or to the moon as moon. So their remaining does not necessitate that the name "perished" not be applied to them.

Then they argued for the remaining of the parts of the world by His saying: ﴿On the day the earth will be changed to other than the earth﴾ (Ibrahim: 48). This is explicit that those parts remain, except that they have become characterized by another attribute. This is what is said on this point.

**Second issue:** The People of Tawhid (Ahl al-Tawhid, those who affirm the absolute oneness of God) argued from this verse that God Most High is a thing (shay'). They said: because He made an exception from His saying ﴿everything﴾, an exception which removes what, were it not for it, would necessarily or validly be included under the word. Therefore He is a thing. This is reinforced by what we mentioned in Surah al-An'am, namely His saying: ﴿Say: "What thing is greatest in testimony?" Say: "God"﴾ (al-An'am: 19).

As for their argument that He is not a thing, based on His saying: ﴿There is nothing like Him﴾ (al-Shura: 11), with the kaf meaning "like", the sense of the verse would be: "There is nothing like the like of Him." And the like of the like of God is God. Therefore God must not be a thing. The answer: the kaf is an extra (zā'idah) particle.

**Third issue:** The Anthropomorphists (al-Mujassimah) used this verse to argue that God Most High is a body (jism), on two grounds.

First: they said: the verse is explicit in affirming the Face, and that entails corporeality.

Second: His saying ﴿and to Him you will be returned﴾. The word "ila" ("to") is for the end of a limit, and that is not conceivable except in bodies.

The answer: if this statement were valid, it would necessitate that all His limbs perish and that nothing remain of Him except the Face. Some of the Anthropomorphists among the Rafidah (Rafidites) have indeed committed to this, namely Bayan ibn Sam'an, and no rational person would say this. Then, among people, there is one who said: "the Face" means the existence and the reality, as one says: "the face of this matter is such-and-such," meaning its reality. And among them is one who said: "the Face" is a filler (silah), and the meaning is "everything perishes except He." As for "ila" ("to"), the meaning is: "to the place of His judgment and decree you will be returned."

**Fourth issue:** The Mu'tazilah used this verse to argue that Paradise and Hell are not created. They said: because the verse requires the annihilation of everything, if the two were created they would perish. This contradicts His saying, in describing Paradise: ﴿its food is eternal﴾ (al-Ra'd: 35).

The answer: this is countered by His saying, in describing Paradise: ﴿prepared for the God-fearing﴾ (Al 'Imran: 133), and in describing Hell: ﴿its fuel is people and stones; it is prepared for the disbelievers﴾ (al-Baqarah: 24). Then either His saying ﴿everything is perishing﴾ is understood as referring to the majority, as in His saying: ﴿and she has been given of everything﴾ (al-Naml: 23), or His saying ﴿its food is eternal﴾ is understood as meaning that since the time of their passing away is short relative to the time of their remaining, the word "eternity" (dawam) is applied to it.

**Fifth issue:** His saying ﴿everything is perishing﴾ indicates that the essence is an actual essence (dhat bi'l-fi'l), because He passed the judgment of perishing upon the thing, which indicates that the thing, in its being a thing, is capable of perishing. Therefore the non-existent must not be a thing. And God knows best. Praise be to God, Lord of the worlds.

Then, those who interpreted the verse in this way said: this is preferable, because He, glorified is He, has judged them to be perishing at present. According to our view, they are perishing at present. According to what you say, that they will perish, not that they are perishing at present, our statement is preferable.

Furthermore, the possible (mumkin), when it exists, considered in itself, is not entitled either to existence or to non-existence by its own essence. This entitlement is what is due to it from its essence. As for existence, it comes to it from outside. So existence is for it like a borrowed garment. And considered in itself, it is like the poor man who borrowed a garment from a wealthy man: the poor man does not, by this means, cease to be poor. Likewise, the possibles are devoid of existence considered in themselves, and existence is only a garment that they acquired by loan. Therefore it is correct that they are always perishing considered in themselves.

As for those who understood it to mean that they will be annihilated, they argued by saying: "Perishing (al-halak) in the language has two meanings:

First: the thing's going out of being benefited by.

Second: passing away and non-existence."

It is not permissible to take the word in the first sense, because their perishing in the sense of going out of the limit of benefit is impossible; for even if their parts are dispersed, they are still beneficial, because the intended benefit is that they are such that one can infer from them the existence of the eternal Creator. This benefit remains, whether they remain dispersed or assembled, and whether they remain existent or become non-existent. When it is impossible to take perishing in this sense, it is necessary to take it in the sense of passing away.

Those who took perishing to mean dispersal responded: the perishing of a thing is its going out of the benefit for which the thing is desired. So when a human dies, it is said he has perished, because the desired attribute of him is his life and his intellect. And when a garment is torn, it is said to have perished, because its purpose is its suitability for wear. Thus when the parts of the world are dispersed, the heavens, the stars, the mountains, and the seas go out of their attributes for which they were beneficial in a particular way. Therefore it is rightly said of them that they have perished. As for the correctness of inferring the Creator, glorified is He, from them, this benefit is not a benefit specific to the sun as sun, or to the moon as moon. Then they argued for the remaining of the parts of the world by His saying: ﴿On the day the earth will be changed to other than the earth﴾ (Ibrahim: 48). This is explicit that those parts remain, except that they have become characterized by another attribute. This is what is said on this point.

They said: because He made an exception from His saying ﴿everything﴾, an exception which removes what, were it not for it, would necessarily or validly be included under the word. Therefore He is a thing. This is reinforced by what we mentioned in Surah al-An'am, namely His saying: ﴿Say: "What thing is greatest in testimony?" Say: "God"﴾ (al-An'am: 19).

The answer: if this statement were valid, it would necessitate that all His limbs perish and that nothing remain of Him except the Face. Some of the Anthropomorphists among the Rafidah (Rafidites) have indeed committed to this, namely Bayan ibn Sam'an, and no rational person would say this. Then, among people, there is one who said: "the Face" means the existence and the reality, as one says: "the face of this matter is such-and-such," meaning its reality. As for "ila" ("to"), the meaning is: "to the place of His judgment and decree you will be returned."

The answer: this is countered by His saying, in describing Paradise: ﴿prepared for the God-fearing﴾ (Al 'Imran: 133), and in describing Hell: ﴿its fuel is people and stones; it is prepared for the disbelievers﴾ (al-Baqarah: 24). Then He said: ﴿Everything is perishing except His Face﴾, and in this there are issues:

First issue: They differed regarding His saying: ﴿Everything is perishing﴾. Among people, some explained "perishing" as non-existence, meaning that Allah, exalted is He, annihilates everything other than Him. Among them, some explained perishing as removing a thing from being beneficial, either by causing it to die or by dispersing its parts, even if its parts remain, for it is said "the garment perished" and "the goods perished," and they do not mean by it the annihilation of its parts, but its removal from being beneficial. Among them, some said: the meaning of its being perishing is its being capable of perishing in its essence, for everything other than Him is possible in existence by its essence, and whatever is possible in existence is capable of non-existence, so it is capable of perishing; so the name perishing is applied to it considering this aspect.

Know that when the theologians wished to establish the proof that everything other than Allah, exalted is He, accepts non-existence and perishing, they said: it is established that the world is originated, and whatever is originated, its reality is capable of existence and non-existence, and whatever is like that must remain in this state forever, because possibility is a necessary property of quiddity, and the necessary property of quiddity never ceases. However, when we examined this proof, we did not find it adequate for this purpose; for they only established the proof for the origination of bodies and accidents. If they were able to establish the proof that whatever is other than Allah, exalted is He, is either a spatially located entity or subsisting in a spatially located entity, their aim would have been achieved. But the opponent affirms existents that are neither spatially located nor subsisting in what is spatially located. So the proof that demonstrates the origination of the spatially located and what subsists in the spatially located does not demonstrate the origination of everything other than Allah, exalted is He, except after establishing the proof negating that third category. For them, in negating this third category, there are two methods:

One: their saying, "there is no proof for it, so it must be negated." This is a feeble method, whose invalidity we have explained in the theological books.

The second: their saying, "If such an existent were found, it would share with Allah, exalted is He, in negating place, time, and possibility; and if that were so, it would become a like of Allah, exalted is He," and this is weak; because it may be said: although they share in this negation, each of them is distinguished from the other by a quiddity and reality. Given this, it is clear that their rational proof does not suffice to establish that everything perishes except His Face. What is relied upon in this matter is that we say: it is established that the Creator of the world is necessarily existent in His essence, so the existence of another existent necessary in its essence is impossible; otherwise both would share in necessity and each would be distinguished from the other by its particularity, and what makes them share is other than what makes them distinct, so each of them would be composed of what makes them share and what makes them distinct; and every composite is possible and needs its parts. Then, if both parts were necessary, they would share in necessity and be distinguished by another aspect, so each of them would also be composite, and this entails infinite regress, which is impossible. And if they were not both necessary, then what is composed of them and needs them is even more deserving of not being necessary. Thus it is established that the necessary existent is one, and that everything other than Him is possible; and every possible thing must have a determinant, and its need for a determinant is either in the state of its non-existence or in the state of its existence. If it is the first

It has been established that it (the contingent existent) is originated (muhdath). If it is the second case, then the existent's need for an effecting agent (mu'aththir) is either at the moment of its origination or at the moment of its continuance. The second is false, because it would necessitate the bringing into existence of something already existent, and that is impossible. Thus it is established that the need arises only at the moment of origination. It is also established that everything other than God Most High is originated, whether it is a spatial entity (mutahayyiz), or subsists in a spatial entity, or is neither a spatial entity nor subsists in one.

If you object to this proof by pointing to the essence of God and His attributes, know that there is a strong difference. Once it is established that everything other than Him is originated, and that everything originated is capable of non-existence, this compelling proof establishes that everything is perishing except His Face, meaning that it is capable of perishing and non-existence.

Then, those who interpreted the verse in this way said: this is preferable, because He, glorified is He, has judged them to be perishing at present. According to our view, they are perishing at present. According to what you say, that they will perish, not that they are perishing at present, our statement is preferable.

Furthermore, the possible (mumkin), when it exists, considered in itself, is not entitled either to existence or to non-existence by its own essence. This entitlement is what is due to it from its essence. As for existence, it comes to it from outside. So existence is for it like a borrowed garment. And considered in itself, it is like the poor man who borrowed a garment from a wealthy man: the poor man does not, by this means, cease to be poor. Likewise, the possibles are devoid of existence considered in themselves, and existence is only a garment that they acquired by loan. Therefore it is correct that they are always perishing considered in themselves.

As for those who understood it to mean that they will be annihilated, they argued by saying: "Perishing (al-halak) in the language has two meanings:

First: the thing's going out of being benefited by.

Second: passing away and non-existence."

It is not permissible to take the word in the first sense, because their perishing in the sense of going out of the limit of benefit is impossible; for even if their parts are dispersed, they are still beneficial, because the intended benefit is that they are such that one can infer from them the existence of the eternal Creator. This benefit remains, whether they remain dispersed or assembled, and whether they remain existent or become non-existent. When it is impossible to take perishing in this sense, it is necessary to take it in the sense of passing away.

Those who took perishing to mean dispersal responded: the perishing of a thing is its going out of the benefit for which the thing is desired. So when a human dies, it is said he has perished, because the desired attribute of him is his life and his intellect. And when a garment is torn, it is said to have perished, because its purpose is its suitability for wear. Thus when the parts of the world are dispersed, the heavens, the stars, the mountains, and the seas go out of their attributes for which they were beneficial in a particular way. Therefore it is rightly said of them that they have perished. As for the correctness of inferring the Creator, glorified is He, from them, this benefit is not a benefit specific to the sun as sun, or to the moon as moon. So their remaining does not necessitate that the name "perished" not be applied to them.

Then they argued for the remaining of the parts of the world by His saying: ﴿On the day the earth will be changed to other than the earth﴾ (Ibrahim: 48). This is explicit that those parts remain, except that they have become characterized by another attribute. This is what is said on this point.

**Second issue:** The People of Tawhid (Ahl al-Tawhid, those who affirm the absolute oneness of God) argued from this verse that God Most High is a thing (shay'). They said: because He made an exception from His saying ﴿everything﴾, an exception which removes what, were it not for it, would necessarily or validly be included under the word. Therefore He is a thing. This is reinforced by what we mentioned in Surah al-An'am, namely His saying: ﴿Say: "What thing is greatest in testimony?" Say: "God"﴾ (al-An'am: 19).

As for their argument that He is not a thing, based on His saying: ﴿There is nothing like Him﴾ (al-Shura: 11), with the kaf meaning "like", the sense of the verse would be: "There is nothing like the like of Him." And the like of the like of God is God. Therefore God must not be a thing. The answer: the kaf is an extra (zā'idah) particle.

**Third issue:** The Anthropomorphists (al-Mujassimah) used this verse to argue that God Most High is a body (jism), on two grounds.

First: they said: the verse is explicit in affirming the Face, and that entails corporeality.

Second: His saying ﴿and to Him you will be returned﴾. The word "ila" ("to") is for the end of a limit, and that is not conceivable except in bodies.

The answer: if this statement were valid, it would necessitate that all His limbs perish and that nothing remain of Him except the Face. Some of the Anthropomorphists among the Rafidah (Rafidites) have indeed committed to this, namely Bayan ibn Sam'an, and no rational person would say this. Then, among people, there is one who said: "the Face" means the existence and the reality, as one says: "the face of this matter is such-and-such," meaning its reality. And among them is one who said: "the Face" is a filler (silah), and the meaning is "everything perishes except He." As for "ila" ("to"), the meaning is: "to the place of His judgment and decree you will be returned."

**Fourth issue:** The Mu'tazilah used this verse to argue that Paradise and Hell are not created. They said: because the verse requires the annihilation of everything, if the two were created they would perish. This contradicts His saying, in describing Paradise: ﴿its food is eternal﴾ (al-Ra'd: 35).

The answer: this is countered by His saying, in describing Paradise: ﴿prepared for the God-fearing﴾ (Al 'Imran: 133), and in describing Hell: ﴿its fuel is people and stones; it is prepared for the disbelievers﴾ (al-Baqarah: 24). Then either His saying ﴿everything is perishing﴾ is understood as referring to the majority, as in His saying: ﴿and she has been given of everything﴾ (al-Naml: 23), or His saying ﴿its food is eternal﴾ is understood as meaning that since the time of their passing away is short relative to the time of their remaining, the word "eternity" (dawam) is applied to it.

**Fifth issue:** His saying ﴿everything is perishing﴾ indicates that the essence is an actual essence (dhat bi'l-fi'l), because He passed the judgment of perishing upon the thing, which indicates that the thing, in its being a thing, is capable of perishing. Therefore the non-existent must not be a thing. And God knows best. Praise be to God, Lord of the worlds.

As for the correctness of inferring the Creator, glorified is He, from them, this benefit is not a benefit specific to the sun as sun, or to the moon as moon. So their remaining does not necessitate that the name "perished" not be applied to them.

Then they argued for the remaining of the parts of the world by His saying: ﴿On the day the earth will be changed to other than the earth﴾ (Ibrahim: 48). This is explicit that those parts remain, except that they have become characterized by another attribute. This is what is said on this point.

**Second issue:** The People of Tawhid (Ahl al-Tawhid, those who affirm the absolute oneness of God) argued from this verse that God Most High is a thing (shay'). They said: because He made an exception from His saying ﴿everything﴾, an exception which removes what, were it not for it, would necessarily or validly be included under the word. Therefore He is a thing. This is reinforced by what we mentioned in Surah al-An'am, namely His saying: ﴿Say: "What thing is greatest in testimony?" Say: "God"﴾ (al-An'am: 19).

As for their argument that He is not a thing, based on His saying: ﴿There is nothing like Him﴾ (al-Shura: 11), with the kaf meaning "like", the sense of the verse would be: "There is nothing like the like of Him." And the like of the like of God is God. Therefore God must not be a thing. The answer: the kaf is an extra (zā'idah) particle.

**Third issue:** The Anthropomorphists (al-Mujassimah) used this verse to argue that God Most High is a body (jism), on two grounds.

First: they said: the verse is explicit in affirming the Face, and that entails corporeality.

Second: His saying ﴿and to Him you will be returned﴾. The word "ila" ("to") is for the end of a limit, and that is not conceivable except in bodies.

The answer: if this statement were valid, it would necessitate that all His limbs perish and that nothing remain of Him except the Face. Some of the Anthropomorphists among the Rafidah (Rafidites) have indeed committed to this, namely Bayan ibn Sam'an, and no rational person would say this. Then, among people, there is one who said: "the Face" means the existence and the reality, as one says: "the face of this matter is such-and-such," meaning its reality. And among them is one who said: "the Face" is a filler (silah), and the meaning is "everything perishes except He." As for "ila" ("to"), the meaning is: "to the place of His judgment and decree you will be returned."

**Fourth issue:** The Mu'tazilah used this verse to argue that Paradise and Hell are not created. They said: because the verse requires the annihilation of everything, if the two were created they would perish. This contradicts His saying, in describing Paradise: ﴿its food is eternal﴾ (al-Ra'd: 35).

The answer: this is countered by His saying, in describing Paradise: ﴿prepared for the God-fearing﴾ (Al 'Imran: 133), and in describing Hell: ﴿its fuel is people and stones; it is prepared for the disbelievers﴾ (al-Baqarah: 24). Then either His saying ﴿everything is perishing﴾ is understood as referring to the majority, as in His saying: ﴿and she has been given of everything﴾ (al-Naml: 23), or His saying ﴿its food is eternal﴾ is understood as meaning that since the time of their passing away is short relative to the time of their remaining, the word "eternity" (dawam) is applied to it.

**Fifth issue:** His saying ﴿everything is perishing﴾ indicates that the essence is an actual essence (dhat bi'l-fi'l), because He passed the judgment of perishing upon the thing, which indicates that the thing, in its being a thing, is capable of perishing. Therefore the non-existent must not be a thing. And God knows best. Praise be to God, Lord of the worlds.
